time.basis: "perhaps sometime during the sixth or seventh centuries" (formal community naming)

location.label: China (general placeholder — Xi'an/Chang'an; no specific city named for the community's origin)

note: Chan. (J. Zen; K. Sŏn; V. Thiền.) Meditation lineage that crystallizes as a distinct Chinese school by the sixth or seventh century under six patriarchs starting with the legendary Indian monk Bodhidharma — ending in a bitter contest over the sixth patriarchy between Shenxiu's gradualist Northern school and Huineng's subitist Southern school. Splits into five houses, seven schools; spreads to Korea as Sŏn, Japan as Zen, Vietnam as Thiền, and briefly to the Tibetan court, where the monk Moheyan loses the Bsam yas debate.

time.basis: "roughly four centuries after the Buddha's death" (chronology convention), widened per the entry's own hedge that firm epigraphic evidence is five centuries after the first sūtras

location.label: India (general placeholder — Magadha; no specific origin site named)

note: Mahāyāna. ("Great Vehicle.") Movement emerging roughly four centuries after the Buddha's death around new sūtras claiming to be his actual word, each proclaiming its own supremacy through the doctrine of skillful means. Sets the bodhisattva path — not personal arhatship — as the ideal, teaching perfection of wisdom, buddha-nature, and pure lands. Despite becoming the dominant form of Buddhism in China, Korea, Japan, Tibet, and Mongolia, Chinese pilgrims report it remained a minority movement within India itself.

time.basis: term's Mahāyāna sense "already in use... by at least the first century BCE"

note: Bodhisattva. ("Enlightenment being.") In mainstream schools, the term for Śākyamuni himself before his awakening; in Mahāyāna, from at least the first century BCE, anyone who vows to seek buddhahood for the sake of all beings. Trains over three incalculable eons through ten stages and six perfections, motivated by great compassion, opting for it over the faster individual liberation of an arhat. Advanced bodhisattvas — Avalokiteśvara, Mañjuśrī, Vajrapāṇi — become objects of devotion in their own right.

Arhat. ("Worthy one.") The highest of four grades of Buddhist saint in the mainstream schools — one who has severed all ten fetters binding beings to rebirth and will enter nirvāṇa at death. Ranks above the stream-enterer, once-returner, and nonreturner; the Buddha himself is described as an arhat. Mahāyāna texts rank the arhat below the bodhisattva, having overcome only afflictive obstructions, not the subtler obstructions to omniscience — though East Asian monasteries still shrine sixteen named arhats as objects of devotion.

time.basis: "Indian scholastics of the fourth to fifth centuries CE" (Asaṅga and Vasubandhu)

location.label: India (general placeholder — Magadha; entry says "in India" but names no city)

note: Yogācāra. ("Practice of yoga.") One of the two great Mahāyāna philosophical schools of India, alongside Madhyamaka — founded in the fourth to fifth century CE by the half-brothers Asaṅga and Vasubandhu. Teaches that experience is "representation-only": what seems like an external world is produced by a foundational storehouse consciousness carrying the imprints of past action. Liberation reprograms this consciousness into a buddha's mirrorlike wisdom. Widely influential in Tibet and East Asia, shaping Huayan and even Chan.

time.basis: founding coincides with the first sermon, via chronology convention

location.label: Sarnath, India (named directly in the entry)

note: Saṃgha. ("Community.") The order of Buddhist monks and nuns, one of the Three Jewels of refuge — founded at Sarnath with the ordination of the first five monks after the Buddha's first sermon. Formal ordination and the twice-monthly recitation of monastic rules developed as the order grew; a saṃgha proper requires at least ten monks in settled regions, five in remote ones. Narrower senses restrict the term to those who have reached one of eight or twenty levels of spiritual attainment, setting an "ultimate" saṃgha of the awakened apart from the ordinary ordained.

time.basis: Upagupta, whose five disciples produced the five vinaya recensions, was "the fifth successor... about a century following [the Buddha's] death"

location.label: India (general placeholder — Magadha; Upagupta traditionally linked to Mathurā, but that's outside this entry's own text, so flagged as uncertain rather than asserted)

note: Vinaya. ("Discipline.") The corpus of monastic regulations for fully ordained monks and nuns, and the canonical texts that record them — one of the three baskets of the Buddhist canon. Five major recensions descend from disciples of the Buddha's fifth successor Upagupta; only the Pāli version survives complete in an Indian language, while the massive Mūlasarvāstivāda recension — four times longer than the rest — survives complete only in Tibetan. Each rule is traditionally said to have been formulated only after an actual infraction occurred.

Dharma. A term with as many as ten meanings in Buddhist literature, from the Sanskrit root "to hold." Most often it means the Buddha's teaching itself — the second of the Three Jewels, first "turned" at his inaugural sermon. Just as often it means the opposite: not a teaching about reality but reality's own constituent building blocks, the individual "factors" analyzed by abhidharma. A third sense denotes a quality or characteristic, as in dharmakāya, the Buddha's "body" of transcendent qualities.

time.basis: the Buddha's enlightenment, age thirty-five, per this entry; converted via chronology convention

location.label: Bodhgayā, India (named directly in this entry)

note: Nirvāṇa. ("Extinction.") The soteriological goal of the Buddhist path — literally the blowing-out of the flame of craving, hatred, and delusion, and with it the causes of future rebirth. Achieved in life as "nirvāṇa with remainder," while mind and body persist; achieved finally at death as "nirvāṇa without remainder," ending rebirth altogether. Not a place or a state of existence, since either would still belong to saṃsāra — traditions describe it only apophatically, by what it is not. Mahāyāna texts later locate the Buddha in an "unlocated nirvāṇa," neither in saṃsāra nor apart from it.

time.basis: split from Sthaviranikāya "as early as a century or two following the first schism, but certainly no later than the first century CE"

location.label: Kashmir (Srinagar) — named directly in the entry as where the school became dominant

note: Sarvāstivāda. ("Teaching that all exists.") One of the most influential mainstream (non-Mahāyāna) schools of Indian Buddhism, distinguished by the doctrine that all conditioned factors exist across past, present, and future alike. Built an elaborate seventy-five-category abhidharma that shaped both Nāgārjuna's critique of it and Yogācāra's own scholastic system. Split from the Sthaviranikāya by around the first century BCE–CE; became dominant in Kashmir, Gandhāra, and along the Silk Road, making it the mainstream school best known to East Asian Buddhism.

Abhidharma. ("Pertaining to dharma" or "higher dharma.") The genre of technical, impersonal analysis that complements the sūtras' worldly parables — scholars debate whether it grew out of numbered mnemonic lists of doctrine or out of catechistic dialogue clarifying difficult points. Compiled into the Abhidharmapiṭaka, one of the three baskets of the canon alongside sūtra and vinaya. Tradition holds the Buddha first taught it to his deceased mother in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, repeating it daily to Śāriputra, who became its foremost master.

Dhyāna. ("Meditative absorption.") Sanskrit source of the term Chan/Zen — the state in which the mind withdraws from sensory awareness into full concentration on its object. Divides into four stages of subtle-materiality absorption, each shedding a mental factor as concentration deepens, then four further immaterial absorptions named for ever-subtler objects: infinite space, infinite consciousness, nothingness, and neither-perception-nor-nonperception. Builds the concentration needed for insight but doesn't by itself grant it — sustained absorption alone only leads to rebirth as a long-lived divinity.

time.basis: first Buddhist council, shortly after the Buddha's death (chronology convention)

note: Sūtra. ("Aphorism.") A discourse delivered by the Buddha or spoken with his sanction — opening formulaically with "Thus have I heard," certifying the first-person report of his attendant Ānanda. Tradition holds the sūtras were first recited into fixed form by Ānanda at the first Buddhist council, shortly after the Buddha's death. Centuries later, hundreds of new Mahāyāna sūtras began appearing in India claiming the same authority, sparking a genre-wide anxiety about proving they too were the Buddha's actual word.

time.basis: Nāgārjuna, its founder, "c. second century CE" per this entry

location.label: South India (general — per the Nāgārjuna entry, not stated here directly)

note: Madhyamaka. ("Middle Way.") Mahāyāna philosophical school founded on the works of the second-century philosopher Nāgārjuna, charting a middle way between the extremes of eternalism and annihilationism through the doctrine of emptiness — the claim that all phenomena, being dependently arisen, lack any independent, intrinsic nature. Tibetan exegetes later split it into Prāsaṅgika (Buddhapālita, Candrakīrti) and Svātantrika (Bhāvaviveka, Śāntarakṣita) branches; in East Asia its texts founded the "Three Treatises" school. Traditionally ranked in Tibet as the highest of the four Indian philosophical schools.

Saṃsāra. ("Wandering.") The beginningless cycle of birth, death, and rebirth across all realms of existence, propelled by karman and craving — the condition nirvāṇa brings to an end. One of Buddhism's most foundational terms, so ubiquitous elsewhere in the tradition that the dictionary's own entry for it is a single line.

time.basis: "worship dates back at least as far as the early centuries of the Common Era"; first Chinese translation "mid-second century CE"

note: Amitābha. ("Limitless Light.") Buddha of the western pure land Sukhāvatī, among the most widely worshipped buddhas in the Mahāyāna world — attained buddhahood after eons of vows, including the promise that anyone who recalls his name with trust at death will be reborn in his pure land. His Indian origins are genuinely obscure; worship is attested by the mid-second century CE, when his foundational sūtra was first translated into Chinese. Became so pervasive in East Asia that reciting his name — "Homage to Amitābha Buddha" — transcended sectarian lines entirely.

Kleśa. ("Afflictions" or "defilements.") Mental factors — greed, hatred, delusion at the core, expanding into fuller lists depending on the school — that disturb the mind and drive unwholesome action, and that must be eliminated to escape rebirth. Sarvāstivāda counts six "fundamental afflictions" universal to all defiled thought plus ten of "limited extent"; Yogācāra instead names six root kleśas — including the five wrong views — plus twenty derivative ones. The taxonomies differ, but the target is the same: uproot these, and the actions they incite stop generating karman.

time.basis: Madhyamaka's systematized sense, via Nāgārjuna, "second century CE"

note: Śūnyatā. ("Emptiness.") In its early sense, one aspect of suffering — the body's lack of anything worth grasping as "mine." Nāgārjuna and the Madhyamaka school, from the second century CE, radically broadened it: emptiness becomes the absence of intrinsic nature (svabhāva) in every phenomenon whatsoever, equated with dependent origination itself — not nonexistence, but the absence of a falsely imagined kind of existence. Yogācāra later reinterprets it through the three natures; in Tibet, the precise meaning of emptiness became the subject of the rang stong/gzhan stong debate.

Karman. ("Action.") The doctrine that virtuous and nonvirtuous deeds of body, speech, and mind ripen into future happiness or suffering — potentially lifetimes later, but never lost, the way energy is conserved in a physical process. Originally a Vedic term for ritual action, redefined by the Buddha as intention itself: "having intended, one acts through body, speech, and mind." Crucially, the person who experiences a karman's fruit is neither identical to nor entirely different from the person who performed it — a middle position meant to preserve moral cause-and-effect without smuggling back in a permanent self.

Samādhi. ("Concentration.") The capacity to fix and sustain one-pointed attention on a single object — one of five determinative mental factors in Abhidharma psychology, and the final step of the eightfold path. Distinguished from the stability of a merely calm mind by its power to cut through ignorance, samādhi ranges from the preparatory concentration of a session's start through to full absorption (dhyāna). Mahāyāna sūtras describe well over a hundred named samādhis attained by advanced bodhisattvas, each a distinct meditative state.

time.basis: traditional lifespan, corrected long chronology (see buddhavarṣa entry) — not restated in this entry itself

location.label: Lumbini area, Nepal-India border (per this entry: "Śākya clan flourished in the foothills of the Himālayas, near the border between present-day Nepal and India")

note: Śākyamuni. ("Sage of the Śākya clan.") The most common Mahāyāna epithet for the historical Buddha, born Siddhārtha Gautama into the kṣatriya Śākya clan in the Himalayan foothills near today's Nepal-India border. The dictionary treats his biography deliberately non-linearly — the tradition itself didn't attempt a single connected life story until centuries after his death — scattering the birth, renunciation, enlightenment under the Bodhi tree, and forty-five years of teaching across separate entries rather than one continuous narrative.

Karman. ("Ecclesiastical proceeding.") Formal monastic business — ordination, the fortnightly confession ceremony, the robe-giving at the close of the rains retreat, adjudication of rule violations — conducted by motion before the assembled congregation of monks and approved by silent assent. Distinguished in Chinese by using a transcription (jiemo) rather than the translation used for karman-as-action, to keep the two senses of the same Sanskrit word apart. For serious infractions, the vinaya sets out seven distinct proceedings, from simple reprimand up to expulsion from the order.

time.basis: "earliest portions... composed as early as the first or second centuries of the Common Era"

location.label: India (general placeholder — Magadha; no specific composition site named)

note: Saddharmapuṇḍarīkasūtra. ("Sūtra of the White Lotus of the True Dharma" — the Lotus Sūtra.) Among the most influential Mahāyāna sūtras, composed in India from as early as the first or second century CE and later expanded with interpolated chapters. Its parable of the burning house recasts the Buddha's earlier teaching of three separate vehicles as mere skillful expedients — there is truly only one vehicle, leading all beings to buddhahood — while its parable of the dying father reveals the Buddha's apparent death as itself only a display. Became the founding scripture of Tiantai in China and Tendai in Japan, and the sole authoritative text for Nichiren Buddhism.

time.basis: Zhiyi's dates, given directly as "de facto founder"

location.label: Mt. Tiantai, Zhejiang, China (named directly in the entry)

note: Tiantai zong. ("Terrace of Heaven School.") Major Chinese Buddhist school named for its headquarters on Mt. Tiantai in Zhejiang, given its systematic form by Zhiyi (538–597) around the Lotus Sūtra and the doctrine that a single thought-moment perfectly contains the entire cosmos. Zhiyi's "three truths" — emptiness, provisional reality, and the mean — and his claim that even hell-denizens possess buddha-nature became foundational across East Asia. Transmitted to Korea and, as Tendai, to Japan, where Mt. Hiei trained the founders of nearly every major Kamakura-era school before Tendai itself declined.

time.basis: "first transmitted to Japan in the late twelfth century by Myōan Eisai"

location.label: Japan (general placeholder — Tokyo/Kantō; no specific site named)

note: Zen. The Japanese branch of the East Asian Chan tradition, first transmitted from China in the late twelfth century by Myōan Eisai. Three surviving lineages call themselves Zen schools: Rinzai (koan-focused, from Eisai), Sōtō (founded by Dōgen on "just sitting"), and the smaller, later Ōbaku. In the twentieth century, thinkers like D.T. Suzuki recast "Zen" in the West as a culture-transcending "pure experience" — a framing the dictionary notes has little to do with how the tradition understands itself in Japan or elsewhere in East Asia.

time.basis: origin, shortly after the Buddha's death, per this entry's own account

location.label: Kuśinagarī (one of the ten original relic-distribution sites named in this entry)

note: Stūpa. ("Reliquary.") A hemispherical monument enshrining the relics of the Buddha or a saint — begun, per tradition, when the Buddha's own remains were divided into ten portions and enshrined at sites including Kapilavastu, Kuśinagarī, Rājagṛha, and Vaiśālī shortly after his death. Emperor Aśoka reportedly reopened these and redistributed the relics into eighty-four thousand stūpas in the third century BCE. Evolved regionally into the dagoba and pagoda; by the seventh century, Indian stūpas increasingly enshrined not physical relics but tablets stamped with a verse encapsulating the Buddha's teaching on causation.

time.basis: first Chinese translation, by Buddhabhadra, dated directly in the entry

location.label: Khotan (named directly: the sūtra was "brought from Khotan")

note: Avataṃsakasūtra. ("Garland Scripture" — the Huayan jing.) Foundational text of the East Asian Huayan school, first brought to China from Khotan and translated by Buddhabhadra in 421 CE. An encyclopedic compilation of originally independent texts (including the Daśabhūmikasūtra and Gaṇḍavyūha) — no complete Sanskrit version has ever been found, suggesting possible Central Asian origins. Presents the cosmos as Indra's Net, a canopy of jewels each reflecting all the others, and closes with the pilgrim-boy Sudhana's visits to fifty-two spiritual guides.

time.basis: "first texts appearing sometime between the first century BCE and the first century CE"

note: Prajñāpāramitā. ("Perfection of wisdom.") Both the wisdom of buddhahood — understanding that no agent, object, or action is ultimately real — and the genre of sūtras expounding it, among the earliest Mahāyāna scriptures, appearing between the first century BCE and first century CE. Individual sūtras are named simply for their length in verses: eight thousand lines, twenty-five thousand, a hundred thousand. Its central figure is paradoxically gendered female in Sanskrit, giving rise to Prajñāpāramitā as a goddess venerated as the mother of all buddhas.

Pure land. An English umbrella term (no single Sanskrit equivalent) covering at least five related ideas: any buddha-field purified for rebirth; specifically Amitābha's Sukhāvatī; the broader Mahāyāna textual tradition describing such fields; the East Asian and Tibetan practice tradition aimed at rebirth there; and the Jōdoshū/Jōdo Shinshū schools of Japan. Notably, there was never an institutional "pure land school" in India itself — rebirth in Sukhāvatī was simply one widespread goal among many Mahāyāna practitioners, only later consolidating into distinct sectarian schools in Japan.

Prajñā. ("Wisdom," closer to "gnosis" or "awareness.") Accurate discernment of reality that goes beyond ordinary understanding — one of five mental factors accompanying all virtuous states of mind, and the third of the three trainings alongside morality and concentration, likened to a sword cutting through the web of ignorance. Distinguished into three grades: wisdom from hearing teachings, from one's own reflection on them, and from meditative cultivation — the last being the deepest. Compounds with pāramitā to form prajñāpāramitā, the perfection of wisdom that yields buddhahood itself.

Skandha. ("Heap" or "aggregate.") The five constituents into which Buddhist analysis decomposes a person: form, sensation, perception, conditioning factors, and consciousness — the last four together called "name," paired with form as "name-and-form." Nowhere among these five is there a self to be found, yet the mind habitually mistakes one or another of them for exactly that — the root wrong view that perpetuates suffering and rebirth.

Srotaāpanna. ("Stream-enterer.") The first of four stages of sanctity in mainstream Buddhism, attained by severing the first three of ten fetters binding beings to rebirth: belief in a perduring self, doubt about the path's efficacy, and faith in the power of rites and rituals. Having "entered the stream" toward liberation, the stream-enterer is guaranteed never again to be reborn as an animal, ghost, or hell-denizen, and will reach arhatship within at most seven more lifetimes.

time.basis: "texts called tantras began to appear in India in the late seventh and early eighth centuries CE"

location.label: India (general placeholder — Magadha; no specific site named)

note: Tantra. ("Continuum.") A genre of esoteric Buddhist manual — mantras, maṇḍalas, initiations, fire sacrifices — aimed at both mundane and supramundane powers, appearing in India from the late seventh century in a nonstandard, colloquial Sanskrit. Exegetes classed the Mahāyāna into two modes: the pāramitānaya of the sūtras and the mantranaya of the tantras, the latter promising the same buddhahood by a faster route — the vajra vehicle. Later Indian scholiasts sorted the corpus into a fourfold hierarchy: kriyā, caryā, yoga, and anuttarayoga tantra.

time.basis: given directly in the entry

location.label: Chang'an (Xi'an), China — named directly as where he built the Dayan Ta pagoda

note: Xuanzang. (600/602–664 CE.) Chinese monk and pilgrim who, defying an imperial travel ban, journeyed the Silk Road to India in 627, studied Sanskrit and Yogācāra for years at Nālandā, and returned to Chang'an in 645 with over six hundred manuscripts. Directed an eighteen-year imperial translation bureau that produced seventy-six works in 1,347 rolls — nearly four times Kumārajīva's output — inaugurating Chinese Buddhism's rigorously philological "new translation" era. Patriarch of the Chinese Yogācāra (Faxiang) school; his pagoda, the Dayan Ta, still stands in Xi'an.

time.basis: Vasubandhu, its author, "c. fourth or fifth century CE"

note: Abhidharmakośabhāṣya. ("A Treasury of Abhidharma, with Commentary.") Influential scholastic treatise by Vasubandhu (c. 4th–5th century CE), pairing a verse root text with his own prose autocommentary — a format that becomes standard for later Sarvāstivāda abhidharma literature. Systematizes Sarvāstivāda doctrine across eight chapters while repeatedly critiquing it from the more progressive Sautrāntika position, provoking a fierce rebuttal from Saṃghabhadra. Its Sanskrit text was lost for centuries, rediscovered in Tibet only in 1934–36.

time.basis: the Buddha's first sermon, via chronology convention

location.label: Sarnath (site of first sermon — not restated in this entry, cross-referenced from the saṃgha entry's account of the same event)

note: Four noble truths. A translation that obscures the original sense — "noble" describes those who understand the truths, not the truths themselves. First taught in the Buddha's inaugural sermon at Sarnath: existence is suffering (duḥkha); suffering has a cause, craving (samudaya); suffering has an end, nirvāṇa (nirodha); and there is a path to that end, the eightfold path (mārga). Traditionally elaborated into sixteen aspects, four per truth, each countering a specific inverted view — though some Mahāyāna sūtras caution that clinging to the four truths as ultimately true is itself a failure to grasp the Buddha's deeper point.

time.basis: "name dates back to the beginning of the Common Era"

location.label: India (general placeholder — Magadha; no specific site named for his origin)

note: Avalokiteśvara. ("Lord who Looks Down in Empathy.") The bodhisattva of compassion, most widely worshipped of all Mahāyāna bodhisattvas, emerging around the turn of the Common Era as the Buddhist successor to the Vedic god Brahmā. Said to have been born from a beam of light from Amitābha's forehead — hence Amitābha's image in his crown. Reached China by the first century CE as Guanyin, where he underwent a striking transformation into a female form; became Tibet's patron deity, with the Dalai Lamas identified as his incarnation and the Potala Palace named for his mythical abode.

time.basis: Padmasambhava "visited Tibet during the eighth century"

location.label: Tibet (general placeholder — Lhasa; no specific founding site named)

note: Rnying ma. ("Ancient.") Oldest of the four major Tibetan Buddhist schools, tracing its founding to the eighth-century arrival of Padmasambhava, who reportedly concealed teachings as "treasures" (gter ma) for later discovery. Named "ancient" only in retrospect, once the Bka' brgyud, Sa skya, and Dge lugs schools arose using newer translations from Tibet's later dissemination of Buddhism. Ranks the Great Perfection (rdzogs chen) as its highest teaching — an unmediated, non-conceptual recognition of the mind's own primordially pure nature — and, alone among the major schools, stayed largely outside state politics.

time.basis: the cult's rise, "during the early centuries of the Common Era"

note: Maitreya. ("The Benevolent One.") The next buddha, currently awaiting his final rebirth in Tuṣita heaven until the dharma has been forgotten entirely — traditionally calculated at 5.67 billion years after Śākyamuni's death. A minor figure in early Indian Buddhism, his cult grew into one of the most popular in Asia during the early centuries of the Common Era, the first bodhisattva to become an object of worship in his own right and the model for later cults of Avalokiteśvara and Mañjuśrī. In China and Japan he later merged with the folk figure Budai, becoming the pot-bellied "laughing Buddha."

time.basis: given directly in the entry

location.label: South India (general placeholder — Andhra Pradesh; entry says only "South India," no city named)

note: Nāgārjuna. (c. 2nd century CE.) Indian philosopher traditionally credited as founder of the Madhyamaka school, active in South India — almost nothing else about his life is secure, though two verse letters of advice to a king suggest real contemporary renown. His Mūlamadhyamakakārikā systematizes the poetic, paradoxical emptiness-talk of the perfection-of-wisdom sūtras into rigorous philosophy: emptiness is not nonexistence but the absence of independent, intrinsic existence (svabhāva), inseparable from dependent origination. Also compiled a sūtra anthology used by scholars to help date which Mahāyāna texts existed in his lifetime.

Deva. ("Radiant" or "shining one.") A divinity or god — one of the rebirth destinies of saṃsāra, and the reason Buddhism is said to have gods but no God. Rebirth as a deva rewards past virtue but remains temporary, not eternal: even the highest heavens are way stations within saṃsāra, not final escape from it. Twenty-seven categories of devas populate three cosmological realms; the six heavens of the sensuous realm alone are stacked from the slopes of Mount Sumeru up into the sky above its summit.

Daśabhūmi. ("Ten grounds" or "ten stages.") The ten highest stages of the bodhisattva path to buddhahood, most systematically laid out in the Daśabhūmikasūtra — each stage paired with mastery of one of ten perfections, from giving on the first ground through knowledge on the tenth. As the bodhisattva ascends, his powers multiply by orders of magnitude: on the first ground he can see a hundred buddhas at once, by the tenth a number equal to the specks of dust in countless universes. Competing traditions (Yogācāra's five-path system, Tiantai's vehicle correlations) map their own schemas onto the same ten stages, producing genuinely different accounts of what happens at each one.

time.basis: "no later than the early-ninth century during the Silla dynasty" (pilgrims bringing the tradition to Korea)

location.label: Korea (general placeholder — no specific site named)

note: Sŏn. The Korean branch of the East Asian Chan tradition, brought to the peninsula by pilgrim-monks no later than the early ninth century. At least nine returning pilgrims founded their own lineages, together known as the Nine Mountains school. Flourished under Pojo Chinul during the Koryŏ dynasty, developed a distinctive "questioning meditation" focused on the Linji lineage, and survived centuries of Chosŏn-era suppression to remain the dominant strand of Korean Buddhism today, in the Chogye and T'aego orders.

Vairocana. ("Resplendent.") Central buddha of the Avataṃsakasūtra and Huayan tradition, personifying the dharmakāya and the universal truth that every phenomenon interpenetrates every other. Originates as a minor solar deity in the Hindu tradition before being absorbed into Buddhism; became one of East Asian Buddhism's principal buddhas as the Avataṃsakasūtra's popularity grew, with colossal images erected at the Longmen Grottoes near Luoyang and at Tōdaiji in Nara. Also central to esoteric Buddhism as the axis of the vajradhātu and garbhadhātu maṇḍalas — though there he is often conflated with the distinct, if closely related, Mahāvairocana.

Darśanamārga. ("Path of vision.") The third of the five paths to liberation, following the paths of accumulation and preparation — the adept's first direct, unmediated perception of reality, severing the first three of the ten fetters binding one to rebirth. In the Sarvāstivāda system, it unfolds across sixteen precisely sequenced moments of realizing the four noble truths; Yogācāra reframes it as dissolving the false subject-object split, while Madhyamaka treats it as the first direct realization of emptiness. Marks the technical threshold at which a practitioner becomes a "noble person."

time.basis: "the term mārga occurs in the Buddha's first sermon"; converted via chronology convention

location.label: Sarnath (site of first sermon; not restated in this entry, cross-referenced from saṃgha/four noble truths)

note: Mārga. ("Path.") The route from suffering to liberation — a road the Buddha claims to have rediscovered, not invented, since every past buddha found and then lost the same path before the next one reopens it. Introduced in the first sermon at Sarnath as the fourth noble truth, the eightfold path between self-indulgence and self-mortification. Elsewhere elaborated as the three trainings of morality, concentration, and wisdom, or as five sequential paths shared by the śrāvaka, pratyekabuddha, and bodhisattva vehicles alike, each ending in a different fruit.

time.basis: Tsong kha pa "founded Ri bo Dga' ldan monastery in 1409"

location.label: Ganden Monastery, Tibet (named directly in the entry)

note: Dge lugs. ("System of Virtue.") Youngest and eventually most powerful of Tibet's four major Buddhist sects, founded by Tsong kha pa with his 1409 monastery at Ganden. Three more foundational monasteries followed within decades, and Tsong kha pa's disciple Dge 'dun grub was later recognized as the first Dalai Lama. After 1642, the fifth Dalai Lama's government made the Dge lugs Tibet's de facto ruling party, backed by a rigorous scholastic examination system that still produces its abbots and incarnate lamas today.

Majjhimanikāya. ("Collection of Middle-Length Discourses.") The second of five divisions of the Pāli Suttapiṭaka, containing 152 discourses across three parts. Preserves some of the earliest versions of the Buddha's enlightenment narrative — its account of his renunciation, unlike later embellished versions, is a spare first-person statement with no chariot rides or four sights. Its Sarvāstivāda Sanskrit counterpart, the Madhyamāgama, overlaps substantially but not completely with it, sharing 98 of its 222 sūtras.

Mantra. ("Spell" or "charm.") A syllable or string of syllables, often semantically meaningless, whose recitation is held to be efficacious — folk-etymologized by Indian exegetes as "mind protector." Appears in sūtras as well as tantras, most famously in the Heart Sūtra, and is central to tantric visualization practice, where its letters are imagined within the meditator's own body. The most widely recited of all is Avalokiteśvara's six-syllable Oṃ maṇi padme hūṃ; Japan's Shingon school takes its very name from the term's Sinitic translation, "true word."

Maṇḍala. ("Circle.") A structured diagram — imagined, painted, or built — in which significance increases toward the center, typically the residence of a primary deity surrounded by an assembly of attendants. Functions simultaneously as cosmological map, meditative visualization, and ritual space that initiates are said to "enter." Scaled up, entire monuments, monasteries, and even mountains (Borobudur, Bsam yas, Wutaishan) are understood as maṇḍalas; scaled into the West, Carl Jung adopted the maṇḍala as a model of psychological wholeness.

Citta. ("Mind," "mentality," or "thought.") General consciousness itself — synonymous with "name" as opposed to form, and present during any conscious activity at all. Sarvāstivāda abhidharma counts ten mental factors that accompany every single moment of citta; Yogācāra expands the concept to encompass all dharmas, not just mentality, giving that school its alternate name "mind-only." At enlightenment, citta is said to be freed from its habitual identification with a self, becoming — per the Buddha's own words — inherently "luminous."

Anātman. ("No self" or "nonself.") One of the three marks of existence, alongside impermanence and suffering — the insight that the "person" is nothing but an imputed continuity across five ever-changing aggregates, the way "chariot" names an arrangement of parts with no separate chariot-essence inside it. Rebirth is neither the same person continuing nor a different one beginning, but a causal chain linking the two. Mahāyāna extends the doctrine from persons to all phenomena, partly in direct response to Sarvāstivāda's claim that dharmas themselves exist eternally across past, present, and future.

Pāramitā. ("Perfection.") A virtue cultivated by a bodhisattva on the path to buddhahood — canonically a set of six (giving, morality, patience, effort, concentration, wisdom), expanded to ten in the Daśabhūmikasūtra by adding method, vow, power, and knowledge, one perfected per stage of the ten bodhisattva grounds. Some Madhyamaka commentators insist these only count as true perfections when practiced with an understanding of emptiness — giving a gift, for instance, without clinging to any notion of giver, gift, or recipient.

time.basis: "By the eleventh century CE, what is today designated as the Theravāda became the dominant form of Buddhism in Sri Lanka"

location.label: Sri Lanka (general placeholder — no specific site named)

note: Theravāda. ("Way of the Elders.") A modern name — not adopted in its current sense until the early twentieth century — applied to the Buddhism of Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia, which became the region's dominant tradition by the eleventh century CE. The dictionary is unusually blunt about the term's shaky pedigree: "Theravāda" isn't securely attested in Indian sources, the name largely displaced the pejorative "Hīnayāna" only in the 1950s by resolution of the World Fellowship of Buddhists, and — despite popular belief — its Pāli scriptures were often redacted later than much of the "newer" Mahāyāna literature they're assumed to predate.

time.basis: "most scholars placing him in the fourth or fifth century CE"

location.label: Peshawar, Pakistan (ancient Puruṣapura, Gandhāra — named directly in the entry)

note: Vasubandhu. (c. 4th–5th century CE.) Born in Puruṣapura, Gandhāra (modern Peshawar) — one of Buddhism's most consequential authors, and the only major figure to shape both the mainstream schools and the Mahāyāna. Composed the Abhidharmakośa from within Sarvāstivāda-Vaibhāṣika orthodoxy, then critiqued it from a Sautrāntika angle in his own prose commentary. Converted to Mahāyāna after encountering his half-brother Asaṅga, becoming a foundational Yogācāra author whose Triṃśikā underlies Xuanzang's massive Chengweishi lun — the root text of the Chinese Faxiang school.

Nianfo. ("Recollection... of the Buddha.") A Chinese translation of buddhānusmṛti, an early meditative practice of recalling the Buddha's qualities that evolved, in East Asia, into reciting his name outright — most often "Homage to Amitābha Buddha." Widely practiced across schools and social classes in China and Korea, not confined to any single pure land tradition, though later exegetes retroactively cast certain monks as its patriarchs. In Japan, became the central, sometimes exclusive practice of Hōnen and Shinran's Jōdoshū and Jōdo Shinshū — which debated whether one sincere recitation sufficed, or many were required.

time.basis: "founded the original edifice underlying the Po ta la Palace in 637"

location.label: Lhasa, Tibet (the entry itself)

note: Lha sa. ("Place of the gods.") Capital of Tibet and its religious center, founded as Srong btsan sgam po's new capital in 637 around the original Potala Palace and Jokhang temple. The area was first called Ra sa ("place of the goats," for the pack animals used in construction) before being renamed following the Jokhang's consecration in 647. Ringed by pilgrimage circuits and the three great Dge lugs monasteries — Dga' ldan, 'Bras spungs, Se ra — it became the seat of the Dalai Lamas' government after the seventeenth century.

time.basis: Mar pa "brought to Tibet from India... in the eleventh century"

location.label: Tibet (general placeholder — Lhasa; no specific founding site named)

note: Bka' brgyud. ("Oral Lineage.") One of Tibet's four major Buddhist sects, tracing to the tantric teachings Mar pa brought from India in the eleventh century — received from his teacher Nāropa, in a chain reaching back through Tilopa to the tantric buddha Vajradhara. Less a single institution than a loose federation: unlike Sa skya or Dge lugs, it has no single sectarian head, and its many subsects vary widely in autonomy. Mar pa's student Mi la ras pa — a layman, like Mar pa himself — became Tibet's most celebrated yogin-poet; a later disciple built the sect's first true monastery, giving an itinerant movement of lay practitioners its monastic backbone.

Bodhi. ("Awakening" or "enlightenment.") The consummate knowledge of the four noble truths that ends the cycle of rebirth — occurring in three grades: that of a perfect buddha, a solitary pratyekabuddha, and an ordinary śrāvaka disciple, the first two achieved independently and the third only through a teacher's guidance. Mahāyāna commentaries hold that buddhas actually achieve full enlightenment not under the Bodhi tree at all, but in the Akaniṣṭha heaven as an eternal enjoyment-body — the scene at Bodhgayā being a conjured display staged to inspire the world.

time.basis: "probably dating from the late-Tang dynasty"

location.label: China (general placeholder — Xi'an/Chang'an; no specific site named)

note: Gong'an. ("Public case" — kōan in Japanese.) Originally a legal term for a magistrate's precedent, adapted by the Chan school for the enigmatic sayings and exchanges of past masters used as objects of contemplation. Practice of commenting on these "old cases" began around the late Tang dynasty, developing into elaborate collections — pointer, case, prose and verse commentary — like the Biyan Lu and Wumen Guan. Dahui Zonggao systematized a further method of fixating on just a case's "keyword" (huatou), most famously the single syllable "wu" — no.

time.basis: the Buddha's death, via chronology convention

location.label: Kuśinagarī (not restated in this entry, cross-referenced from the stūpa entry's account of the Buddha's death)

note: Parinirvāṇa. ("Final nirvāṇa.") The last passage into nirvāṇa at the death of a buddha or arhat, distinguished from the "nirvāṇa with remainder" attained earlier at enlightenment, when the causes of future rebirth end but the current body and mind live on to complete their natural term. At parinirvāṇa, that remainder itself is extinguished — no physical or mental constituents remain to be reborn. The term is used above all for Śākyamuni's own death, one of the most depicted scenes in Buddhist art, conventionally shown as the Buddha reclining.

Śīla. ("Morality.") Restraint of unwholesome deeds of body and speech — one of the three trainings alongside concentration and wisdom, and the second of the six perfections. Takes graduated forms across the tradition: five precepts for laypeople, an expanded eight for occasional lay observance, ten for novices, and the full monastic code for ordained monks and nuns. In the bodhisattva path, its scope widens further still, into the distinct bodhisattva precepts.

time.basis: "fl. eighth century," given directly

location.label: Swat Valley, Pakistan (Oḍḍiyāna — "a region some scholars associate with the Swat Valley," per this entry)

note: Padmasambhava. (fl. 8th century.) Indian tantric master revered in Tibet as "Guru Rinpoche," the "Precious Guru," and honored by the Rnying ma sect as its founder and a "second buddha." Traditional accounts place his miraculous lotus-birth in Oḍḍiyāna, a region some scholars locate in Pakistan's Swat Valley; historically, he's credited with subduing Tibet's indigenous deities and helping establish Bsam yas, the country's first monastery, alongside Śāntarakṣita and King Khri srong lde btsan. Said to have hidden teachings as "treasures" for future discovery, and believed by devotees to still reside in a paradise he never truly left.

Śrāvaka. ("Listener" or "disciple.") In Mahāyāna usage, one who seeks personal liberation as an arhat rather than full buddhahood — grouped with the pratyekabuddha as followers of the lesser vehicle, and pointedly contrasted with the bodhisattva. Mahāyāna texts disagree sharply on their fate: the Lotus Sūtra has the Buddha prophesy future buddhahood for famous śrāvakas like Śāriputra, while other traditions treat arhatship as a genuine dead end. Frequently appear as the Buddha's interlocutors and audience throughout Mahāyāna sūtras, sometimes visibly out of their depth — as when several balk at visiting the layman Vimalakīrti, dreading his superior grasp of the dharma.

Tathāgatagarbha. ("Womb" or "embryo of the tathāgatas" — buddha-nature.) The claim that the potential for buddhahood is innate in all sentient beings, merely concealed by adventitious afflictions rather than absent. Evolves across Mahāyāna sūtras from a simple assurance that awakening is possible into something closer to genetic destiny — the Laṅkāvatāra even gives it the thirty-two physical marks of a buddha. Provoked real anxiety about smuggling back a forbidden permanent self: Candrakīrti insists it names nothing but the mind's own emptiness, while others, like the Jo nang, defended it as an ultimately real, if obscured, nature — a live fault line between Tibetan schools to this day.

Anāgāmin. ("Nonreturner.") The third of four grades of Buddhist saint, having eliminated the first five of ten fetters binding beings to rebirth and substantially weakened the rest. Guaranteed never to be reborn in the sensuous realm again — instead completing the path to arhatship in this life, or in one of the five "pure abodes" at the top of the subtle-materiality realm, typically the Akaniṣṭha heaven. Sits between the once-returner and the arhat in mainstream Buddhism's four-stage ladder of sanctity.

time.basis: "a new religious movement in the fifth century BCE" (coining of the term)

note: Bhikṣu. ("Beggar" — monk.) A fully ordained male Buddhist mendicant, coined as a term in the fifth century BCE to distinguish Buddhism's wandering renunciants from rival śramaṇa movements like the Jainas and Ājīvakas. Reached through a two-stage process — novice ordination, then full ordination — after which a bhikṣu is bound by the complete monastic code: 227 rules in the Pāli vinaya, 250 in the Dharmaguptaka, 253 in the Mūlasarvāstivāda. Permitted, by rule if rarely in practice, only four or eight personal possessions, and dependent on lay donors in exchange for serving as their "field of merit."

time.basis: Song-dynasty consolidation by named successors (e.g. Fengxue Yanzhao, b. 896); Linji Yixuan's own Tang-dynasty dates aren't given in this entry

location.label: China (general placeholder — no specific site named)

note: Linji zong. One of the Five Houses and Seven Schools of mature Chinese Chan, tracing to the Tang-dynasty master Linji Yixuan and consolidated by Song-dynasty successors including Shishuang Chuyuan, whose two disciples founded the lineage's two enduring branches, the Huanglong and Yangqi. Dahui Zonggao, in the Yangqi line, developed the practice of fixating on a single gong'an's "keyword" into what became kanhua Chan; his branch also sparred publicly with the rival Caodong lineage over meditation method. Survives today as the ancestor of Japan's Rinzai and Korea's Imje traditions.

time.basis: "at the time of the Buddha"; chronology convention

location.label: Śrāvastī (Sahet-Mahet), Uttar Pradesh, India — the entry itself

note: Śrāvastī. Capital of Kośala and one of India's major cities during the Buddha's lifetime, where he is said to have spent twenty-five rainy-season retreats — more than anywhere else. Ruled by his patron King Prasenajit; home to his wealthiest lay donor, Anāthapiṇḍada, who gave him the Jetavana grove where hundreds of sūtras are set. Also the site of two of the Buddha's most spectacular recorded miracles: multiplying himself across the heavens and earth, and rising into the air emitting fire and water simultaneously.

Abhidharmapiṭaka. The third of the three canonical "baskets," compiled from early attempts to resolve inconsistencies in the Buddha's sūtra teachings, adapted as he was to different audiences. At least seven Indian schools had their own recension; only two survive complete — the Pāli version (seven texts, the only one extant in an Indian language) and the Sarvāstivāda version (seven different texts, complete only in Xuanzang's seventh-century Chinese translation). In the Sarvāstivāda canon, one text, the Jñānaprasthāna, is treated as the "body" with the other six as its supporting "feet."

Vijñāna. ("Consciousness.") Technically, the six types of sensory consciousness — eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind — that constitute the fifth of the five aggregates and give the observable universe its knowability. Most schools accept exactly six; Yogācāra adds two more, an afflicted mentality that mistakenly generates the sense of self, and a foundational storehouse consciousness beneath it. Each form of consciousness arises dependent on three conditions, tying vijñāna directly into the broader Buddhist analysis of causation.

Caitta. ("Mental concomitants" or "mental factors.") The states — sensation, volition, faith, envy, doubt, and dozens more — that accompany the mind and its six sensory consciousnesses in every act of awareness. Schools disagree sharply on the count: Vaibhāṣika lists forty-six, Pāli abhidhamma fifty-two, mature Yogācāra fifty-one sorted into six categories running from universal factors present in every thought to afflictions present only in defiled ones. The precise inventory functions as each school's working model of how a mind actually operates, moment to moment.

Duḥkha. ("Suffering" or "unsatisfactoriness.") The first of the four noble truths — not just pain, but the built-in unsatisfactoriness of anything impermanent, since even pleasure inevitably passes and pain unpredictably arrives. Enumerated in lists of three (misery from suffering itself, from change, and from mere conditionedness), four (birth, aging, sickness, death), or eight types; some texts count as many as a hundred and ten. The teaching's purpose isn't despair but reorientation: recognizing duḥkha in ordinary life is what first turns a person toward nirvāṇa.

time.basis: split from Mahīśāsaka "probably sometime around the late second or early first centuries BCE"

location.label: Kashmir-Gandhāra (Peshawar placeholder) — named as where the school was "most active"

note: Dharmaguptaka. One of the eighteen traditional mainstream schools of early Indian Buddhism, splitting off — by one account — from the Mahīśāsaka school around the late second or early first century BCE, and most active in Kashmir-Gandhāra and Sri Lanka. Distinctively held that the Buddha stands apart from the saṃgha altogether, so that gifts to him outrank gifts to the community — a view that fueled its emphasis on stūpa veneration. Its vinaya, the "Four-Part Vinaya," translated into Chinese in 405, remains the monastic code still followed across East Asia today.

location.label: Kashmir (Srinagar placeholder) — named as where the school was especially based

note: Vaibhāṣika. ("Followers of the Vibhāṣā.") The Sarvāstivāda abhidharma specialists of Kashmir-Gandhāra and Bactria, named for their allegiance to the school's massive encyclopedic treatise, the Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā — which they held to be the Buddha's own word, its dialogic structure explained by divine interlocutors he summoned for the occasion. Maintained that all seventy-five constituent factors of reality are both real and eternal, enduring across past, present, and future — a position so committal that a rival faction split off entirely, calling itself Sautrāntika, "those who adhere to the sūtras instead."

Rūpadhātu. ("Realm of subtle materiality" or "form realm.") The middle of Buddhist cosmology's three realms, between the sensuous realm below and the immaterial realm above — accessible only by mastering one of four meditative absorptions in a prior life. Its inhabitants, classed as Brahmā gods, retain only the barest trace of physicality: three senses instead of five, ever taller bodies and longer lifespans at each of seventeen ascending sublevels. Its fourth and subtlest heaven is considered an ideal springboard to nirvāṇa — the Buddha's own mind is said to have passed through it on the way to his final extinction.

time.basis: "written by the exegete Buddhaghosa... in the fifth century CE"

location.label: Anurādhapura, Sri Lanka (Mahāvihāra — named directly in the entry)

note: Visuddhimagga. ("Path of Purity.") Buddhaghosa's fifth-century compendium of Theravāda doctrine and practice, composed at the Mahāvihāra monastery in Anurādhapura, Sri Lanka, and organized around the three trainings of morality, concentration, and wisdom. Legend holds the monks tested him by having him write a commentary from scratch three times, after gods repeatedly hid the manuscript — all three versions came out word-for-word identical. Remains the closest Pāli equivalent to the Sarvāstivāda's own encyclopedic Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā.

time.basis: born "the same day" as the Buddha (chronology convention) and died "when Ānanda was 120 years old," per this entry

location.label: Kapilavastu (named directly in this entry as the Śākya home town)

note: Ānanda. ("Bliss.") The Buddha's cousin, longtime personal attendant, and cousin of Devadatta — said to have been born the same day as the future Buddha into the same Śākya clan. Served the Buddha for twenty-five years on his own carefully negotiated terms, meant to prove he received no special treatment; successfully lobbied, against the Buddha's initial refusal, for women to be admitted to the saṃgha. Renowned for perfect memory, he recited the entirety of the Buddha's teachings at the first council shortly after the Buddha's death — becoming an arhat only the night before, famously attaining enlightenment in none of the four traditional postures.

Ālayavijñāna. ("Storehouse consciousness.") Yogācāra's eighth and foundational form of consciousness, solving a real tension in Buddhist thought: how can there be moral cause-and-effect across lifetimes if there's no permanent self to carry it? An ethically neutral repository holds the karmic "seeds" of every past action, releasing them as experience while itself persisting from moment to moment and across death and rebirth. Attacked by Madhyamaka philosophers like Candrakīrti as smuggling in a disguised self, and eventually said to be transformable, once purified, into the "immaculate consciousness" of a buddha's mind.

Bodhicitta. ("Thought of enlightenment.") The intention to achieve buddhahood in order to liberate all beings — the aspiration that opens the bodhisattva path. Some schools treat it as already latent in every mind as an "innately pure" nature; others hold that not all beings are so endowed. Distinguished into "conventional" bodhicitta (the aspiration itself, further split into vowing and actually setting out) and "ultimate" bodhicitta (direct realization of emptiness) — and, in tantric contexts, taken on an additional, more literal meaning as well.

time.basis: "fl. c. 370–450 CE," given directly

location.label: Anurādhapura, Sri Lanka (Mahāvihāra — named directly in the entry)

note: Buddhaghosa. (fl. c. 370–450 CE.) The preeminent Pāli commentator, whose origins are genuinely uncertain — competing legends claim him as Burmese or as an Indian brāhmaṇa converted after losing a debate to a Buddhist monk. Traveled to the Mahāvihāra monastery in Anurādhapura, Sri Lanka, to translate the Sinhalese commentaries on the Pāli canon back into Pāli, producing along the way his masterwork, the Visuddhimagga. Later attributions credit him with a large body of further commentary, though modern scholarship is confident only in the Visuddhimagga and the four nikāya commentaries as genuinely his.

time.basis: contemporary of the Buddha (died "several months before the Buddha"); no specific dates given in this entry, so chronology convention used

location.label: Rājagṛha (Nālaka nearby) — named directly in the entry as his birthplace

note: Śāriputra. ("Son of Śārī.") The Buddha's first chief disciple, renowned above all for wisdom, paired with Mahāmaudgalyāyana (chief in supernormal powers) — the two became stream-enterers together on hearing a single four-line verse from the monk Aśvajit before either had even met the Buddha. Recognized as second only to the Buddha in his grasp of the dharma, and said to be the one who received and transmitted the abhidharma after the Buddha first taught it to his mother in heaven. In Mahāyāna sūtras he's repeatedly outmaneuvered — turned into a woman by a goddess, humbled by questions he can't answer — dramatizing that even the mainstream tradition's wisest arhat falls short of Mahāyāna insight. Died months before the Buddha, at Nālaka near Rājagṛha.

Tripiṭaka. ("Three baskets.") The standard organizing schema of the Buddhist canon — discourses (sūtrapiṭaka), monastic discipline (vinayapiṭaka), and scholastic analysis (abhidharmapiṭaka) — named for the baskets once used to store palm-leaf manuscripts. Each mainstream school kept its own version; only the Pāli recension survives complete in an Indian language. Mahāyāna sūtras were never organized under this scheme at all, though some later exegetes reinterpreted the three baskets figuratively, as corresponding to the three trainings in morality, meditation, and wisdom.

time.basis: "the fundamental insight on the night of his enlightenment"; chronology convention

location.label: Bodhgayā (site of enlightenment; not restated in this entry, cross-referenced from nirvāṇa/Śākyamuni)

note: Pratītyasamutpāda. ("Dependent origination.") The principle that nothing arises except in dependence on something else — according to tradition, the Buddha's core insight on the seventh night after his enlightenment at Bodhgayā. Formalized as a twelvefold chain running from ignorance through to old age and death, each link conditioning the next; a shorter ten-link version in some texts suggests the standard twelve developed over time. Charts a genuine middle way between eternalism (a soul persists unchanged) and annihilationism (the person simply ends) — when asked "who is reborn," the Buddha reframes the question entirely: not who, but what conditions what.

Bhūmi. ("Ground" or "stage.") A stage of training on the bodhisattva (or, in some contexts, śrāvaka) path — most often enumerated as ten, following the Daśabhūmikasūtra, with the first ground coinciding with the path of vision and the remaining nine with the path of cultivation. Buddhahood itself is sometimes described as an eleventh, tathāgata ground. Competing enumerations exist — seven shared stages common to all three vehicles, or seven bodhisattva-specific ones — reflecting a doctrine still being actively organized and re-organized across different texts and schools.

Indriya. ("Faculty" or "dominant factor.") Most often the five or six sense bases — sight, hearing, smell, taste, touch, and mind — but also, soteriologically, the five spiritual "dominants" of faith, effort, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom that drive progress on the path. Vaibhāṣika abhidharma expands both senses into a comprehensive list of twenty-two faculties, adding faculties of sex, life-force, feeling, and three grades of purifying insight — an entire taxonomy of what actually governs a being's experience, moment to moment.

Jhāna. The Pāli counterpart of Sanskrit dhyāna — meditative absorption achieved by withdrawing the mind from sensory input into single-pointed concentration on one object. Eight stages total: four increasingly refined absorptions of the subtle-materiality realm, each shedding a mental factor as it deepens, followed by four immaterial absorptions named for ever-more-attenuated objects, from infinite space to neither-perception-nor-nonperception. Builds the concentration that makes insight possible, without by itself constituting insight — and can lead, if mistaken for the goal, merely to rebirth as a long-lived divinity in the corresponding heaven.

time.basis: "(c. 300–232 BCE; r. c. 268–232 BCE)," given directly

location.label: India (general placeholder — Magadha/Pāṭaliputra, the Mauryan capital; not named in this specific entry)

note: Aśoka. (c. 300–232 BCE; r. c. 268–232 BCE.) Mauryan emperor whose inscribed edicts — found from northern Pakistan to Bengal to South India — are among the earliest deciphered writing on the subcontinent. Turned to dharma after a bloody war of conquest in Kalinga, but the ethical code he promulgated was a multireligious civic program, not a specifically Buddhist one — a fact obscured for centuries because the edicts themselves weren't translated until the nineteenth century. The Buddhist legend of Aśoka, built instead from later Pāli and Sanskrit chronicles, casts him as an exclusively Theravāda patron who purged the saṃgha and convened the third Buddhist council — a portrait the actual inscriptions don't support.

Dharmakāya. ("Truth body.") One of the two or three bodies of a buddha — originally referring simply to the collected auspicious qualities and teachings that make up the Buddha's legacy, later evolving in Mahāyāna into a cosmic principle: the true nature of the Buddha from which all his other forms derive. Perfection-of-wisdom commentators split over whether it names an ultimate "own-nature body" or divides further into a "knowledge truth body" distinct from that own-nature — a technical dispute with real consequences for how Tibetan and Indian exegetes understood what, exactly, becomes enlightened.

Pratyekabuddha. ("Solitary buddha.") One who achieves arhatship through his own effort, without a teacher, but — unlike a fully enlightened buddha — declines to teach others, having never developed the requisite great compassion. Distinguished from a śrāvaka not just by self-sufficiency but by the sheer time required: a pratyekabuddha must accumulate enough merit across lifetimes to succeed entirely alone. Mahāyāna groups the pratyekabuddha and śrāvaka paths together as the "lesser vehicle," contrasted with the bodhisattva's path to full buddhahood.

Kāmadhātu. ("Sensuous realm" or "desire realm.") The lowest of Buddhism's three cosmological realms, encompassing six rebirth destinies from hell through hungry ghosts, animals, humans, demigods, and lesser divinities — all bound by sensuality and possessing a comparatively coarse physical body. Rebirth here, at whatever level, reflects a specific mix of past unwholesome and wholesome deeds. Above it sit the subtler realm of form (rūpadhātu) and the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), where the pull of desire progressively loosens.

Anitya. ("Impermanence.") The first of the three marks of existence, alongside suffering and nonself — the fact that anything compounded by causes and conditions is destined to change and eventually cease. Distinguished into two grains: impermanence marked by an elapsed span (a life ending, daylight fading) and impermanence occurring at every single thought-instant, an unbroken flux even before any visible ending arrives. Mistaking the impermanent for permanent is one of Buddhism's four fundamental inverted views, and precisely what meditation on this mark is meant to correct.

time.basis: the title "originated during the sixteenth century when Altan Khan... bestowed the title"

location.label: Tibet (general placeholder — Lhasa; no single site names the institution)

note: Dalai Lama. ("Ocean teacher" — a Mongolian-Tibetan hybrid title.) An incarnation lineage within the Dge lugs sect, its holders traditionally revered as manifestations of the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara. The name itself dates only to the sixteenth century, when the Mongol ruler Altan Khan translated the name of the Dge lugs teacher Bsod nams rgya mtsho — literally "ocean" — into Mongolian; he became the third Dalai Lama, with his two predecessors recognized only posthumously. Despite the common assumption abroad, the Dalai Lama has never held the formal headship of the Dge lugs sect — that position belongs to a separate office, the "Throneholder of Ganden Monastery."

Huayan zong. ("Flower Garland School.") Chinese exegetical tradition named for its central scripture, the Avataṃsakasūtra, with a lineage of patriarchs — Dushun, Zhiyan, Fazang, Chengguan, Guifeng Zongmi — retrospectively constructed by later followers. Systematizes the sūtra's vision of infinite, mutually interpenetrating world-systems into the doctrine of "dependent origination of the dharmadhātu," where every phenomenon simultaneously creates and is created by every other. Transmitted to Japan in 740 as Kegon and influential in Korea through Ŭisang and Wŏnhyo; weakened in China after the Huichang persecution but continues to shape modern Buddhist environmentalism and engaged Buddhism.

time.basis: founder Myōan Eisai's dates (1141–1215) and the school's "early Kamakura period" establishment

location.label: Japan (general placeholder — Tokyo/Kantō; no specific site named)

note: Rinzaishū. Japanese Zen school established in the early Kamakura period, tracing to the Chinese master Linji Yixuan via Myōan Eisai's two trips to China. Virtually the entire tradition descends from the Yangqi collateral line of the Linji lineage; twenty-four transmission lineages reached Japan, twenty-one of them Rinzai. Rose to prominence under shogunal and imperial patronage through the state-organized "five mountains" (gozan) temple system, declined by the Edo period, and was revitalized by Hakuin Ekaku, whose systematized kōan curriculum still structures Rinzai training today.

Ratnatraya. ("Three jewels" — the triple gem.) The Buddha, dharma, and saṃgha, together the three objects of Buddhist veneration and the object of a formula — "I go to the Buddha/dharma/saṃgha for refuge" — that formally identifies someone as a Buddhist upon its threefold recitation. Each term admits multiple readings: "Buddha" can mean the historical Śākyamuni, any Mahāyāna buddha, or innate buddhahood itself; "dharma" in this specific context is often narrowed to just the third and fourth noble truths; "saṃgha" here technically means only its noble, awakened members, not the ordained at large.

time.basis: the instruction-class literature, "dating from the eleventh to fourteenth centuries"

location.label: Tibet (general placeholder — Lhasa; entry describes it as "a Tibetan innovation" with no single site)

note: Rdzogs chen. ("Great perfection.") A Tibetan meditative and philosophical tradition centered in the Rnying ma sect but embraced to varying degrees elsewhere, including the non-Buddhist Bon religion — despite legendary claims of a lineage running back through Padmasambhava and Vimalamitra to a primordial buddha, historically appears to be a genuine Tibetan innovation blending native belief with imported Chinese and Indian teachings. Its literature developed in three phases — mind, space, and instruction classes — with the eleventh-to-fourteenth-century instruction-class texts fully absorbing tantric technique into what had begun as a doctrine explicitly suspicious of formal practice.

time.basis: "Dkon mchog rgyal po founded Sa skya monastery in 1073"

location.label: Sakya, Tsang, Tibet (named directly in the entry)

note: Sa skya. ("Gray earth.") One of Tibet's four major Buddhist sects, founded with its namesake monastery in 1073 by Dkon mchog rgyal po, and built around tantric teachings — the Hevajratantra and "path and result" system — brought from India via the adept Virūpa. Politically dominant in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries after Sa skya Paṇḍita struck a political alliance with the Mongol ruler Godan Khan, later extended by his nephew 'Phags pa with Qubilai Khan. Uniquely among the major sects, Sa skya's leadership passes hereditarily within the 'Khon family rather than through incarnation.

Dharmadhātu. ("Dharma realm.") In Abhidharma, one of the eighteen elements — the category of whatever can be an object of cognition. In Mahāyāna, something far grander: the infinite domain in which all phenomena occur, a virtual synonym for ultimate reality itself. Huayan philosophy elaborates it into four ascending levels of realization, from the mundane realm of phenomena up to their unimpeded, mutual interpenetration with one another — the same vision, framed differently, that animates the entire Huayan system.

time.basis: "first comes to prominence in the Vimalakīrtinirdeśa, which probably dates no later than the first century CE"

location.label: Wutaishan, China (named directly and extensively in the entry as his associated site)

note: Mañjuśrī. ("Gentle Glory.") The bodhisattva of wisdom, one of Mahāyāna's two most important bodhisattvas alongside Avalokiteśvara — first prominent in the Vimalakīrtinirdeśa (by the first century CE), the only figure with courage enough to debate the wise layman Vimalakīrti. Wields a flaming sword of wisdom and a lotus-borne volume of the Prajñāpāramitā; some texts claim he inspired Śākyamuni, and every past buddha, to set out on the bodhisattva path in the first place. Closely tied to Wutaishan in China, a pilgrimage site drawing seekers of his visionary presence from across Asia since at least the Northern Wei dynasty.

Āgama. ("Text" or "scripture.") A general term for the received scriptural tradition, paired with reasoning as the two means of arriving at truth, and with realization as the two divisions of the buddhadharma — the verbal tradition versus what practice manifests. More specifically, the four scriptural collections of the mainstream tradition — long, medium, connected, and numerically-arranged discourses, attributed to the Buddha and his close disciples and now lost in Sanskrit but preserved in Chinese — that correspond, with real differences in content, to the four Pāli nikāyas. A fifth Pāli collection, the miscellaneous "Minor Collection," has no equivalent among the surviving Chinese āgamas, though similar miscellanies are known to have existed in several mainstream schools.

Ārya. ("Noble" or "superior.") A term appropriated from earlier Indian culture to denote someone who has directly perceived reality — at minimum, a stream-enterer in the fourfold path system, or one who has reached the path of vision in the fivefold system. Both Sarvāstivāda and Theravāda scholastics recognize seven types of noble ones, ranked by whether liberation comes chiefly through faith, doctrine, or a combination of meditative absorption and wisdom; Mahāyāna sources expand candidate lists further, up to forty-eight or more noble bodhisattvas. Also lends its name, via the Indian master Ārya Nāgārjuna, to one of two esoteric Guhyasamājatantra exegetical traditions.

time.basis: "the first Tibetan gter ma appear sometime after the start of the second dispensation (phyi dar), c. 1000"

location.label: Tibet (general placeholder — the tradition is Tibet-wide, centered on the Rnying ma sect)

note: Gter ma. ("Hidden treasures.") Tibetan Buddhist and Bon manuscripts, relics, and ritual objects said to have been concealed — most famously by Padmasambhava, before the ninth-century persecution under Glang dar ma — for discovery by a predestined revealer in a later age. Three types: earth treasures physically unearthed from caves or pillars, mind treasures found within the revealer's own mindstream as seeds from a past life, and pure visions perceived through the mind's innate purity. Authenticity is genuinely contested — some are dismissed as forgeries — but major gter ma cycles, including the Klong chen snying thig, remain foundational to Rnying ma practice, and even the fifth Dalai Lama's political legitimacy was grounded in gter ma he himself revealed.

time.basis: "(c. late-fourth to early-fifth centuries)", given directly

location.label: Songshan, China (Shaolinsi — named directly as where he sat in meditation for nine years)

note: Bodhidharma. (c. late fourth–early fifth century.) The Indian (or perhaps Central Asian) monk revered as Chan's first patriarch — a legend built up over centuries from a little-known émigré into an elaborate hagiography. Said to have sailed to South China, unsettled the devout emperor Wu of Liang by declaring that his monastery-building had earned him no merit at all, then crossed the Yangtze on a reed to the north, where he sat facing a wall in a cave at Shaolinsi for nine years — his disciple Huike reportedly proving his sincerity by cutting off his own arm. Long confused with the translator Bodhiruci and the monk Dharmatrāta, and credited, without real evidence, as founder of the Shaolin martial arts tradition.

Prātimokṣa. ("Code" or "rules.") The disciplinary code governing fully ordained monks and nuns, or the text setting it out — probably the oldest layer of the various Buddhist vinayas, recited communally to maintain monastic cohesion. Its pre-Buddhist meaning is uncertain, perhaps "a promise to be redeemed"; in Buddhist usage it comes to denote a binding obligation and, by extension, formal monastic regulation itself.

Ātman. ("Self" or "I.") A perduring substratum of being posited as the agent of actions, possessor of mind and body, and the thing that passes from lifetime to lifetime. Buddhism treats belief in such a self — and in a correlate "mine" — as the root misconception injecting a self-referential point of view into all perception, generating clinging toward what one likes and hatred toward what one doesn't. Diagnosed as fundamental ignorance and the root cause of suffering, it's countered by the teaching of nonself, whose precise meaning and implications the various philosophical schools work out in exhaustive, often conflicting detail.

Dhātu. ("Element.") A polysemous term spanning several distinct Buddhist taxonomies. In epistemology, the eighteen elements of sensory experience — six sense organs, six objects, six resulting consciousnesses. In cosmology, the three realms of existence that comprise all of saṃsāra. Physically, the four (or six) constituent elements of matter — earth, water, fire, wind, sometimes space and consciousness. And, in mortuary contexts, a synonym for bodily relics, sometimes differentiated into corporeal relics, relics of use, and relics of commemoration — the same word doing duty across physics, cosmology, and the cult of the dead.

time.basis: the "magnum opus of the second-century Indian master Nāgārjuna"

note: Mūlamadhyamakakārikā. ("Root Verses on the Middle Way.") Nāgārjuna's second-century masterwork, 448 verses across twenty-seven chapters subjecting causation, motion, self, time, and nirvāṇa itself to a relentless four-cornered analysis that finds none of them possessing independent, intrinsic existence. Preserved complete only within Candrakīrti's Sanskrit commentary the Prasannapadā, and hugely influential in East Asia as one of the Three Treatises school's core texts. Its most quoted line — that there is not the slightest difference between saṃsāra and nirvāṇa — argues that emptiness doesn't negate causation but is precisely what makes change and transformation possible at all.

Hīnayāna. ("Lesser vehicle.") A pejorative coined by Mahāyāna Buddhists for the doctrines of rival mainstream śrāvakayāna schools — never used self-referentially, and never a synonym for the contemporary Theravāda tradition, despite common confusion. Variously used to mean those who reject the Mahāyāna sūtras as authentic word of the Buddha, the combined paths of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who seek liberation for themselves alone, or the roughly eighteen non-Mahāyāna schools of Indian Buddhism collectively.

time.basis: the earliest Sanskrit version "was likely compiled in Kashmir... in the third century CE"

location.label: Kashmir (compilation site of the earliest Sanskrit version, per this entry)

note: Mahāparinirvāṇasūtra. ("Discourse on the Great Decease.") The Mahāyāna retelling of the Buddha's final teachings and passage into parinirvāṇa, compiled in Kashmir by the third century CE and radically different in content from its mainstream counterpart. Its central, provocative claim is that all beings — even "incorrigibles" in the longer recension — possess buddha-nature, and that the Buddha's own nirvāṇa is not annihilation but an eternal, blissful, pure state endowed with a "great self," directly inverting the standard no-self teaching by recasting it as a merely conventional truth. Survives complete only in Chinese and Tibetan translation, in versions differing enough that scholars believe Mahāyāna material was progressively layered onto a shorter, non-Mahāyāna original.

Śamatha. ("Calmness" or "serenity.") One of the two chief branches of Buddhist meditative cultivation alongside insight — the specific degree of concentration needed to generate insight into reality and thereby destroy the afflictions. Cultivated across nine stages in which eight counteracting forces overcome five hindrances (laziness, forgetfulness, restlessness, under- and over-application of antidotes), moving from effortful desire and faith toward a self-sustaining stream of tranquility marked by physical rapture and mental ease. In monastic law the same word is also used technically for the formal settlement of disputes within the saṃgha.

Vipaśyanā. ("Insight.") An understanding of reality, conceptual or nonconceptual, sustained at a level of mental concentration equal to or exceeding śamatha — the feature that distinguishes the wisdom born of meditation from mere calm. This insight is what actually destroys the afflictions and opens the path to liberation from rebirth; calmness alone, however deep, cannot do it.

time.basis: contemporary of the Buddha (converted by the elder Mahānāma, later visited the Buddha in person); no specific dates given, chronology convention used

location.label: Kāsī (Varanasi region placeholder) — Citta was treasurer of Macchikāsaṇḍa in the kingdom of Kāsī, named directly

note: Citta. A lay treasurer of Macchikāsaṇḍa in the kingdom of Kāsī, named for the shower of colored flowers that reportedly fell at his birth, and celebrated in Pāli sources as foremost among laymen who preached the dharma. Converted on encountering the elder Mahānāma, he built him a monastery and attained nonreturner status while listening to a sermon on the six senses; his own recorded exchanges with monks and rival teachers, including Mahāvīra, fill an entire chapter of the Saṃyuttanikāya. On his deathbed he declined the gods' offer of heavenly rebirth as an unworthy, impermanent reward — preaching one last time to the assembled divinities and kin before he died.

time.basis: "officially transcribed into written form in Sri Lanka during the reign of King Vaṭṭagāmaṇi Abhaya in the first century BCE"

location.label: Sri Lanka (Anurādhapura placeholder — seat of King Vaṭṭagāmaṇi Abhaya, named in the entry)

note: Dīghanikāya. ("Collection of Long Discourses.") The first division of the Pāli sutta collection, thirty-four lengthy discourses grouped loosely into three sections and including such influential texts as the Aggaññasutta and Mahāparinibbānasutta. Tradition holds it was first recited orally at the first council after the Buddha's death and officially committed to writing in Sri Lanka in the first century BCE. A closely related Sanskrit recension, the Dīrghāgama, survives only in a 413 CE Chinese translation attributed to the Dharmaguptaka school, plus fragments rediscovered in Afghanistan in the 1990s.

Dveṣa. ("Aversion," "ill will," or "hatred.") One of Buddhism's most pervasive defilements, appearing across nearly every list of afflictions — the six fundamental kleśas, the ten fetters, the ten proclivities, the three poisons — and counted among the core mental factors in every major abhidharma system. Arises when contact with a displeasing sensory object occurs without proper introspection, and branches into derivative emotions including anger, enmity, agitation, envy, and harmfulness, all sharing aversion as their common root.

Śarīra. ("Body," and by extension, "relic.") A term for a corpse — especially the Buddha's or a monk's — before and after cremation, whose remains were divided by the brāhmaṇa Droṇa among north Indian kingdoms and later said to have been redistributed by Aśoka into eighty-four thousand stūpas. Relics are classed as whole-body (mummified remains of eminent masters) or partial-body (a finger bone, a tooth, crystalline residue from cremation believed to condense a sage's sanctity), and were venerated as an ongoing presence and power from the time of the Buddha's own parinirvāṇa onward. By extension, Buddhist scriptures themselves came to be enshrined and worshipped as "relics of the dharma-body."

Foxing. ("Buddha-nature," rendering Sanskrit buddhadhātu.) In the East Asian Yogācāra tradition, split into a universal "buddha-nature of principle" — the true, unproduced nature of all factors, discoverable by anyone through wisdom — and a "functional buddha-nature," a latent seed within the storehouse consciousness that only some beings possess and that must be activated to reach buddhahood. The Foxing lun elaborates a further threefold scheme: buddha-nature simply inherent in deluded minds, buddha-nature emerging through practice once the aspiration for enlightenment arises, and buddha-nature fully attained at the completion of the bodhisattva path.

time.basis: arose "about a century after the Buddha's death, at the so-called second Buddhist council" (chronology convention: Buddha's death c. 480 BCE)
