location.label: Vaiśālī (site of the second Buddhist council, named directly)

note: Mahāsāṃghika. ("Great Congregation.") A major mainstream school that split from the Sthaviranikāya at the second Buddhist council in Vaiśālī, roughly a century after the Buddha's death, over ten disputed points of monastic conduct — including handling money, drinking unfermented wine, and holding incomplete assemblies — which the larger faction judged not to be violations at all. Emphasized the supramundane nature of the Buddha, treating his career as Śākyamuni as mere display, and taught a "root consciousness" underlying the six senses that likely anticipated the Yogācāra storehouse consciousness. Its Lokottaravāda branch produced the celebrated Buddha biography, the Mahāvastu; the school spread across India and Afghanistan before dying out as an ordination lineage.

Sakṛdāgāmin. ("Once-returner.") The second of the four grades of noble person, above the stream-enterer and below the nonreturner and arhat — one who has fully abandoned the first three of ten fetters binding beings to rebirth (self-view, doubt, and belief in the efficacy of rites) and substantially weakened the fourth and fifth (sensual craving and malice). Destined for at most one more rebirth in the sensuous realm, though possibly further rebirths in the higher realms of form or formlessness before reaching nirvāṇa — a status defined entirely by exactly how many of the nine levels of affliction have been eliminated.

Sukhāvatī. ("Blissful" — rendered in Chinese as "ultimate bliss.") The buddha-field or pure land of Amitābha, described across the three core pure land sūtras and known in East Asia as "the western pure land." In India, rebirth there appears to have circulated as a general soteriological goal somewhat independent of devotion to Amitābha specifically, appearing in Mahāyāna sūtras such as the Samādhirājasūtra, which likely dates to the second century CE — though its own fullest description appears in the larger Sukhāvatīvyūhasūtra.

Āyatana. ("Sense-fields" or "bases of cognition.") The twelve bases for the production of consciousness — six internal sense organs and six external sense objects — whose contact generates specific sensory consciousnesses. Subsumed as the first twelve of the eighteen elements, and, alongside the aggregates and elements, one of three major early taxonomies of factors found in the sūtras, representing a more primitive stage of classification than later abhidharma analysis. In the twelvefold chain of dependent origination, the term narrows to mean just the six sense bases.

Bhāvanāmārga. ("Path of cultivation.") The fourth of five stages in the Sarvāstivāda path schema, following the path of vision and preceding the adept stage requiring no further training. Where the path of vision eliminates gross afflictions in fifteen swift thought-moments, cultivation works through eighty-one deeply rooted levels of affliction across the three realms — a slow process that may span several lifetimes — destroying each in a two-step act of elimination followed by the knowledge that it has been eliminated, until the subtlest affliction finally falls and the adept is freed from rebirth entirely.

time.basis: period of greatest prominence, as capital of Magadha during the Buddha's lifetime (chronology convention)

location.label: Rājagṛha (modern Rajgir, Bihar, India) — named directly as the entry's subject

note: Rājagṛha. Capital of the kingdom of Magadha under King Bimbisāra, the Buddha's first royal patron, and — together with Śrāvastī — one of the two most important centers of the Buddha's ministry. Site of the Veṇuvanavihāra ("Bamboo Grove Monastery") where the Buddha spent several rains retreats, of Vulture Peak where the Prajñāpāramitā sūtras were said to be delivered, and of the first Buddhist council held immediately after the Buddha's death. Also where the great monastic university of Nālandā later arose on its outskirts — though by the time the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang visited in the seventh century CE, the city itself lay in ruins.

time.basis: founding activity of Kuiji, "traditionally regarded as the first Faxiang patriarch" (632–682), building on Xuanzang's return from India

location.label: China (Chang'an placeholder — base of Xuanzang and Kuiji's translation activity)

note: Faxiang zong. ("Dharma Characteristics School.") The most important of three Chinese Yogācāra strands, built on Xuanzang's Chinese translation of the Cheng weishi lun and systematized by his disciple Kuiji, the school's first patriarch. Its own preferred self-designation was "Consciousness-Only School"; the pejorative "Faxiang" name came from rivals. Transmitted to Korea, where the monk Wŏnch'ŭk's rival interpretive lineage sparked intense controversy with Kuiji's own line, and to Japan as Hossōshū, where it survived but never rivaled Tendai or Shingon in influence — known above all for its exhaustive hundred-factor taxonomy of all possible phenomena.

time.basis: "(1158–1210)", given directly

location.label: Kaesŏng, Korea (birthplace region, named directly in the entry)

note: Pojo Chinul. (1158–1210.) The premier Sŏn master of the Koryŏ dynasty, alongside Wŏnhyo one of the two most influential monks in Korean Buddhist history, who preferred his own cognomen "Oxherder." After ordination and a series of awakening experiences reading the Platform Sūtra, Li Tongxuan's Huayan commentary, and the recorded sayings of Chan master Dahui Zonggao, he founded the Samādhi and Prajñā Retreat Society, later renamed Susŏnsa. Renowned for reconciling scriptural study with Sŏn practice through a scheme of sudden awakening followed by gradual cultivation, and for introducing "questioning meditation" (kanhwa Sŏn) into Korea, where it has held pride of place ever since.

Śraddhā. ("Faith" or "confidence.") Ranges from mental clarity and positive disposition toward the Buddha to conviction in the path's efficacy to active commitment to follow it — with real cognitive, conative, and affective dimensions, the latter epitomized by the disciple Vakkali's rapturous devotion. Listed first among both the wholesome mental factors and the five spiritual faculties, faith is deliberately kept in tension with wisdom via mindfulness: unchecked faith risks blind acceptance, unchecked wisdom risks corrosive skepticism. Its four proper objects are karmic cause-and-effect, the conditioned nature of the world, the three jewels, and the prospect of nirvāṇa itself.

Anuttarayogatantra. ("Unsurpassed yoga tantra.") The highest of four tantra classes in the Indo-Tibetan system, encompassing texts such as the Guhyasamājatantra, Hevajratantra, and Cakrasaṃvaratantra, and split into "mother" tantras emphasizing wisdom and "father" tantras emphasizing method and the illusory body. Tibetan exegetes hold that buddhahood can be achieved only through this class of practice, which divides into a generation stage and a completion stage, the latter typically incorporating sexual yoga. The historically latest of these texts, the Kālacakratantra — which alludes to Muslim invaders in India — provoked real disagreement among Tibetan scholars over whether it even counts as a Buddhist tantra at all.

time.basis: "(c. 320–c. 390 CE)", given directly

location.label: Puruṣapura, modern Peshawar, Pakistan (birthplace, named directly)

note: Asaṅga. (c. 320–c. 390 CE.) Indian scholar traditionally credited as a founder of the Yogācāra school, born to a brāhmaṇa family in Peshawar and originally trained under Sarvāstivāda teachers before converting to the Mahāyāna and, by tradition, converting his own younger brother Vasubandhu in turn. Said to have received Yogācāra teachings directly from the future buddha Maitreya after twelve years of meditation retreat — teachings modern scholars debate as possibly the work of a historical Maitreyanātha rather than a literal revelation. Author of the Abhidharmasamuccaya and Mahāyānasaṃgraha and the vast Yogācārabhūmiśāstra, whose influence on Yogācāra philosophy, tathāgatagarbha thought, and Buddhist practice across India, Tibet, and East Asia is virtually unmatched in breadth.

Dhāraṇī. ("Mnemonic device," "code" — from √dhṛ, "to hold.") A verbal formula, meaningful or not, believed to encapsulate and let its user retain the fuller doctrine it condenses. The sixth-century Chinese exegete Jingying Huiyuan classified dhāraṇī into four types tied to teachings, meaning, spells, and acquiescence, the first two functioning essentially as memory codes for Buddhist doctrine. In Prajñāpāramitā literature a single letter of the alphabet could serve as a dhāraṇī, standing in for an entire technical term.

time.basis: "Chinese translation made by Gautama Saṃghadeva between 397 and 398"

note: Madhyamāgama. ("Medium [Length] Scriptures.") The Sanskrit sūtra collection corresponding to, but substantially larger than, the Pāli Majjhimanikāya — no longer extant in an Indic language but preserved whole in a Chinese translation completed in 397–398, with scattered Sanskrit fragments recovered at Turfan. Ascribed to the Sarvāstivāda school on the strength of those surviving fragments, its 222 sūtras overlap heavily not just with the Majjhimanikāya but with suttas scattered across all four other Pāli nikāyas.

time.basis: attributed to Maitreyanātha, "c. 350 CE"

note: Abhisamayālaṃkāra. ("Ornament of Realization.") A Mahāyāna scholastic treatise attributed to Maitreyanātha, mapping the vast Perfection of Wisdom in Twenty-Five Thousand Lines onto the stages of the Buddhist path via eight categories of realization — three wisdoms accessible to any adept, four stages of the path proper, and a final realization of the buddha-body. Regarded as the "hidden teaching" underlying the prajñāpāramitā sūtras, it went largely unnoticed in East Asia but became central to Tibetan monastic curricula, especially the Dge lugs sect, which treats it as the definitive account of the path's stages, and spawned over twenty Indian commentaries plus a long Tibetan exegetical tradition.

Apocrypha. A term borrowed from Judeo-Christian scholarship for indigenous sūtras composed outside India but modeled on translated Indian scripture — some genuinely revelatory, many deliberately forged under the Buddha's name to gain authority. Chinese bibliographers policed the canon by demanding proof a text had actually arrived from "Outer Regions" India or Central Asia, branding unverifiable texts "suspect" or outright "spurious"; in Tibet, comparable treasure texts drew authority instead from claimed revelatory discovery. In one of Buddhism's stranger ironies, some of East Asia's most influential scriptures — the Humane Kings Sūtra, the Awakening of Faith — turned out to be exactly this kind of homegrown apocrypha, not genuine imports at all.

time.basis: site of Śākyamuni's enlightenment; chronology convention

location.label: Bodhgayā, Bihar, India (named directly as the entry's subject)

note: Bodhgayā. The most sacred site in the Buddhist world, where Śākyamuni became a buddha meditating beneath the Bodhi tree — and, by tradition, where every buddha of this world system does the same, each under his own species of tree. One of the four great pilgrimage sites sanctioned by the Buddha himself, it drew Aśoka's patronage and a shrine as early as the third century BCE, flourished under Gupta and Pāla support, then fell into ruin after the Muslim invasions of the thirteenth century. Restored beginning in 1880 under British administration and championed by Anagārika Dharmapāla's Mahābodhi Society, the Mahābodhi Temple now anchors a cluster of national monasteries built by Buddhist countries from Bhutan to Vietnam, and was named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2002.

Jñāna. ("Gnosis," "knowledge," or "understanding.") A cognitive grasp of an object's specific nature, following perception and related to but more general than perfected wisdom (prajñā) — jñāna covers the ordinary knowledge proper to a śrāvaka, pratyekabuddha, or buddha alike. Yogācāra maps four or five such knowledges onto transformations of the eight consciousnesses upon enlightenment: mirror-like knowledge, the knowledge of equality, discerning knowledge, the knowledge that one's task is done, and the knowledge of the dharma-realm's true nature — each in turn personified as one of the five buddha-families.

time.basis: "(c. 740–795)", given directly

location.label: Bsam yas, Tibet (site of the famous debate central to this entry, and where he later died)

note: Kamalaśīla. (c. 740–795.) A leading late Indian Madhyamaka author and disciple of Śāntarakṣita, invited to Tibet to debate the Chinese Chan monk Heshang Moheyan after his teacher's death — the celebrated Bsam yas debate, in which the Tibetan king judged Kamalaśīla's gradual path victorious and banished the Chinese faction (Chinese sources tell it the other way). His three Bhāvanākrama treatises, composed in response, set out a step-by-step cultivation of bodhicitta, calmness, and insight toward buddhahood, sharply opposed to Chan's sudden-awakening model. His independent masterwork, the Madhyamakāloka, argues that Yogācāra's mind-only doctrine is merely a provisional teaching en route to the Madhyamaka view — and Kamalaśīla is said to have been assassinated in Tibet by partisans of the Chinese side he had defeated.

time.basis: "(344–409/413)", given directly

location.label: Kucha (birthplace and royal-family connection, named directly)

note: Kumārajīva. (344–409/413.) The single most influential translator of Buddhist texts into Chinese, born into the royal family of the Central Asian kingdom of Kucha, converted from Sarvāstivāda to Mahāyāna at Kashgar, then held hostage for eighteen years by Chinese warlords — time he used to master fluent Chinese. Installed at Chang'an in 402 to head an imperial translation bureau, he produced around seventy-four texts in 384 rolls, including the Lotus Sūtra, Vimalakīrtinirdeśa, Diamond Sūtra, and Nāgārjuna's Root Verses — translations so clear and readable that they remain, to this day, the versions still read across East Asia wherever a rival translation exists.

Rūpa. ("Body," "form," or "materiality.") Broadly, whatever has shape and is composed of matter — the objects of the five physical senses and the first of the five aggregates, covering all of a person's physical constituents. Narrowly, just the colors and shapes seen by visual consciousness specifically, the sense in which rūpa counts among the twelve sense-fields and eighteen elements. In the compound "name and form," rūpa denotes the entire physical body set against the four mental aggregates grouped under "name" — and in some Mahāyāna sūtras, since form heads every standard list of factors, "form and so on" becomes shorthand for the emptiness of all dharmas whatsoever.

time.basis: "committed to writing in Sri Lanka at the end of the first century BCE"

location.label: Sri Lanka (Anurādhapura placeholder — where the Pāli canon was first committed to writing)

note: Sūtrapiṭaka. ("Basket of discourses.") One of the three divisions of the canon, a sprawling collection of thousands of texts attributed to the Buddha or spoken with his sanction. The Pāli version splits into five groups running from thirty-four long discourses to nearly ten thousand brief numerically-organized texts, preserved orally for centuries before being committed to writing in Sri Lanka at the end of the first century BCE; other Indian schools' Chinese and Tibetan translations use "āgama" instead of "nikāya" for the same groupings, with real differences in content despite the parallel titles.

time.basis: set forth in "the Buddha's first sermon after his enlightenment"; chronology convention

note: Āryāṣṭāṅgamārga. ("Noble eightfold path.") The fourth noble truth, first set out in the Buddha's inaugural sermon as a middle way between asceticism and indulgence: right view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness, and concentration. Often collapsed into the simpler "three trainings" of morality, concentration, and wisdom, and in later formulations treated less as a behavioral prescription than as eight qualities already present in a mind that has understood nirvāṇa. A Mahāyāna reading folds it into the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, reached only after the path of vision has already occurred.

Brahmā. An Indian divinity absorbed into the Buddhist pantheon as a protector of the teachings and king of the Brahmā-realm. In the form Sahāṃpati, he plays a pivotal role just after the Buddha's enlightenment: sensing the newly awakened Buddha's doubt about whether anyone could grasp his insight, Brahmā descends and persuades him that some people have "little dust in their eyes" and could understand — prompting the first sermon. Buddhaghosa insists the compassionate Buddha never truly hesitated, but that being entreated by so revered a god lent his mission needed credibility; depicted with four faces and four arms, Brahmā later fuses in various traditions with bodhisattvas like Avalokiteśvara and Tibetan protector deities.

time.basis: "(c. 600–650)", given directly

location.label: South India (general placeholder — entry states only "he was from south India", no city named)

note: Candrakīrti. (c. 600–650.) A Madhyamaka master, probably a monk of Nālandā, whose commentaries on Nāgārjuna and Āryadeva later defined what Tibetan scholars would retrospectively call the Prāsaṅgika branch of Madhyamaka. In his Prasannapadā he argues that Madhyamaka should refute rivals only through drawing out absurd consequences, never through autonomous syllogisms — the very distinction Tibetans used to split Madhyamaka into Svātantrika and Prāsaṅgika camps. Barely read in the centuries after his death and untranslated into Chinese until the 1940s, his Madhyamakāvatāra was revived in eleventh-century Kashmir and went on to become the single most important Madhyamaka text studied in Tibet, a core text of the Dge lugs curriculum.

time.basis: founder Saichō's dates, "(767–822)", who "laid the doctrinal and institutional foundations"

location.label: Mt. Hiei / Enryakuji, Japan (the school's institutional base, named directly)

note: Tendaishū. The Japanese counterpart of Chinese Tiantai, founded on the doctrinal and institutional groundwork laid by the pilgrim-monk Saichō, centered like its parent tradition on the Lotus Sūtra and Zhiyi's commentaries, and later distinctive for its doctrine of original enlightenment. Its Mt. Hiei headquarters, Enryakuji, became both a major religious center and a political force at the Kyōto court — and, crucially, an incubator: Genshin, Hōnen, Shinran, Dōgen, and Nichiren, founders of Japan's later Kamakura schools, all trained there first. Rivalry with Kūkai's Shingon esoteric teachings pushed Tendai to absorb its own esoteric practices (Taimitsu), securing its dominance through the medieval and Tokugawa periods.

Akuśala. ("Unwholesome" or "unvirtuous.") Physical, verbal, and mental actions — commonly enumerated as ten — driven by greed, hatred, or delusion, that lead to unfavorable rebirths as hell denizens, hungry ghosts, animals, or demigods. The ten split into three bodily misdeeds (killing, stealing, sexual misconduct), four verbal (lying, slander, harsh speech, idle chatter), and three mental (covetousness, ill will, wrong views) — a comprehensive catalogue of exactly what generates bad karma.

Avidyā. ("Ignorance.") The root cause of suffering and the first link in the twelvefold chain of dependent origination, sustaining the entire cycle of rebirth. Closely related to but distinguished from generic "delusion" (moha): Asaṅga's analogy has twilight (delusion) fall over a coiled rope (reality), which someone then wrongly conceives to be a snake — that active misconstruction is avidyā. Under its influence, beings mistake nonself for self and impermanence for permanence; it is progressively weakened at each stage of the noble path and only fully eliminated at arhatship.

Dāna. ("Giving" or "generosity.") The foundational lay virtue, prized for weaning practitioners from attachment to possessions while materially sustaining the saṃgha — exemplified in legend by Prince Viśvantara, who gave away his kingdom, his wife, and his children. Generates merit accruing to both this life and future ones, and is ranked among three types by object (material goods, freedom from fear, or the dharma itself, held to be the greatest gift of all) and heads both the Mahāyāna's six perfections and the Pāli tradition's ten. Someone incapable of even minimal generosity is, in some schools, considered to have severed their wholesome roots entirely.

time.basis: "widely assumed to be an indigenous Chinese text... composed in the sixth century"

note: Dasheng qixin lun. ("Awakening of Faith According to the Mahāyāna.") A Chinese treatise nominally attributed to the Indian Aśvaghoṣa but now generally regarded as an indigenous Chinese apocryphon, seeking to reconcile two seemingly incompatible Mahāyāna doctrines: tathāgatagarbha (innate enlightenment) and ālayavijñāna (a storehouse consciousness that explains why enlightened minds still become deluded). Its solution splits the mind into "true thusness" and "production-and-cessation" aspects, permanently grounded in each other, so the mind is simultaneously always enlightened and always in need of actualizing that enlightenment through practice. One of the most influential texts in all of East Asian Buddhism, it later drew major commentaries from Wŏnhyo, Fazang, and Jingying Huiyuan.

time.basis: identifies the family name of Śākyamuni Buddha; chronology convention

location.label: Lumbini area, southern Nepal (homeland of the Śākya tribe, named directly)

note: Gautama. The clan name of the historical Buddha — Śākya was his tribe, Gautama his family or clan, and Siddhārtha his given name. "Gotama" ("Excellent Cow") was a common brāhmaṇa lineage name in ancient India, also borne by a poet of the Ṛg Veda, unrelated to the Buddha's own family beyond the shared name. Pāli literature typically calls him Gotama Buddha; Mahāyāna sources prefer Śākyamuni.

time.basis: period of use during the Buddha's ministry; he "passed nineteen rains retreats there"; chronology convention

location.label: near Śrāvastī (named directly)

note: Jetavana. ("Prince Jeta's Grove.") A park outside Śrāvastī donated to the Buddha by the banker Anāthapiṇḍada, who purchased it from the reluctant Prince Jeta by literally covering its grounds in gold coins — Jeta, impressed, donated the entrance himself. The Buddha's favorite residence, where he is said to have spent nineteen rains retreats in a chamber called the "perfumed chamber," alternating with another monastery built nearby by the laywoman Viśākhā. A later, unrelated monastery at Anurādhapura in Sri Lanka also bears the name Jetavana, built after a schism with the Mahāvihāra sect.

time.basis: the night of Gautama's enlightenment; chronology convention

location.label: Bodhgayā, Bihar, India (site of the current Bodhi tree, named directly)

note: Bodhi tree. The tree species beneath which each buddha in turn attains enlightenment — a pipal, or fig tree, in Gautama's case, rooted at the "diamond seat" in Bodhgayā. Repeatedly destroyed by hostile kings, including Saśāṅka of Bengal in the seventh century, and replanted from cuttings taken as far as Sri Lanka in the third century BCE — a lineage of clippings that has since spread the original tree's descendants to Buddhist sites worldwide. Its large seeds are commonly strung into Buddhist prayer rosaries.

time.basis: "legend has it that in 366 CE" the first cave was excavated there

location.label: Dunhuang, Gansu, China (named directly as the entry's subject)

note: Dunhuang. A garrison oasis town on the Silk Road's edge, today famous for the nearby Mogao and Qianfo Dong cave complexes, whose excavation legend holds began in 366 CE with a monk's vision of a thousand golden buddhas and continued for nearly a thousand years. Sealed inside a side chamber, Cave 17, was a hoard of manuscripts and silk paintings discovered in the early twentieth century — tens of thousands of texts in over a dozen languages, including the world's earliest dated printed book, an 868 CE copy of the Diamond Sūtra, making the find one of history's richest paper archives.

time.basis: "(638–713)", given directly

location.label: Xinzhou, Guangdong, China (birthplace, named directly)

note: Huineng. (638–713.) The legendary sixth and final patriarch of the Chan school, whose historical life is barely documented but whose hagiography in the Platform Sūtra is foundational to Chan literature. An illiterate woodcutter converted on hearing the Diamond Sūtra recited, he reportedly won a poetry contest against the learned monk Shenxiu with a verse on emptiness so sharp the fifth patriarch Hongren secretly transmitted Bodhidharma's robe and bowl to him overnight, then sent him into hiding. Settled at Baolinsi on Caoxishan, he is claimed as founder of Chan's "Southern school" of sudden awakening, and virtually every later Chan lineage traces its pedigree back to him.

time.basis: founder Shinran's dates, "(1173–1262)"

location.label: Kyōto, Japan (Honganji, the school's central monastery)

note: Jōdo Shinshū. ("True Pure Land school.") The tradition founded on the teachings of Shinran, distinguished from earlier Jōdoshū by permitting clergy to marry and eat meat, and by teaching complete reliance on Amitābha's grace rather than one's own effort — Shinran held that a single sincere invocation of Amitābha's name sufficed, against rivals who urged continuous recitation. Consolidated under the monastery Honganji, particularly through Rennyo's leadership in the fifteenth century, before splitting into the Nishi and Higashi Honganji branches that still anchor the tradition's two main lineages today.

Saṃyojana. ("Fetter.") Ten defilements binding beings to rebirth, eliminated in stages as one advances through the noble path: the first three (self-view, doubt, attachment to rites) vanish at stream-entry; craving for sensuality and malice weaken at once-returning; craving for existence in the realms of form and formlessness, pride, restlessness, and ignorance persist until arhatship finally dissolves them all. A precise checklist, in other words, of exactly what separates each stage of awakening from the next.

time.basis: founder Kūkai's dates, "(774–835)"

location.label: Kōyasan, Japan (major center Kūkai established, named directly)

note: Shingonshū. ("True Word School.") Japan's major esoteric Buddhist tradition, built by the monk Kūkai around ritual access to the cosmic buddha Mahāvairocana through maṇḍala visualization, mantra recitation, and mudrā — techniques said to let a practitioner achieve buddhahood in this very body. Kūkai's political skill secured him control of ordination platforms at Nara and Kyōto and imperial grants of Tōji and Mt. Kōya, the latter surviving Oda Nobunaga's destruction of rival Buddhist centers by successfully appealing to Toyotomi Hideyoshi. Suppressed during the Meiji persecution, its scattered lineages later reunified under the single Shingonshū banner.

Upāya. ("Method" or "stratagem.") One of the two essential components of the bodhisattva path alongside wisdom — the active deeds performed on behalf of all beings, said to fructify as a buddha's form-body just as wisdom fructifies as the dharma-body. In tantra, method is gendered male against wisdom's female, and the superiority of the esoteric vajrayāna over the exoteric path is explained by the sheer sophistication of its methods compared to those the sūtras offer.

Āryapudgala. ("Noble person.") An enlightened being who has reached at least the path of vision, classed in a standard fourfold hierarchy — stream-enterer, once-returner, nonreturner, arhat — each further split into a "candidate" and "fruition" stage for eight grades total. Advancing through these ranks means progressively shedding the ten fetters that bind beings to rebirth: self-view, doubt, and ritualism first, then sensual craving and malice, and finally craving for the higher realms, pride, restlessness, and ignorance, eliminated completely only at arhatship.

time.basis: the tantra "probably appeared toward the end of the eighth century"

note: Cakrasaṃvaratantra. ("Binding of the Wheel Tantra.") A major anuttarayogatantra centered on the deity Heruka and his consort Vajravārāhī, emerging from a literature of female yoginī and ḍākinī divinities and showing close ties — skull imagery, cremation-ground settings — to Śaiva Kāpālika practice, whether through direct appropriation or a shared wandering-siddha milieu. Focused overwhelmingly on ritual technique for attaining mundane powers like flight and invisibility rather than doctrine, it was transmitted to Tibet through the siddha Nāropa and remains important across the Sa skya, Bka' brgyud, and Dge lugs sects.

Gati. ("Destiny" or "bourne.") The five or six places within saṃsāra where rebirth occurs, ranked from hell denizens through hungry ghosts, animals, humans, demigods, and divinities, spanning all three cosmological realms. The bottom three destinies are called the "evil bournes," dominated by suffering from past unwholesome deeds; divine realms are dominated by pleasure from virtuous ones — but the human destiny alone offers the balanced mix of suffering and happiness that makes it, paradoxically, the ideal condition for recognizing impermanence and pursuing liberation.

time.basis: contemporary of the Buddha, presiding over the first council after the Buddha's death; no specific dates given, chronology convention used

location.label: Magadha (general placeholder — birthplace, named directly)

note: Mahākāśyapa. Foremost among the Buddha's disciples in ascetic practice, born Pipphali to a brāhmaṇa family in Magadha, who married only reluctantly and, with his equally renunciation-minded wife Bhaddā, abandoned a shared estate after both were separately moved to pity by insects killed in ordinary farm work. Ordained on the road to Rājagṛha, he exchanged robes with the Buddha himself — a gesture read as marking him successor — and presided over the first Buddhist council after the Buddha's death, sharply interrogating Ānanda over his conduct. Revered in Chan tradition as the first patriarch, the sole disciple who understood the Buddha's silent "flower sermon" and thus received the first mind-to-mind transmission.

time.basis: founded by King Śakrāditya, "sometimes identified as the fifth-century ruler Kumāragupta I (r. 415–455)"

location.label: Nālandā, Bihar, India (named directly as the entry's subject)

note: Nālandā. India's most renowned Buddhist monastic university, founded near Rājagṛha under Gupta patronage and flourishing from the sixth to twelfth centuries CE, hosting as many as ten thousand students and fifteen hundred teachers at its height, supported by the tax revenue of a hundred neighboring villages. Nearly every major figure of late Indian Mahāyāna and Madhyamaka philosophy — Asaṅga, Vasubandhu, Dharmakīrti, Candrakīrti, Śāntideva — is said to have taught or studied there, and its curriculum spanned Buddhist philosophy alongside Hindu thought, mathematics, and medicine. Sacked by Turkic troops in 1192, its library reportedly smoldered for months, and the institution never recovered.

Smṛti. ("Mindfulness" or "memory.") The ability to stay focused on a chosen object without forgetting or drifting, classed by Sarvāstivāda abhidharma among five "determinative" mental factors that together aid the mind in fixing on its object. Uniquely among the five spiritual faculties, mindfulness can never be excessive — it is precisely what keeps faith from collapsing into blind belief, wisdom from curdling into skepticism, and effort from swinging between restlessness and sloth. As the seventh element of the noble eightfold path and the first of the seven factors of enlightenment, it underlies virtually every account of Buddhist meditative training.

time.basis: "(982–1054)", given directly

location.label: Bangladesh (general placeholder — born "into a royal family in what is today Bangladesh")

note: Atiśa Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna. (982–1054.) Bengali-born monk revered as the leading figure of Buddhism's later dissemination in Tibet, ordained at twenty-nine after years as a married tantric practitioner, and trained at Nālandā, Vikramaśīla, and other great North Indian monasteries before studying bodhicitta for twelve years under a teacher in Sumatra. Invited to Tibet in 1042 by kings seeking to correct corrupted practice, he composed the Bodhipathapradīpa ("Lamp for the Path to Enlightenment") at Tho ling monastery — the founding text of the entire lam rim "stages of the path" genre — before settling near Lhasa, where he died and his disciples founded the Bka' gdams sect in his name.

Dharmapāla. ("Protector of the dharma.") Wrathful divinities, often originally local deities converted into Buddhist service, tasked with defending the teachings and guarding practitioners from harm. Tibetan tradition credits Padmasambhava with instituting their worship in the early eighth century by subduing hostile local spirits along his route into Tibet and sparing only those who agreed to become protectors. Classed as either "mundane" — worldly beings who protect the dharma — or "supramundane" — already-enlightened beings appearing in wrathful guise for the same purpose, with the eight classes of nonhuman beings (nāgas, yakṣas, and the like) sometimes listed among them.

time.basis: "(530–561)", given directly

location.label: Nālandā, India (where he became chief instructor, the entry's central setting)

note: Dharmapāla. (530–561.) One of India's ten great Yogācāra philosophers, born to a South Indian government minister's family, who fled his own wedding to become a monk and rose, despite his youth, to chief instructor at Nālandā. His interpretation of consciousness as always split into a "seeing part" and a "seen part" — against rivals who saw that split as purely imaginary — became orthodox doctrine in China after Xuanzang studied it under Dharmapāla's disciple Śīlabhadra and carried the lineage home, where it shaped the entire Chinese Faxiang school. He died at twenty-nine, having retired to Asaṃbodhi monastery.

time.basis: "(643–712)", given directly

location.label: Chang'an, China (site of his major translation and imperial-court activity)

note: Fazang. (643–712.) Tang-dynasty monk of Sogdian immigrant descent, third-generation patriarch of the Huayan zong and its de facto founder, who studied under Zhiyan and assisted in retranslating the Avataṃsakasūtra and Laṅkāvatārasūtra. A favorite lecturer of Empress Wu Zetian on dependent origination, he systematized his teacher's vision of the Avataṃsakasūtra using indigenous Chinese concepts drawn partly from the Dasheng qixin lun, effectively giving Huayan philosophy its lasting doctrinal vocabulary. His close friendship with the Korean monk Ŭisang helped carry Huayan teaching to Korea and, through further transmission, to Japan as Kegon.

Kanhua Chan. ("Chan of investigating the topic of inquiry.") A meditative technique systematized by the Song-dynasty master Dahui Zonggao out of the growing practice of studying old "public case" anecdotes (gong'an), using a single fragment — a "topic of inquiry" or huatou — as an object of concentrated doubt rather than intellectual puzzle-solving. The most famous example is Zhaozhou's one-word answer "no" to whether a dog has buddha-nature; sustained investigation builds an intensifying doubt that eventually "explodes," dissolving conceptual thought and the boundary between self and other. Transmitted to Korea by Pojo Chinul as kanhwa Sŏn, where it remains the dominant contemplative method, and popularized in Japanese Rinzai Zen through Hakuin Ekaku's elaborate kōan curriculum.

Kuśala. ("Wholesome" or "virtuous.") Actions of body, speech, and mind — enumerated as ten — free of greed, hatred, or delusion, that lead to favorable rebirths as humans or divinities. The ten wholesome courses invert their unwholesome counterparts point for point: sustaining life instead of killing, giving instead of stealing, truthful and harmonious speech instead of lying and slander, and unselfishness, goodwill, and right views in place of their opposites.

Lobha. ("Craving" or "greed.") One of Buddhism's most pervasive defilements, appearing on nearly every standard list of afflictions and counted among the core mental factors in every major abhidharma system. Arises when sensory contact occurs without proper introspection, and can target virtually anything — sensual pleasure, possessions, loved ones, fame, even one's own future existence or nonexistence — functioning, per the āgamas, as a self-imposed yoking of mind to object that leaves the mind "mired" and "burdened" by desire.

Nāraka. ("Hell denizen.") The lowest of the six rebirth destinies, inhabiting an elaborate cosmography of eight burning hot hells and eight freezing cold hells beneath the earth, each successively more agonizing, plus four neighboring hells of embers, corpses, razors, and a river impossible to ford. Crucially, Buddhist hells are temporary places of rebirth, not eternal damnation — however long a sentence, once a hell denizen's karmic lifespan expires, rebirth continues elsewhere, a point vividly illustrated in Chinese cave art showing tormented sinners finally served a cup of tea before moving on.

Bodhicittotpāda. ("Generating the aspiration for enlightenment.") The pivotal moment marking entry into the Mahāyāna and the start of the bodhisattva path, triggered by any of several conditions across different texts — witnessing a miracle, hearing a teaching on enlightenment, fearing the dharma's decline, or simply seeing beings suffer. Tsong kha pa taught two techniques for cultivating it: a "seven cause and effect" sequence tracing back to Atiśa, built on recognizing all beings as having once been one's mother, and an "equalizing self and other" method from Śāntideva, built on the shared, symmetrical wish for happiness. Mahāyāna texts generally hold that three full "incalculable eons" of practice follow this initial aspiration before buddhahood is reached.

time.basis: attributed to Maitreya/Asaṅga, "c. fourth century CE"

note: Bodhisattvabhūmi. ("The Bodhisattva Stages.") A Yogācāra treatise on the entire bodhisattva vocation, attributed to Asaṅga, laying out a seven-stage path correlated with thirteen "abodes" — a scheme that developed independently of, and awkwardly maps onto, the ten-stage path of the Daśabhūmikasūtra. Its chapter on precepts is foundational for Mahāyāna monastic ethics, organizing bodhisattva vows into three sets — restraint from wrongdoing, active cultivation of virtue, and direct service to other beings — a framework later echoed in the Chinese apocryphal Fanwang jing and, in Tibet, forming a core text of the Bka' gdams sect.

Buddhakṣetra. ("Buddha field.") The domain belonging to a specific buddha, produced through his accumulated merit, knowledge, and personal vow upon enlightenment. Impure buddha-fields are ordinary world systems where unenlightened beings, including animals and hell denizens, still suffer; pure buddha-fields — "pure lands" like Sukhāvatī or Abhirati — exclude the unfortunate rebirth realms entirely, so that even the birds singing there are buddha-emanations rather than reborn creatures. In the Vimalakīrtinirdeśa, the Buddha reveals that Śākyamuni's own world only appears impure to inspire disciples toward liberation — touching the earth with his toe instantly transforms it into a pure field.

Cakra. ("Wheel.") A wide-ranging Buddhist symbol, from the dharma-wheel the Buddha "turned" in his first sermon to the thousand-spoked wheel marking a buddha's or universal emperor's palms and soles, to the "wheel of existence" depicting saṃsāra's six realms ringed by the links of dependent origination. In tantric physiology, cakra also names energy centers strung along a central channel running the length of the body, visualized as lotus blossoms where the flanking left and right channels form knots — much tantric practice aims at loosening these knots to let vital energies flow freely into the center.

Jātaka. ("Birth" or "nativity.") Narratives of a buddha's previous lives, one of the classical genres of Buddhist scripture and, at 547 stories in the Pāli collection alone, among the most popular forms of Buddhist literature — especially with the laity, thanks to their entertaining plots and moral payoff. A typical tale has the Buddha recount a past-life story demonstrating some virtue, then identify the story's characters as past incarnations of people in his present audience, his rival Devadatta included. Many plots trace back to shared Indian folklore also found in Hindu and Jaina literature, simply repurposed with a Buddhist frame.

Moha. ("Delusion" or "confusion.") A synonym for ignorance denoting basic confusion about the true nature of the person and the world, counted among the "three poisons" alongside greed and hatred and, in Sarvāstivāda abhidharma, first among six fundamental afflictions tainting every defiled thought. Its opposite, nondelusion, is one of the eleven wholesome factors in the Yogācāra hundred-dharma list — delusion and clarity treated as the two poles around which a mind's entire moral character turns.

Nāga. Serpent-bodied beings — human-headed and torsoed but tailed and hooded like a cobra — said to inhabit an underwater kingdom of treasure and magnificent palaces, appearing in Buddhist literature as both allies and adversaries. A nāga princess's instant transformation into a buddha in the Lotus Sūtra is cited as proof that women can attain enlightenment; the nāga Mucilinda sheltered the newly enlightened Buddha from a storm; and Nāgārjuna is said to have recovered the massive Perfection of Wisdom in One Hundred Thousand Lines from safekeeping among the nāgas at the bottom of the sea.

time.basis: founder Dōgen Kigen's dates, "(1200–1253)"

location.label: Eiheiji, Echizen (Fukui), Japan (the monastery Dōgen founded as the tradition's center)

note: Sōtōshū. One of Japanese Zen's three major branches, tracing its lineage through Dōgen Kigen, who brought the Chinese Caodong line back from China in 1227 and, driven out of Kyōto by rival Tendai and Rinzai institutions, founded Eiheiji in rural Echizen instead. Revitalized by "second patriarch" Keizan Jōkin, who folded local kami worship into Sōtō practice and founded the second head monastery, Sōjiji, the school expanded through the medieval period by serving rural communities with bridges, irrigation, and funerals largely neglected by court Buddhism. Its central practice, "just sitting" (shikan taza), treats meditation itself as the direct manifestation of buddhahood rather than a means toward it, and the school remains one of Japan's largest, with over fourteen thousand temples today.

time.basis: śramaṇa movements "derive from historical persons who all flourished around the sixth century BCE"

note: Śramaṇa. ("Renunciant" or "mendicant.") A category of itinerant ancient Indian religious founded by historical figures flourishing around the sixth century BCE, challenging Brahmanical orthodoxy and its Vedic ritual authority — Buddhism and Jainism among them. Six rival śramaṇa teachers are named in early Buddhist texts, each championing a different position (antinomianism, fatalism, materialism, atomism, agnosticism, and the Jaina teacher Mahāvīra's asceticism), all dismissed by the Buddha as "heterodox." In Buddhism the term also broadens generically to mean any monk, including the Buddha himself, distinguished carefully from śrāmaṇera, a mere novice.

time.basis: "(538–597)", given directly

location.label: Mt. Tiantai, Zhejiang, China (the mountain and monastery from which the school he founded takes its name)

note: Tiantai Zhiyi. (538–597.) De facto founder of the Tiantai zong, orphaned by wartime turmoil and ordained at eighteen, who studied under Nanyue Huisi before retiring to Mt. Tiantai for eleven years of intensive meditative practice and writing. His three great commentaries — the Fahua xuanyi, Fahua wenju, and Mohe zhiguan, the latter composed after returning to lecture at the invitation of Sui royalty — systematized Lotus Sūtra doctrine and meditation into the framework that has defined Tiantai (and Japanese Tendai) ever since, earning him the imperial title "Great Master Zhizhe."

Abhijñā. ("Superknowledges.") Six supranormal powers arising as by-products of deep meditation: magical abilities like passing through walls, clairvoyance, clairaudience, memory of one's own past lives, telepathic knowledge of others' minds, and — alone among the six — the supramundane knowledge of the extinction of one's own corrupting influences. The first five are attainable through sheer meditative refinement and carry no guarantee of wisdom; only the sixth, reached through insight into reality itself, marks genuine liberation.

time.basis: "origins... traced back to the founding of Rwa sgreng monastery in 1056"

location.label: Rwa sgreng (Reting) monastery, Tibet (named directly as the sect's founding site)

note: Bka' gdams. An early Tibetan Buddhist sect founded at Rwa sgreng monastery in 1056 by Atiśa's chief disciple and interpreter, and organized around three lineages of transmission — authoritative treatises, essential instruction, and oral instruction — each emphasizing a different mode of study. Known for strict discipline but also, through its Gsang phu ne'u thog branch, for rigorous scholarship in logic and epistemology, and for originating the influential "stages of teaching" genre based on Atiśa's own Bodhipathapradīpa. The sect eventually dissolved into the rising Dge lugs sect, whose founder Tsong kha pa revered Atiśa as the ideal teacher and whose early followers were even known as the "new Bka' gdams pa."

time.basis: founder Mahāvīra's death date, "(d. c. 488 BCE)"

location.label: Magadha (general placeholder — the region of Mahāvīra's activity, contemporary with the Buddha)

note: Jaina. ("Followers of the Victor.") One of the major non-Buddhist śramaṇa movements of ancient India, founded in the tradition of Mahāvīra, a direct contemporary of the Buddha, and the śramaṇa group closest to Buddhism in belief and practice — close enough that the Buddha regularly used Jaina teachings as a foil for his own. Jainas share a doctrine of karman with Buddhism but treat it as an actual physical substance binding the soul, requiring rigorous bodily purification through a five-vow moral code that closely parallels Buddhism's own five precepts.

time.basis: "probably composed around the last half of the first-century BCE"

note: Jñānaprasthāna. ("Foundations of Knowledge.") The central canonical text of Sarvāstivāda abhidharma, attributed to Kātyāyanīputra, around which the school's six other treatises are organized as supporting "feet." Its systematic eight-section structure — covering afflictions, knowledge, karma, elements, faculties, meditative absorption, and vision — set out doctrines that came to define mature Sarvāstivāda, including the claim that factors exist across all three time periods, and later drew a massive commentary, the Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā, whose adherents named themselves "Vaibhāṣika" after it. Distinctively focused on advanced stages of the path rather than the preliminary ethical training emphasized in Pāli abhidhamma.

time.basis: founder Hōnen's dates, "(1133–1212)"

location.label: Kyōto, Japan (Chion'in, built at Hōnen's grave site and the branch's eventual headquarters)

note: Jōdoshū. ("Pure Land school.") The first indigenous Japanese Buddhist school founded outside imperial court sponsorship, built on Hōnen's teaching that reciting the nenbutsu alone opens an "easy path" to rebirth in Amitābha's pure land. His disciples split over how often that recitation needed repeating — from Shōkū's reported sixty thousand times daily down to Kōsai and Shinran's radical claim that a single sincere invocation would suffice — factional splits that produced the Chinzei and Seizan branches, with Chinzei eventually dominant under Tokugawa patronage. Shinran's more radical single-recitation position later broke off entirely as its own school, Jōdo Shinshū.

Sādhana. ("Method" or "technique.") A tantric ritual for receiving attainments from a deity, performed either by inviting the deity to appear and be worshipped, or by the meditator directly visualizing themselves as the deity, already possessed of an enlightened body, speech, and mind. Elaborate sādhanas follow a set architecture: a sevenfold preliminary service of homage and confession, taking refuge and generating bodhicitta, meditation on emptiness, construction of a maṇḍala, and the invitation of actual "wisdom beings" to merge with their visualized "pledge being" doubles — ending, after the requested boons are sought, with the entire visualization dissolving back into emptiness.

location.label: Emeishan, Sichuan, China (named directly as the center of his worship)

note: Samantabhadra. A principal Mahāyāna bodhisattva personifying the perfection of good works, standing at Śākyamuni's side opposite Mañjuśrī and serving, in the Gaṇḍavyūha, as the final and culminating teacher in Sudhana's long search for guidance — the one who sets forth the ten vows of the famous Bhadracarīpraṇidhāna. His Chinese cult centers on Emeishan in Sichuan, where legend has him arriving astride his signature white elephant. In the Rnying ma sect of Tibetan Buddhism he takes on an entirely different role as the primordial buddha, depicted naked and blue in union with his consort, embodying the eternal union of awareness and emptiness at the root of the Atiyoga teachings.

Śrāmaṇera. ("Novice.") The preliminary ordination stage every man must pass through before full ordination as a monk, entered through a simple ceremony of shaving, robing, and a threefold recitation of the refuges. Bound to ten precepts in Pāli tradition (expanded to thirty-six under Mūlasarvāstivāda), a novice cannot yet attend the formal recitation of the monastic code or participate in official ecclesiastical acts, and must live under a teacher's guidance until reaching full ordination — with disqualifying categories for admission ranging from convicted criminals to those with communicable disease.

Svabhāva. ("Self-nature" or "intrinsic existence.") In Madhyamaka, a falsely hypostatized independent essence that ignorance wrongly attributes to phenomena — so central to refute that the school calls itself the "Proponents of No Svabhāva." Yogācāra instead sorts all phenomena into three natures — imaginary, dependent, and consummate — while the Laṅkāvatārasūtra multiplies the term into seven distinct senses of "nature," from causal origination to the fully realized buddha-nature underlying reality. The same word, in other words, names either the illusion Madhyamaka dismantles or the structure Yogācāra builds up, depending entirely on which school is using it.

Trāyastriṃśa. ("[Heaven] of the thirty-three.") The second-lowest of the six sensuous-realm heavens, sitting atop Mount Sumeru and ruled by Śakra, king of the gods, presiding over thirty-two other male divinities in golden palaces with thirty-million-year lifespans. Here, in the seventh year after his enlightenment, the Buddha spent a rains retreat teaching the abhidharma to his deceased mother, later descending to earth on a jeweled ladder — and here Śakra is said to have enshrined a lock of hair Prince Siddhārtha cut off at his renunciation. Scholars note its thirty-three-god roster likely echoes the Ṛgveda's own pantheon, suggesting Buddhist cosmology absorbing pre-Buddhist Indian religion wholesale.

Vimokṣa. ("Liberation" or "deliverance.") Freedom from rebirth achieved via the śrāvaka, pratyekabuddha, or bodhisattva paths, classically reached through one of three "doors": emptiness, signlessness, or wishlessness. A separate scheme of eight graded liberations tracks increasingly refined states of meditative absorption, moving from perceiving material form, through the four formless-realm attainments of infinite space, infinite consciousness, nothingness, and neither-perception-nor-nonperception, to the final cessation of consciousness itself — with Mahāyāna abhidharma reinterpreting the earlier stages as a bodhisattva's tool for manifesting different forms to help other beings.

time.basis: "(c. 600–670 CE)", given directly

note: Dharmakīrti. (c. 600–670 CE.) The most influential logician in Buddhist philosophical history, building on his predecessor Dignāga's epistemology through a series of seven treatises defending Buddhist theories of valid knowledge against Brahmanical critics. His key innovation grounds reliable perception in a causal link between sense object and sensory awareness, closing a gap in Dignāga's system, and his works provoked a long line of Indian commentary before becoming the focus of intense, competing interpretive traditions in Tibet — one line descending from Rngog Blo ldan shes rab, the other, more faithful to Dharmakīrti's own text, initiated by Sa skya Paṇḍita's critique of it.

Tathāgata. ("One who has thus come/gone.") One of the Buddha's most common epithets, deliberately ambiguous in Sanskrit between "thus come" and "thus gone," and used by the Buddha himself to refer both to himself and to buddhas of the past. Pāli commentaries offer as many as sixteen explanations, some possibly pre-Buddhist in origin; the most common readings hold that a buddha has "thus come" into the world following the pattern of past buddhas, or "thus gone" on to nirvāṇa as they did — with the term's root also suggesting a more literal claim to understand things "as they truly are."

time.basis: the Pāli vinayapiṭaka "perhaps redacted around the first century CE"

location.label: Sri Lanka (Anurādhapura placeholder — where the Pāli canon was redacted and committed to writing)

note: Vinayapiṭaka. ("Basket of discipline.") One of the three divisions of the canon, and a far richer historical source than its reputation as mere monastic rulebook suggests — since each rule is narratively framed by the specific misconduct that prompted the Buddha to institute it, the vinaya doubles as some of Buddhism's earliest narrative literature. There is no single vinayapiṭaka but many, one per mainstream school, with disputes over correct monastic conduct a major force behind the historical fracturing into eighteen schools; when Ānanda failed to ask the dying Buddha which minor rules could later be dropped, the first council resolved simply to keep them all.

Bhikṣuṇī. ("Nun.") A fully ordained woman bound to a disciplinary code larger than the monks' own equivalent and, uniquely, to eight additional "weighty rules" formally subordinating nuns to the monks' saṃgha. After ten years' standing a bhikṣuṇī becomes an elder eligible to ordain others herself, but the formal ordination lineage died out in South Asia during the medieval period and may never have taken root in Southeast Asia at all — leaving China, Korea, and Taiwan as the only places with unbroken bhikṣuṇī lineages, a gap recent decades have seen concerted efforts to close elsewhere.

time.basis: the Buddha's "first sermon" after his enlightenment; chronology convention

location.label: Deer Park, Ṛṣipatana, Sārnāth (named directly as the site of delivery)

note: Dhammacakkappavattanasutta. ("Discourse on Turning the Wheel of the Dharma.") The Buddha's first sermon, delivered at the Deer Park near Sārnāth to the five ascetics who had abandoned him for giving up self-mortification. Setting out a middle way between indulgence and asceticism — the noble eightfold path — followed by the four noble truths, the sermon converts its first listener, Ājñātakauṇḍinya, into a stream-enterer and the first ordained monk, admitted with the simple formula "come, monk." The site of its delivery became one of Buddhism's four great pilgrimage destinations.

time.basis: "the line of Karma pas originated... with Dus gsum mkhyen pa (1110–1193)"

location.label: Mtshur phu Monastery, Tibet (named directly as the lineage's main seat)

note: Karma pa. A title held by the incarnate lama heading the Karma Bka' brgyud subsect — the first lineage in Tibetan history to institutionalize succession by incarnation, a model every other sect later adopted. Each Karma pa is said to leave a letter predicting the time and place of his own rebirth; the line's black crown, reputedly woven from a hundred thousand ḍākinīs' hair and invisible to the unmeritorious, was physically replicated for the fifth Karma pa by the Ming Yongle emperor. Regarded, like the Dalai Lamas, as emanations of Avalokiteśvara, the seventeen recognized Karma pas have included major scholars, yogins, and — at times, through Mongol and Chinese court ties — political power players, occasionally in tension with the rising Dge lugs sect.

time.basis: the practice of identifying incarnate children "may date from as early as the eleventh or twelfth century"

note: Sprul sku. ("Tulku.") The Tibetan rendering of nirmāṇakāya, a buddha's "emanation body" manifest in the world for others' benefit — extended by usage to mean any recognized "incarnate lama." Unlike ordinary beings, whose rebirth is involuntary and risks a lower destiny, an incarnate lama's rebirth is held to be a deliberate choice, traceable through instructions the dying master leaves behind. By the fifteenth century every Tibetan sect had adopted the practice — the Dalai Lamas its most famous example — creating roughly three thousand recognized incarnation lines and, with them, a durable mechanism for passing religious authority across generations.

Bodhisattvabhūmi. ("Ground" or "stage" of a bodhisattva.) The systematic stages of a bodhisattva's maturation into a buddha, most commonly enumerated as ten following the Daśabhūmikasūtra, mapped onto the broader fifty-two-stage bodhisattva path found in the Avataṃsakasūtra and related scriptures. The first stage begins on the path of vision; the remaining nine unfold across the path of cultivation. A rival seven-stage schema, set out independently in Asaṅga's treatise of (almost) the same name, developed on its own terms and requires real exegetical effort to reconcile with the more standard ten-stage account.

time.basis: "formed in 1938 during the Japanese colonial administration of Korea"

location.label: Chogyesa, Seoul, Korea (the order's headquarters, named directly)

note: Chogye chong. Korea's largest Buddhist order, its name evoking Caoxishan, the mountain where Chan's sixth patriarch Huineng resided, to claim pedigree as a Sŏn-descended tradition while absorbing other strands of Korean Buddhism. Though its constitution traces roots to the ninth-century monk Toŭi and later Pojo Chinul, the order in its present form was founded in 1938 under Japanese colonial rule, and split decisively in the 1950s and 60s "purification movement," when celibate monks broke from the married-clergy tradition imposed under Japanese influence to form the reconstituted, celibate Chogye chong of today.

time.basis: "the earliest complete Buddhist canons in China date from the fifth century"

note: Dazangjing. ("Scriptures of the great repository.") The Chinese term that replaced the Indian "tripiṭaka" once the Chinese canon grew to include not just translated Indian texts but indigenous commentaries, treatises, biographies, and dictionaries composed directly in literary Chinese. Organized by court-library-style shelf categories rather than the Indian threefold division, the earliest complete canons date to the fifth century; by the tenth, woodblock printing enabled full printed editions, of which Korea's meticulously accurate Koryŏ canon — 1,514 texts on over 81,000 woodblocks, still housed at Haeinsa — is especially renowned.

Mudrā. ("Seal," "mark," or "sign.") Ritual hand and arm gestures performed in practice or depicted in Buddhist art, from the earliest "fearlessness" and "earth-touching" gestures of Śākyamuni images to the hundreds of mudrās that proliferated with Mahāyāna and Vajrayāna iconography. In tantric ritual mudrās become dynamic gestures symbolizing offerings or invoking visualized deities, and the term takes on a further, more literal meaning as a sexual consort — visualized or actual — with the "great seal," mahāmudrā, naming the highest realization in certain tantric systems.

Saṃskāra. ("Formation" or "conditioning factor.") In its passive sense, anything brought into being by causes and conditions — the basis of the Buddha's famous seal that "all conditioned things are impermanent." In its active sense, the latent mental imprint left by past action, equivalent to volition and functioning as the second link in dependent origination, perpetuating rebirth. As the fourth of the five aggregates, it also becomes a catch-all category for every mental and non-mental conditioning factor that doesn't fit neatly under materiality, sensation, perception, or consciousness.

Zushi. ("Patriarch.") An eminent teacher in a lineage claimed to trace back to Śākyamuni or earlier buddhas, a concept likely descended from the vinaya's more mundane notion of a "preceptor" who confers ordination and thereby forges a durable teacher-disciple bond. East Asian schools from Chan to Tiantai to Huayan built their legitimacy on such retrospectively constructed lineages, none more scrutinized than Chan's canonical list of twenty-eight Indian and six Chinese patriarchs — genealogies whose fluid, contested membership reveals they were compiled after the fact to authorize specific contemporary teachers, not preserved as settled history.

time.basis: developed "over a period of about two hundred years, from the first century BCE to the first century CE"

location.label: South/Central India (general placeholder — text calls its provenance "obscure" but favors this region)

note: Aṣṭasāhasrikāprajñāpāramitā. ("Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines.") Almost certainly the earliest surviving prajñāpāramitā sūtra and among the very earliest Mahāyāna scriptures, developing gradually enough that its earliest Chinese translations lack the full Mahāyāna vocabulary found in later recensions. Its central figure is Subhūti rather than the more usual Śāriputra, hinting at roots in forest-dwelling ascetic circles outside the mainstream urban monastic establishment; its relentless refrain — that nothing, not even prajñā or bodhisattva or bodhi itself, can be grasped — pushes the doctrine of nonself to its logical, radically self-undermining limit.

Bīja. ("Seed.") A metaphor doing double duty across Buddhist thought: in karma theory, the latent potential an action plants in the mind until it either ripens into experience or is dissolved by wisdom; in tantra, a "seed syllable" visualized and recited to invoke a deity. Yogācāra's Faxiang school elaborates an entire taxonomy of seeds stored in the storehouse consciousness — primordial versus newly acquired, tainted versus untainted — while tantric practice has the meditator visualize a seed syllable blossoming into an entire maṇḍala of deities, then dissolving back into it at the ritual's close.

time.basis: translated by Kumārajīva "between 402 and 406"

location.label: Chang'an, China (site of Kumārajīva's translation activity)

note: Dazhidu lun. ("Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom.") A massive commentary on the Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikāprajñāpāramitāsūtra, attributed to Nāgārjuna but surviving only in Kumārajīva's Chinese translation — no Sanskrit or Tibetan version, nor any reference to it in Indian sources, has ever surfaced, fueling speculation it may actually be the work of a Central Asian Sarvāstivāda convert to Madhyamaka, possibly Kumārajīva himself. An encyclopedic compendium of Buddhist doctrine, legend, history, and geography padded with Kumārajīva's own interlinear glosses for Chinese readers, it became so authoritative that Chinese canon compilers placed it first among all treatise literature.

time.basis: "(780–841)", given directly

location.label: Xichong, Sichuan, China (native place, named directly)

note: Guifeng Zongmi. (780–841.) Chan master, historian, and putative fifth patriarch of the Huayan tradition, celebrated for arguing that Buddhism's scriptural teachings and Chan meditative practice are fundamentally in harmony rather than in tension. Trained first in the Heze line of Chan and later under the Huayan master Chengguan, he retired to a hermitage on Gui peak — the source of his toponym — where he wrote his influential commentary on the Yuanjue jing and a massive, now largely lost history of the Chan school. His synthesis of Sŏn and doctrinal study went on to shape Pojo Chinul and, through him, the entire subsequent Korean Buddhist tradition.

Huayan wujiao. ("Huayan's five classifications of the teachings.") A doctrinal ranking system, in two competing versions by Fazang and later Guifeng Zongmi, sorting the whole of Buddhist teaching into an ascending hierarchy — Hīnayāna teachings at bottom, then Mahāyāna's "elementary" emptiness- and phenomena-focused strands, then more "advanced" teachings on buddha-nature, then Chan's "sudden" methods, capped by Huayan's own "perfect" or "consummate" teaching centered on the Avataṃsakasūtra. A textbook case of a school using comparative doctrine not just to organize Buddhist literature but to install itself, unsurprisingly, at the very top of the resulting pyramid.

Nīvaraṇa. ("Hindrance.") Five obstacles blocking the first meditative absorption, each undermining a specific component of concentration: sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and worry, and skeptical doubt. Each has its own prescribed antidote — contemplating bodily decay against desire, loving-kindness against ill will, recollecting death against sloth — and each is permanently uprooted at a specific stage of the noble path, worry and doubt vanishing at stream-entry, desire and ill will at nonreturning, and the rest only at arhatship.

Pañcamārga. ("Five paths.") The standard Sanskrit Buddhist map of the road to enlightenment: accumulation, preparation, vision, cultivation, and the adept path where nothing more remains to be learned. The path of vision marks the pivotal transition from ordinary person to noble one, corresponding to stream-entry in abhidharma models and to the first bodhisattva ground in Mahāyāna ones; the final adept path culminates in an "adamantine-like concentration" that permanently destroys even the subtlest fetters, whether the destination is arhatship or buddhahood.

Saṃdhinirmocanasūtra. A foundational Yogācāra sūtra best known for its doctrine of the "three turnings of the wheel of dharma": a first turning at Sārnāth teaching the four noble truths to śrāvakas, a second teaching emptiness to bodhisattvas (understood as the perfection of wisdom sūtras), and a third and definitive turning — which the sūtra places itself within — clearly differentiating how things actually exist. By ranking its own teaching above even the perfection of wisdom literature as the Buddha's truest, most refined intention, the sūtra stakes an unusually bold claim to doctrinal supremacy, one hugely influential in shaping how later exegetes classified the entire corpus of Buddhist teaching.

time.basis: arose "about a century after the Buddha's death, at the... second Buddhist council" (chronology convention)

location.label: Vaiśālī (site of the second Buddhist council, named directly)

note: *Sthaviranikāya. ("School of the Elders.") One of the two mainstream factions produced by a dispute over ten points of monastic conduct at the second Buddhist council in Vaiśālī, insisting the disputed rules be strictly observed against the more permissive Mahāsāṃghika. Subsequently splintered into further schools, the earliest being the Vātsīputrīya or Pudgalavāda, notorious among rival mainstream schools for positing a quasi-permanent "person" underlying karmic continuity — a position its critics viewed as a thinly disguised self, yet one that proved durable and widespread despite near-universal reproach.

Vajrapāṇi. ("Holder of the Vajra.") A bodhisattva who began as a lowly yakṣa bodyguard of the Buddha in Pāli sources — tasked with splitting open the skull of anyone who thrice refused to answer the Buddha's questions — before rising through Mahāyāna and tantric literature to become a principal bodhisattva and, alongside Avalokiteśvara and Mañjuśrī, one of the "protectors of the three families" embodying compassion, wisdom, and power. His signature narrative has him subjugating the god Śiva at Vairocana's command, killing him with a mantra only to ensure his rebirth and eventual buddhahood — the template for how fearsome pre-Buddhist deities get absorbed wholesale into the Buddhist pantheon.

Viṃśatiprabhedasaṃgha. ("Twenty varieties of the saṃgha.") A finely graded subdivision of the eight noble persons into twenty, sorting practitioners by faculty and by the specific manner in which each reaches nirvāṇa — those who "enter" versus those who "abide" in each of the four fruits from stream-enterer to arhat. Later Mahāyāna commentators, especially in the perfection of wisdom literature, used this same twenty-fold template as scaffolding to classify as many as forty-eight distinct grades of noble bodhisattva.

Buddhavacana. ("Word of the Buddha.") Teachings accepted as spoken by the Buddha or with his sanction — a category stretched from the start to include material by his disciples or composed after his death, legitimized instead by four criteria for authoritative testimony and by consistency with existing scripture and reality itself. This built-in flexibility meant no Buddhist canon was ever truly closed: entirely new Mahāyāna and Vajrayāna scriptures could be, and were, accepted as authentic buddhavacana on the same grounds — though their legitimacy remained fiercely contested by mainstream schools for the rest of Buddhist history.

Dunwu. ("Sudden awakening.") The Chan claim that simply "seeing one's [buddha-]nature" suffices to realize innate buddhahood, weaponized polemically by Heze Shenhui's "Southern school" to dismiss its gradualist "Northern" rivals as inferior. In two-tiered schemes of "sudden awakening followed by gradual cultivation," this initial breakthrough only confirms that one is already a buddha — full, functioning buddhahood still requires continued practice until knowledge and action fully coincide in a final "realization-awakening." A structurally similar sudden-versus-gradual dispute surfaces even outside East Asia, in Tibet's Bsam yas debate between Kamalaśīla and the Chan monk Heshang Moheyan.

time.basis: "(774–835)", given directly

location.label: Mt. Kōya (Kōyasan), Japan (site of his mausoleum, where he is said to remain in meditation)

note: Kūkai. (774–835.) Founder of Japan's Shingon esoteric tradition, who abandoned a path toward government office to pursue Buddhism, traveled to Tang China in 804 alongside Saichō, and studied tantric ritual and Sanskrit under masters in Chang'an before returning in 806 with the two-realm maṇḍala lineage. Built his teaching around the claim that all acts of body, speech, and mind are direct expressions of the cosmic buddha Mahāvairocana, secured Mt. Kōya and Tōji as twin institutional centers, and is said to remain in eternal meditation in his mountain mausoleum, awaiting the future buddha Maitreya — alongside his other legacies as calligrapher, engineer, and, by tradition, inventor of the kana syllabary.

Māra. ("Maker of Death.") Buddhism's personification of evil, a genuine divinity of the sensuous realm devoted to blocking beings' escape from death and rebirth. His defining defeat comes on the night of the Buddha's enlightenment: unable to dissuade the meditating bodhisattva with armies, seductive daughters, or the challenge of who could vouch for his accumulated merit, Māra is routed when the earth goddess herself is called to testify, quaking the ground in confirmation. Scholastic literature later expands him into four metaphorical forms — the aggregates, the afflictions, death itself, and the literal deity — a comprehensive taxonomy of everything standing between a being and liberation.

Phala. ("Fruition," "effect," or "result.") A term spanning three registers: the physical or mental effect of any cause, the fruition of the four supramundane paths from stream-enterer to arhat, and the specific "retributive fruition" of a ripened karmic deed. Sarvāstivāda and Yogācāra abhidharma sort effects into five distinct types — correlative, retributive, disconnective, virile, and predominant — a granular taxonomy of exactly how causes translate into consequences; tantra itself is sometimes called the "fruition vehicle" for building the fruit of buddhahood directly into its practice.

time.basis: "both sūtras are believed to date from the third century CE"

note: Sukhāvatīvyūhasūtra. ("Sūtra Displaying [the Land of] Bliss.") The longer and shorter versions of Pure Land Buddhism's foundational scripture, recounting how the monk Dharmākara, inspired by a vision of countless buddha-fields, vowed to concentrate their finest qualities into a single realm and made forty-eight specific vows describing it — including that anyone who calls his name with sincere faith will be reborn there. Having fulfilled his vow and become the buddha Amitābha, he brought into being the pure land Sukhāvatī exactly as promised: level, lotus-carpeted, radiant with light-born buddhas, and entirely free of suffering's harsher registers.

Upasaṃpadā. ("Higher ordination.") The ceremony admitting a novice into full monkhood or nunhood, requiring a candidate of at least twenty, a qualified preceptor of ten years' standing, and an assembly of at least ten (or five, outside India) monks convened within a consecrated boundary. After three formal requests and a round of disqualifying questions, silence from the assembly signals approval; women additionally undergo a double ordination, first before the order of nuns and then before the order of monks. A lengthy list of disqualifying conditions — from criminal record to physical disability — governs who may be admitted at all.

Upoṣadha. A fortnightly monastic observance, held on the new and full moon, in which the community assembles to confess faults and recite the prātimokṣa code — a practice of pre-Buddhist origin, likely adapted from other Indian ascetic movements, originally tied to fasting before a Vedic sacrifice. Only four or more monks trigger a full recitation; laypeople often mark the day by voluntarily taking eight precepts that temporarily turn them into monks or nuns for the day, while a long list of disqualified categories of people may not even be present at a monk's version of the ceremony.

time.basis: "composed in Sanskrit, probably sometime between the second and fourth centuries CE"

note: Vajracchedikāprajñāpāramitāsūtra. ("Diamond Sūtra.") One of Mahāyāna Buddhism's most famous and commented-upon texts, staging a dialogue between the Buddha and the arhat Subhūti that repeatedly collapses ordinary categories — "A is in fact not A, therefore it is called A" — to argue that even a bodhisattva's most generous act is worthless if tainted by any residual notion of self, giver, or recipient. Its self-promoting claim that reciting even four lines earns incalculable merit helped fuel what scholars call a "cult of the book," evidenced by the world's earliest dated printed text — an 868 CE Dunhuang copy — and a monumental rock carving on Mt. Tai; in Chan legend, it was hearing this very sūtra that triggered Huineng's enlightenment.

time.basis: "the compilation of the work of a number of scholars... during the fourth century CE"

note: Yogācārabhūmiśāstra. ("Treatise on the Stages of Yogic Practice.") The encyclopedic master treatise of Indian Yogācāra, traditionally credited to Asaṅga though likely a multi-author compilation, structured in five sections covering the entire path across all three vehicles. Its longest section on the "multiple stages" includes two of Buddhist literature's most influential standalone texts, the Śrāvakabhūmi and Bodhisattvabhūmi, and its later sections work systematically through the sūtras to standardize Yogācāra's core terminology — a text so foundational that Xuanzang's translation of it helped define the entire shape of Chinese Yogācāra.

Abhiṣeka. ("Anointment" or "empowerment.") A term borrowed from the ritual investiture of Indian kings and applied to a buddha's symbolic anointing of a bodhisattva who has vowed to achieve buddhahood — sprinkling the crown of the head just as a monarch anoints his heir. In tantric practice, abhiṣeka becomes a formal initiation permitting entry into a maṇḍala and access to a deity's mantras and gestures, elaborated in anuttarayogatantra into a sequence of four distinct empowerments; a related consecration ceremony is also used to ritually "awaken" a newly made buddha image into a living object of worship.

Caitya. ("Cairn," "sanctuary," or "shrine.") A commemorative structure distinguished from a stūpa by the absence of an actual relic inside — though usage is loose enough that the terms often overlap. Early Indian cave monasteries centered their worship on a rectangular "caitya hall" holding a stūpa in an apse, a form later superseded once monasteries shifted to enshrining a buddha image instead. The Diamond Sūtra even declares that any spot where a mere four-line verse from it is taught becomes, by that fact alone, a caitya worthy of veneration.

time.basis: "inscriptional evidence places the school in the Andhra region of India in the early second century CE"

location.label: Andhra region, India (named directly via inscriptional evidence)

note: Caitya. ("The Caitya Worshippers.") A subgroup of the Mahāsāṃghika school, attested by second-century inscriptions in India's Andhra region and likely linked to the group Pāli sources collectively call the Andhakā. Named for its distinctive devotion to shrine-worship, the school traces its founding to a second monk named Mahādeva, who revisited the controversial five theses about arhatship first raised by an earlier, unrelated Mahādeva blamed for the original schism between the Mahāsāṃghika and Sthaviranikāya.

Caodong zong. One of the "five houses and seven schools" of mature Chinese Chan, named by combining syllables from its two founding Tang-dynasty masters, Caoshan Benji and Dongshan Liangjie (the disciple's name placed first purely for euphony). Distinctive for Dongshan's "five ranks," a compressed dialectical framework for the whole of Mahāyāna insight, and later for the "silent illumination" meditation revived by Hongzhi Zhengjue — a technique built on the premise that since enlightenment is already the mind's natural state, sitting quietly without striving is itself sufficient practice, a claim its Linji-school rival Dahui Zonggao attacked sharply. Transmitted to Japan by Dōgen as Sōtōshū, it barely registered in Korea, where Imje (Linji) lineages dominated instead.

time.basis: composed "after his return to China in 645," when Xuanzang "set to work translating"

location.label: Chang'an, China (Xuanzang's translation base)

note: Cheng weishi lun. ("Demonstration of Consciousness-Only.") The foundational text of Chinese Yogācāra, compiled by Xuanzang from ten Indian commentaries on Vasubandhu's Thirty Verses but built almost entirely around Dharmapāla's interpretation, which Xuanzang considered orthodox — a choice likely inherited from his own teacher Śīlabhadra, himself Dharmapāla's student.
