Its central claim is that consciousness always splits into a "seeing part" and "seen part," both ultimately mere projections of mind, whose recognition triggers a fundamental "transmutation of the basis" ending the illusion of subject and object entirely — a text detailed enough that it doubles as the school's primer on Yogācāra's hundred-dharma taxonomy.

time.basis: "(1089–1163)", given directly

location.label: Ningguo, Xuanzhou (Anhui), China (native place, named directly)

note: Dahui Zonggao. (1089–1163.) The most influential Song-dynasty Linji Chan master, who inherited Yuanwu Keqin's lineage, revived Linji Yixuan's teachings, and championed "investigating the topic" (kanhua Chan) meditation in sharp public opposition to Hongzhi Zhengjue's rival "silent illumination" method — even while the two remained personally cordial. Exiled for years on a false charge of collaborating with the invading Jin dynasty, he used the time to compose his magnum opus, the Zhengfayanzang, before returning to favor as teacher to Emperor Xiaozong and receiving the posthumous title "Chan Master Pujue."

time.basis: the ḍākinī "first appears in Indian sources during the fourth century CE"

note: Ḍākinī. A class of female tantric beings evolving from cannibalistic demons and local shamanic figures into guardians of secret tantric doctrine, and eventually into fully enlightened goddesses embodying both fearsome power and the highest beauty. Classed as outer (ordinary yoginīs), inner (visualized meditation deities), and secret (nondual wisdom itself), and mapped onto the three buddha-bodies, they form the third of Vajrayāna's "inner" three jewels alongside the guru and one's chosen tantric deity — with the consort of Padmasambhava, Ye shes mtsho rgyal, standing as the archetypal Tibetan wisdom ḍākinī.

Gotra. ("Family" or "lineage.") In Mahāyāna, especially Yogācāra, a spiritual disposition determining which of several paths a person is destined to follow — a fivefold scheme running from those bound for buddhahood, through those destined for pratyekabuddha- or arhatship, to those of indeterminate lineage who could still shift paths, down to those without any lineage at all, permanently barred from liberation as "incorrigibles." A further distinction separates gotra that is simply innate from gotra actively cultivated through habit — the raw potential for awakening versus the practical work of realizing it.

time.basis: "internal evidence... makes it possible to date the composition of the tantra rather precisely to between the dates 1025 and 1040 CE"

location.label: Northern India (general placeholder — text specifies composition there, coinciding with Mahmud of Ghazni's invasions)

note: Kālacakratantra. ("Wheel of Time Tantra.") A late, highly elaborate anuttarayogatantra composed in northern India during the Muslim invasions of Mahmud of Ghazni, whose apocalyptic vision of a future Buddhist army sweeping out of the mythical kingdom of Śambhala to defeat the invaders directly reflects that historical trauma. Distinctively organized into outer (cosmology and astrology), inner (embryology and physiology), and "other" (initiation and practice) sections, it culminates in a unique six-branched yoga producing a body of "empty form" — and its 1027 calendar system still underlies the Tibetan calendar used today, while its public initiation has been bestowed by the fourteenth Dalai Lama around the world as a peace ritual.

Mahāmudrā. ("Great seal.") The crowning tantric realization in the Bka' brgyud sect's Tilopa-to-Mi la ras pa lineage, in which phenomenal appearance and emptiness are recognized as already unified — a state reached not by rejecting the ordinary mind but by recognizing that its natural lucidity was there all along, underneath even its most deluded thoughts. Structured around the classic threefold rubric of basis, path, and fruition, it remains debated in Tibet as either an exclusively tantric attainment or one with a parallel sūtra-based route tied to tathāgatagarbha teachings, and ranks as the highest of tantra's four "seals."

time.basis: introduced to Japan via Saichō's and Kūkai's returns from China, "804" and "806" respectively

location.label: Kyōto, Japan (Heian capital, center of its early court patronage)

note: Mikkyō. ("Esoteric teachings.") The body of esoteric ritual, text, and iconography Saichō and Kūkai brought back from Tang China in 804 and 806, rooted in late Indian tantric Buddhism transmitted through Central Asia and China. Kūkai's Shingon strand (Tōmitsu) and the Tendai school's own parallel esoteric tradition (Taimitsu) both centered worship on the cosmic buddha Mahāvairocana and promised concrete this-worldly goals — political power, protection, buddhahood in one's own body — gaining rapid favor with the Heian court and eventually shaping Shugendō and local Shintō ritual as well.

Nikāya. ("Group" or "collection.") A term with two distinct senses: the sūtra collections of the Pāli canon (paralleled in Sanskrit by "āgama"), and, separately, any of the mainstream non-Mahāyāna schools of Indian Buddhism — traditionally counted at eighteen, though inscriptions and texts actually attest to thirty-four. "Nikāya Buddhism" specifically denotes monastic Buddhism after the Mahāsāṃghika–Sthaviranikāya split, and is sometimes used as a more neutral substitute for the pejorative "Hīnayāna."

Nirmāṇakāya. ("Emanation body.") One of a buddha's three bodies, the only one visible to ordinary beings — meaning, in Mahāyāna logic, that the entire "historical Buddha," hunger, pain, and all, was itself just a display staged to inspire the world rather than a literal embodied experience. Capable of appearing as a divinity, human, animal, or even an inanimate object like a bridge, nirmāṇakāya splits into three types: the "supreme" emanation exemplified by Śākyamuni himself, the "birth" emanation that simply benefits beings, and the "artisan" emanation appearing as a craftsman or work of art — rendered in Tibetan as sprul sku, the root of "tulku."

time.basis: "(725–788)", given directly

location.label: Zahor, Bengal (birthplace, named directly; modern Bangladesh placeholder)

note: Śāntarakṣita. (725–788.) Bengali-born scholar of Nālandā whose Yogācāra-Madhyamaka synthesis — asserting, with Yogācāra, that external objects are mind-only, but, with Madhyamaka, that consciousness itself lacks ultimate existence — became the most important philosophical development of late Indian Buddhism. Invited to Tibet by King Khri srong lde btsan, he retreated to Nepal after local deities seemed to resist Buddhism's arrival, advised summoning Padmasambhava to subdue them, then returned to found Bsam yas, Tibet's first monastery, and ordain its first monks. He died there in a riding accident around 788, having already predicted the doctrinal dispute that would summon his disciple Kamalaśīla to the famous Bsam yas debate.

Sautrāntika. ("Followers of the Sūtras.") A mainstream school, likely a Sarvāstivāda offshoot, distinguished by rejecting the abhidharma's status as authentic word of the Buddha and advocating that only the present moment truly exists. No independent texts survive; its positions are known mainly through the Abhidharmakośabhāṣya, whose author Vasubandhu — by Tibetan accounts a committed Yogācārin — wrote it from a broadly Sautrāntika standpoint. Grouped with its rival Vaibhāṣika as one of the two "śrāvaka schools" in later Indian and Tibetan classification, the two differ chiefly on whether the mind perceives external objects directly or only through mediating images.

Sparśa. ("Contact.") The sixth link of dependent origination, the mental — not physical — event by which consciousness "touches" an object once sense organ and sense object meet, immediately classifying it as pleasant, unpleasant, or neutral and thereby triggering the next link, sensation. The Buddha traced his own pre-enlightenment inquiry into suffering back to exactly this point: sensation depends on contact, contact depends on the sense organs, and if the sense organs cease functioning, the whole chain collapses with them.

time.basis: "entered the Buddhist pantheon relatively late, around the sixth century, in northern India and Nepal"

location.label: Nepal / northern India (general placeholder, per the entry's own dating)

note: Tārā. ("Savioress.") A female bodhisattva born either from a ray of light in Amitābha's eye or a tear of Avalokiteśvara's compassion, revered — despite her youthful maiden form — as "mother of all buddhas" alongside the goddess Prajñāpāramitā. Best known in her peaceful White and Green forms and her wrathful dancing Kurukullā, she is invoked especially as protector from eight great fears (lions, fire, thieves, and the like) and became central to Tibetan Buddhism from the eleventh century onward through Atiśa's visions and translations, with later tradition identifying her as incarnate in figures from the Nepalese and Chinese princesses who married Srong btsan sgam po to the female tantric master Ma gcig lab sgron.

Vicikitsā. ("Doubt" or "skepticism.") A root affliction across every major abhidharma system, appearing on the standard lists of fetters and hindrances alike — a paralyzing "two-pointedness of mind" that leaves a person unable to act virtuously, likened to trying to sew with a two-pronged needle. Countered by wisdom and scriptural study, it is only temporarily suppressed by meditative absorption but permanently uprooted the moment one becomes a stream-enterer.

Vipassanā. The Pāli counterpart of Sanskrit vipaśyanā — direct insight into impermanence, suffering, and nonself, paired with calm (samatha) as Buddhist meditation's two complementary wings. The Visuddhimagga catalogues eighteen distinct types of insight-knowledge, from basic recognition of impermanence to a final "turning away" from conditioned existence; the popular lay vipassanā movements taught worldwide today, including the lineages descending from the Thai forest tradition and from S. N. Goenka, are modern nineteenth- and twentieth-century Burmese constructions, not ancient unbroken practices, even though they draw on genuine scriptural and commentarial precedent.

Antarābhava. ("Intermediate state.") A transitional existence between death and rebirth, its acceptance genuinely contested among Buddhist schools — the Sarvāstivāda and most Mahāyāna traditions affirmed it on scriptural grounds, while Theravāda scholasticism rejected it outright in favor of an instantaneous "linking consciousness" connecting one life directly to the next. Various durations were proposed, with forty-nine days eventually becoming standard; in Tibet, this state as bar do became the subject of elaborate funerary literature, most famously the text known in the West as The Tibetan Book of the Dead.

Ārūpyadhātu. ("Immaterial" or "formless realm.") The highest of Buddhist cosmology's three realms, home to four classes of divinities whose existence is purely mental, with no material basis whatsoever — spheres of infinite space, infinite consciousness, absolute nothingness, and neither-perception-nor-nonperception. Rebirth at each level depends on having mastered the corresponding formless meditative absorption in a previous life, and even here, beings retain only the barest trace of the last four aggregates.

Dhutaṅga. ("Ascetic practices.") Thirteen voluntary austerities the Buddha sanctioned for monks seeking deeper contentment and detachment — wearing only discarded-cloth robes, eating a single sitting's worth of alms food, dwelling at the root of a tree or in a charnel ground, never lying down to sleep — offered explicitly as a middle way after the Buddha's own failed extreme asceticism as a bodhisattva. Notably, he authorized these as optional precisely while rejecting his rival cousin Devadatta's harsher proposal to make similar austerities mandatory for the entire saṃgha.

time.basis: "(1200–1253)", given directly

location.label: Eiheiji, Echizen (Fukui), Japan (the monastery he founded and renamed)

note: Dōgen Kigen. (1200–1253.) Founder of Japanese Sōtōshū, trained first at Tendai's Mt. Hiei before studying under Myōan Eisai's disciple and eventually traveling to China, where he received dharma transmission from the Caodong master Tiantong Rujing after reportedly awakening on hearing Rujing rebuke a sleeping monk with the phrase "sloughing off body and mind." Driven from Kyōto by rival Rinzai institutional power, he relocated to rural Echizen and founded Eiheiji, where he composed much of his monumental Shōbōgenzō and taught "just sitting" (shikan taza) as the direct enactment, not merely the path toward, one's own buddhahood.

Ekayāna. ("One vehicle.") The Lotus Sūtra's claim that the three separate vehicles of śrāvaka, pratyekabuddha, and bodhisattva are merely expedient devices concealing a single underlying path to buddhahood for all beings — a position genuinely contested elsewhere in Mahāyāna literature, since texts like the Saṃdhinirmocanasūtra and thinkers like Asaṅga held instead that some beings following the lesser vehicles become arhats permanently, never advancing to buddhahood. East Asian schools drew further fine distinctions atop this dispute, with Faxiang splitting the "one vehicle" into an inclusive expedient sense and a stricter derivative sense, while Huayan and Tiantai kept the buddha vehicle conceptually distinct from the bodhisattva vehicle nested within the three.

time.basis: "probably dates from sometime between the second century and the first part of the fourth century CE"

note: Ekottarāgama. ("Numerically Arranged Discourses.") The Sanskrit-tradition counterpart to the Pāli Aṅguttaranikāya, nominally organized by ascending numerical lists though its surviving form reads more topically. Its sectarian origin remains genuinely disputed — proposed candidates include the Mahāsāṃghika, the Prajñaptivāda offshoot, and the Dharmaguptaka, the last suggested partly because the text cites 250 prātimokṣa rules matching the Dharmaguptaka code. Surviving only in a 397 CE Chinese translation, it contains just 471 sūtras against the Pāli collection's 2,198.

Rebirth. A doctrine Buddhism inherited rather than invented, already widespread among the śramaṇa movements of ancient India, describing a beginningless process in which a mental continuum takes new form, lifetime after lifetime, across six possible realms driven entirely by the moral quality of past action. Reconciling this cycle with the denial of a perduring self has occupied Buddhist philosophy since its beginnings — most schools describe the person as simply a shifting sequence of mental and physical processes, transferred at death like a flame passed from one candle to the next, though the controversial Pudgalavāda posited an "inexpressible person" to carry karmic continuity instead.

Jiaoxiang panshi. ("Tenet classification.") An East Asian exegetical practice, flourishing in the fifth through seventh centuries, ranking Buddhist scriptures by relative profundity to explain why texts all claiming the Buddha's authorship offer such different teachings. Tiantai organized its ranking chronologically, by stage of the Buddha's teaching career; Huayan sorted scriptures into five tiers of doctrinal depth, from Hīnayāna at the bottom to its own Avataṃsakasūtra at the summit. Almost without exception, whichever school built the classification placed its own central scripture at the top — turning a hermeneutical tool into an unmistakably polemical one.

Lakṣaṇa. ("Mark," "characteristic," or "sign.") A term covering a striking range of Buddhist ideas: the defining feature of any factor, the three or four marks shared by all conditioned things (impermanence, suffering, nonself, and sometimes the four stages of arising, enduring, decaying, and ceasing), the thirty-two physical marks of a great man on a buddha's body, Yogācāra's three intrinsic natures, and — in Madhyamaka — the falsely perceived "signs" of intrinsic existence that ignorance projects onto things that have none. In epistemology, it narrows further into the specific/particular mark known only through direct nonconceptual perception versus the general/shared mark that appears whenever one merely thinks about something.

time.basis: "(1028/40–1111/23)" — dates disputed among biographies, given directly

location.label: Gung thang, southwestern Tibet (birthplace, named directly)

note: Mi la ras pa. ("Milarepa," 1028/40–1111/23.) Tibet's most beloved yogin, whose life story — practicing black magic to avenge his family's stolen inheritance, then seeking redemption through grueling trials imposed by his guru Mar pa, including single-handedly building and dismantling stone towers — became a foundational template for the possibility of attaining buddhahood in one lifetime despite a troubled past. Renowned for spontaneous songs of realization rather than philosophical discourse, often mocking scholarly pretension, he transmitted Mar pa's tantric teachings, especially mahāmudrā and inner-heat practice, to disciples including Sgam po pa, founder of the Bka' brgyud sect's monastic tradition. Poisoned by a jealous rival monk, he is said to have allowed himself to die despite having already achieved buddhahood, leaving no relics behind.

Mofa. ("Final dharma.") The last of a three-stage East Asian scheme of Buddhism's eschatological decline — true dharma, semblance dharma, and final dharma — a framework original to China rather than inherited from India, its onset variously calculated but generally assumed to have already begun soon after Buddhism reached East Asia. The doctrine supplied ready justification for "easier" practices suited to a degenerate age unable to follow the Buddha's original path, fueling devotion to Amitābha's pure land and the cult of the future buddha Maitreya, and shaping entire traditions including Pure Land, Jōdoshū, and Nichirenshū.

Puṇya. ("Merit.") The store of wholesome karma generated by virtuous deeds, accumulated over lifetimes and deliberately dedicated toward chosen outcomes — a favorable rebirth, rebirth alongside the future buddha Maitreya, or buddhahood itself for the sake of all beings. Pāli sources name three grounds for generating it: giving, morality, and meditative practice, with charity to the saṃgha standing as one of Buddhism's most universally central practices across every culture it has reached.

Rāga. ("Passion" or "desire.") One of the three poisons alongside aversion and delusion, arising whenever contact with an object occurs without proper introspection — a pursuing, grasping reaction toward anything from sensual pleasure to abstract ideologies to the future continuation or annihilation of the self. Crucially, its object must be karmically "contaminated"; this technical restriction is what allows Buddhist texts to insist that the aspiration for enlightenment itself is not a form of desire, since nirvāṇa and buddhahood are, by definition, uncontaminated objects.

Vikalpa. ("[False] discrimination" or "conception.") The mind's conceptualizing activity, generally cast negatively as fantasy or imaginative proliferation and contrasted with the immediate, unmediated knowledge of direct perception. Traditions disagree sharply on its value: some treat structured conceptual analysis as a necessary stepping-stone toward a nonconceptual goal, while Chan's "sudden" approach holds thought-free awareness to be accessible at any moment without passing through concepts first. Yogācāra locates its deepest form in the false split between a perceiving subject and perceived object — a bifurcation gradually dissolved, moving from coarser to subtler levels, on the way to the nonconceptual wisdom that opens the path of vision.

Dharmacakrapravartana. ("Turning the wheel of the dharma.") A general term for the Buddha's teaching activity, rooted in his first sermon at Sārnāth, but expanded by later exegetes into a framework for explaining why different sūtras present seemingly contradictory doctrines — as if the Buddha had "turned the wheel" multiple times for different audiences. The Saṃdhinirmocanasūtra's influential three-turnings scheme (four truths, then emptiness, then Yogācāra's three natures) became a major hermeneutical battleground, with Madhyamaka partisans insisting the second turning was the truly definitive one against the sūtra's own claim that the third was.

time.basis: "probably dates from around the fourth century CE"

note: Laṅkāvatārasūtra. ("Scripture on the Descent into Lanka.") A seminal Mahāyāna sūtra staged as the bodhisattva Mahāmati's wide-ranging questions to the Buddha on behalf of Rāvaṇa, king of Lanka, touching on storehouse consciousness, tathāgatagarbha, and mind-only doctrine — themes central to Yogācāra even though neither Asaṅga nor Vasubandhu ever quote it directly. Also notable for one of Buddhist literature's earliest sustained condemnations of meat-eating, and later claimed retrospectively by the Chan school as scriptural authority for its own lineage, with some accounts even ranking its first translator above Bodhidharma among the Chan patriarchs.

Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra. ("Ornament for the Mahāyāna Sūtras.") One of five treatises tradition holds were delivered to Asaṅga by the bodhisattva Maitreya in Tuṣita heaven, offering a systematic, twenty-one-chapter verse account of the entire bodhisattva path from a Yogācāra standpoint — opening with a defense of the Mahāyāna sūtras' authenticity and closing with the consummation of buddhahood. Covers everything from taking refuge and generating bodhicitta through the six perfections to the methods of teaching the dharma, and remains anchored by Vasubandhu's commentary and Sthiramati's subcommentary as one of Indian Mahāyāna's most important treatises.

Pramāṇa. ("Valid knowledge" or "means of knowledge.") Technically, a consciousness not deceived about its object, with most Buddhist schools recognizing exactly two forms — direct perception and inference — a deliberately narrower list than rival Hindu schools, which also counted scriptural sound (the Vedas) as valid. Dignāga and Dharmakīrti's extensive elaboration of these two categories became hugely influential across medieval India and Tibet, far less so in East Asia, and the term itself came to stand more broadly for the entire discipline of Buddhist epistemology and logic.

Pṛthagjana. ("Ordinary being.") Anyone still bound by the ten fetters who has not yet reached the path of vision or become a stream-enterer — persistently unfavorably contrasted with the noble person in Buddhist texts. One vivid simile captures the gap: the suffering inherent in mere conditioned existence is like a wisp of wool resting unnoticed in an ordinary person's palm, but like a wisp of wool lodged in a noble person's eye — impossible to ignore, demanding immediate action.

Śāstra. ("Treatise.") Buddhist commentarial and exegetical literature attributed to named Indian masters, as distinguished from sūtra, the word of the Buddha himself — the basic split underlying the Tibetan canon's two great divisions. Encompassing everything from verse to prose, of any length, and spanning genres Sanskrit differentiates far more finely than English's single catch-all word "commentary," śāstra typically functions to explain the Buddha's words or intent rather than to speak with independent authority in his voice.

time.basis: identified with the Avataṃsakasūtra's Mt. Qingliang "during the Northern Wei dynasty (424–532)"

location.label: Wutaishan, Shanxi, China (named directly as the entry's subject)

note: Wutaishan. ("Five-Terraces Mountain.") One of China's four great Buddhist mountains, identified since the Northern Wei dynasty with the Avataṃsakasūtra's Mt. Qingliang, the perpetual preaching-ground of the bodhisattva Mañjuśrī — a status that drew pilgrims from across Asia, including Tibet and Korea, whose own Mt. Odaesan is named as its direct analogue. Home to China's first monastery, reputedly founded in the first century CE, and later a major center for Huayan studies under Chengguan and for Tang-dynasty esoteric Buddhism under Amoghavajra, it remained an important hub for Tibetan Buddhism in China as late as the Qing dynasty.

time.basis: legendary compilation "four hundred years after the Buddha's parinirvāṇa" under King Kaniṣka; chronology convention

location.label: Kashmir (traditional site of the compiling council under Kaniṣka)

note: Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā. ("Great Exegesis of Abhidharma.") A massive Vaibhāṣika commentary on Kātyāyanīputra's Jñānaprasthāna, legendarily compiled by five hundred arhats convened by King Kaniṣka four centuries after the Buddha's death, and translated into Chinese by Xuanzang in 200 rolls — one of the single largest works in the entire Buddhist canon. Weaving together the views of four major Sarvāstivāda scholiasts before rendering a definitive judgment, it became the primary influence shaping Vasubandhu's Abhidharmakośabhāṣya, and wasn't translated into Tibetan until the 1940s, when a copy was presented to the young fourteenth Dalai Lama.

Asaṃskṛtadharma. ("Uncompounded factors.") The small handful of phenomena exempt from impermanence because they are not produced by causes and conditions — lists ranging from just nirvāṇa alone in Pāli tradition, to three in Sarvāstivāda (space plus two forms of cessation), to six in Yogācāra's more expansive roster. Nirvāṇa is the one uncompounded factor every Buddhist school accepts, valued precisely because, unlike everything else that exists, it neither produces further effects nor was itself produced by anything — making its attainment a genuine escape from the causal machinery of rebirth rather than just another link in the chain.

time.basis: "constructed... probably circa 779"

location.label: Bsam yas (Samye), central Tibet (named directly as the entry's subject)

note: Bsam yas. Tibet's first Buddhist monastery, founded by King Khri srong lde btsan with Śāntarakṣita as preceptor, after Padmasambhava was summoned to subdue hostile local spirits blocking construction. Modeled on the Indian monastery Odantapurī and laid out as a maṇḍala mirroring the Buddhist cosmos — a central basilica for Mount Sumeru ringed by chapels for the surrounding continents — it hosted the pivotal Bsam yas debate around 797, whose outcome tilted Tibetan Buddhism decisively toward Indian rather than Chinese models. Politically and religiously dominant until the tenth century, it has weathered fires and Cultural Revolution-era destruction and remains a major pilgrimage site today.

time.basis: "(738–839)", given directly

location.label: Wutaishan, China (where he settled from 776 and composed his major works)

note: Chengguan. (738–839.) Putative fourth patriarch of the Huayan tradition, whose massive commentary on Śikṣānanda's translation of the Avataṃsakasūtra came to rival, and perhaps surpass, Fazang's own earlier commentary in influence. Trained broadly across Prajñāpāramitā, Chan, and Vinaya before settling at Wutaishan, Mañjuśrī's earthly abode, he elaborated Dushun's concept of the "realm of reality" into four interlocking perspectives — phenomena, principle, and their mutual, and then their fully reciprocal, nonobstruction — and later collaborated on a new translation of the Gaṇḍavyūha at the Tang capital. His most famous disciple, Guifeng Zongmi, carried his synthesis of doctrine and practice into the next generation.

time.basis: cousin and contemporary of the Buddha; chronology convention

location.label: Gayāśīrṣa, near Gaya, India (site of the monastery built for him, named directly)

note: Devadatta. The Buddha's cousin and Buddhism's archetypal villain, ordained alongside Ānanda but consumed by jealousy after attaining meditative powers without ever reaching enlightenment. Having failed to have the aging Buddha cede him leadership of the saṃgha, he orchestrated a series of assassination attempts — hired archers, a hurled boulder, a maddened elephant — all foiled by the Buddha's own powers, before splitting the saṃgha entirely by demanding stricter ascetic rules the Buddha refused to mandate. Tradition consigns him to the deepest hell for shedding a buddha's blood and causing schism, though even he is promised eventual buddhahood in the Lotus Sūtra — proof, to later exegetes, that no one is beyond redemption.

Hetu. ("Cause.") The primary or main cause of production, working alongside supporting conditions (pratyaya) to jointly generate an effect — a seed as hetu, soil and water as pratyaya, together yielding a tree. The Jñānaprasthāna specifies six distinct types of cause, from a broad generic causation encompassing everything a phenomenon isn't, to a "retributive" cause linking present unwholesome or wholesome deeds to their eventual karmic payoff — and in logic, hetu also names the "reason" step of a formal syllogism.

Khuddakanikāya. ("Miscellaneous Collection.") The fifth and final division of the Pāli sutta collection, a fifteen-book miscellany mixing some of the canon's oldest material with relatively late compositions, including the Dhammapada, Udāna, and Jātaka. Similar "mixed baskets" are known to have existed in other mainstream schools, but none survive and no equivalent appears among the Chinese āgama translations — making the Pāli Khuddakanikāya, expanded to nineteen books in the Burmese recension, a uniquely preserved genre.

time.basis: the largest of the sixteen states that "flourished in northern India between the sixth and third centuries BCE"

location.label: Magadha, northern India (named directly as the entry's subject)

note: Magadha. The largest and, over time, most dominant of ancient northern India's sixteen great states, ruled during the Buddha's lifetime by his patrons Bimbisāra and Ajātaśatru from the capital Rājagṛha before the seat of power shifted to Pāṭaliputra and became the heart of the Mauryan Empire. Often called the birthplace of Buddhism, its regional dialect reputedly the language the Buddha himself spoke, Magadha reached its imperial peak under Aśoka in the third century BCE, when its authority stretched from Bengal to Afghanistan.

headword: Ngag dbang blo bzang rgya mtsho

time.basis: "(1617–1682)", given directly

location.label: 'Phyong rgyas (Chongye), Tibet (birthplace, named directly)

note: Ngag dbang blo bzang rgya mtsho. (The fifth Dalai Lama, 1617–1682.) The first Dalai Lama to unify religious and secular rule over Tibet, consolidating power with Mongol military backing after a bitter struggle against the Bka' brgyud-aligned kings of Gtsang. A gifted scholar, tantric practitioner, and treasure-revealer despite his Dge lugs training, he built the Potala Palace on the site of Srong btsan sgam po's ancient residence, forced doctrinally suspect monasteries into Dge lugs allegiance while still patronizing new Rnying ma institutions, and navigated a fraught relationship with the Qing court that resented being treated as an equal rather than a vassal — a political and religious legacy still felt in Tibet today.

Pañcaśīla. ("Five precepts.") The foundational moral code for lay and monastic Buddhists alike: abstaining from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, and intoxicants, formally undertaken as part of the refuge ceremony that marks becoming a Buddhist. These same five, with celibacy substituted for sexual restraint, form the base layer for progressively stricter codes — the eight lay retreat precepts observed on fasting days, the ten novice precepts, and ultimately the hundreds of specific rules binding fully ordained monks and nuns.

Pañcatathāgata. ("Five tathāgatas" or "five conquerors.") A tantric grouping of five buddhas — Vairocana, Akṣobhya, Amitābha, Ratnasambhava, and Amoghasiddhi — each heading his own buddha "family" and mapped onto a rich set of homologies: the five aggregates, five poisons, five wisdoms, five colors, and the cardinal-plus-center layout of the maṇḍala itself. Developing out of earlier, simpler threefold groupings as Mahāyāna doctrine matured, the five tathāgatas were later folded into the separate concept of a single primordial buddha, especially influential in Newari Buddhism.

Prajñāpāramitāhṛdayasūtra. ("Heart Sūtra.") The most widely recited of all Mahāyāna sūtras despite its extreme brevity, staging the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara's answer to Śāriputra on how to train in the perfection of wisdom as a systematic negation of Buddhism's own core categories — culminating in the celebrated line "form is emptiness, emptiness is form" and the mantra gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā. Genuinely disputed among scholars is whether the shorter, more widely used version is an original Indian composition or actually a Chinese digest of Xuanzang's own translation of the larger perfection-of-wisdom corpus, later back-translated into Sanskrit — which, if true, would make it the single most influential indigenous Chinese scripture ever produced.

Pratyaya. ("Condition.") The subsidiary factors that, alongside a primary cause, jointly produce an effect — heat and moisture supporting a seed's cause in producing a sprout. The Pāli abhidhamma's Paṭṭhāna elaborates an extraordinarily granular list of twenty-four distinct types of condition, from the "root condition" of greed, hatred, or delusion underlying unwholesome states to conditions defined purely by an event's mere presence or impending disappearance — a comprehensive attempt to map, with almost obsessive precision, every way one thing can causally support another.

Pravrajita. ("Going forth.") The act of leaving lay life to enter the monastic community, technically referring to a novice's lower ordination as distinct from the higher ordination of full monkhood — a distinction introduced only after the Buddha's earliest days, when going forth and full ordination were originally a single unified ceremony performed with the simple refuge formula. Performed with a similarly minimal ritual of shaving, robing, and reciting the threefold refuge, the novice stage still carries the same lengthy list of disqualifying conditions found in full ordination, from criminal history to physical disability.

Śakra. Buddhism's own, notably less warlike, version of the Vedic god Indra — chief of the gods of the heaven of the thirty-three and the divinity who appears more often in Buddhist scripture than any other. A devoted, recurring assistant to the Buddha across multiple lifetimes, he catches Prince Siddhārtha's cut-off royal locks and enshrines them in heaven, builds the jeweled ladder for the Buddha's celebrated descent from teaching his mother in the heaven of the thirty-three, and — in one of Buddhist literature's more disarmingly human details — personally carries the dying Buddha's chamber pot during his final illness.

Saṃgīti. ("Recitation" or "council.") Both the communal recitation of scripture and the assembly convened to perform it — the basis for calling the great post-Buddha gatherings "councils," convened to resolve disputes over orthodoxy and to collectively rehearse, agree upon, and codify the canon. In Pāli tradition, a saṃgīti follows the successful purification of the dispensation, expelling false monks and healing schism, so that the newly unified saṃgha can publicly affirm a single, agreed canon; the term is also used more narrowly for the recitation of one specific text, as in the Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti.

Satkāyadṛṣṭi. ("View of a real/existent body.") The mistaken belief that the impermanent aggregates making up a person constitute a real, perduring self — the first of the ten fetters and sixth of the ten root afflictions. Pāli sources multiply this single wrong view into twenty variants, four for each of the five aggregates: believing the self is identical to an aggregate, contained within it, distinct from it, or its owner. Permanently eliminated the moment one becomes a stream-enterer, it is the very first delusion Buddhist practice is designed to dismantle.

time.basis: the custom introduced while Dao'an "resided in Xiangyang... between 365 and 379"

location.label: Xiangyang, Hubei, China (where Dao'an introduced the custom, named directly)

note: Shi. The monastic surname adopted by Chinese Buddhist monks and nuns in place of their family names, taken from the first syllable of the Buddha's own clan name, Śākya. Before the monk Dao'an standardized the practice, ordinands instead took ethnic surnames tied to their teacher's homeland — An for Parthians, Zhu for Indians, Zhi for Kushans, Kang for Sogdians. Adopting "Shi" instead signified a decisive break from one's birth family in favor of a shared identity within the lineage of the Buddha, and became universal practice after 385 once a translated scriptural passage seemed to supply textual justification for it.

Trikāya. ("Three bodies.") Mahāyāna buddhology's central doctrine of a buddha's three aspects: the dharmakāya ("truth body," originally just the sum of a buddha's virtuous qualities, later a transcendent cosmic principle), the saṃbhogakāya ("enjoyment body," a resplendent form marked with the thirty-two signs, visible only to advanced bodhisattvas in a buddha-field), and the nirmāṇakāya ("emanation body," the form that appears to ordinary beings in the world). The scheme resolved a real doctrinal puzzle — since the Buddha's physical body decayed and died, how could it serve as a genuine object of refuge? — by locating ultimate refuge instead in the imperishable body of qualities underlying it.

Tuṣita. ("Contentment.") The fourth of six sensuous-realm heavens, distinguished as the waiting place for bodhisattvas destined for their final rebirth and buddhahood — it was from here that the future Śākyamuni descended into his mother's womb, and here that Maitreya currently resides awaiting his own turn. A single day in Tuṣita equals four hundred earth years, and countless Buddhists across history have aspired to rebirth there simply for the chance to study directly under Maitreya before accompanying him back to earth.

Vedanā. ("Sensation" or "feeling.") The pleasurable, painful, or neutral quality accompanying every moment of sensory consciousness, present universally in the mind according to every major abhidharma system. As the second of the five aggregates and seventh link of dependent origination, it occupies a pivotal causal position — sensation is what conditions craving, making "contemplation of sensations" the second of the four foundations of mindfulness and a direct point of intervention in the chain that otherwise runs on to suffering.

Dṛṣṭi. ("View" or "opinion.") Used almost exclusively pejoratively in Buddhism, denoting attachment to a fixed opinion — the Suttanipāta's earliest strata already treat views in general as sources of conceit and quarrel, a skepticism some scholars see as prefiguring Madhyamaka's later reductio-style demolition of any philosophical position whatsoever. A standard list of five wrong views includes belief in a perduring self, extreme views of permanence or annihilation, denial of karma and causality, and stubborn attachment either to one's own opinions or to the efficacy of rites and rituals.

time.basis: site of the Buddha's ministry (many Mahāyāna and mainstream sūtras delivered there); chronology convention

location.label: Vulture Peak, near Rājagṛha (named directly as the entry's subject)

note: Gṛdhrakūṭaparvata. ("Vulture Peak.") A hill outside Rājagṛha where the Buddha reportedly delivered numerous mainstream sūtras as well as major Mahāyāna scriptures like the Lotus Sūtra and the perfection-of-wisdom texts — a site so sanctified by its sermons that some traditions hold it survives even the fire that consumes the universe at the end of an eon. Also the site of two darker episodes: Devadatta's attempt to kill the Buddha by hurling a boulder down its slope, and, by tradition, the cave where the first Buddhist council was convened after the Buddha's death.

Gter ston. ("Treasure revealer.") The Tibetan title for someone who discovers gter ma — hidden Buddhist or Bon treasures, whether physical objects unearthed from the landscape or teachings surfacing directly within the revealer's own mind. The role carries real religious authority, since a successful revelation is taken as evidence of a karmic connection to the treasure's original concealer, most often Padmasambhava himself.

Kammaṭṭhāna. ("Working ground" — meditative topic.) The Visuddhimagga's catalogue of forty meditation objects, ranging from ten elemental "visualization devices" and ten "loathsome" corpse-decay topics through ten recollections, four immaterial spheres, and four "divine abidings." Different topics were traditionally matched to different temperaments — loathsome topics for the lustful, loving-kindness for the hateful — a diagnostic skill the Buddha himself was said to possess; as later generations lost that ability, the repertoire in active use narrowed dramatically, leaving mindfulness of breathing as by far the most commonly practiced topic today.

time.basis: where Siddhārtha "was raised and lived as a prince until he renounced worldly life"; chronology convention

location.label: Kapilavastu, on the modern Nepal-India border (named directly as the entry's subject)

note: Kapilavastu. Capital of the Śākya tribe and hometown of the Buddha, where he was raised as a prince before renunciation and later returned often as a teacher, converting his cousins Ānanda and Devadatta, his half-brother Nanda, and his own son Rāhula. It was here, after the Buddha ordained the seven-year-old Rāhula without parental consent, that a new rule was created requiring parental permission for ordination — and here that his foster mother Mahāprajāpatī's request to join the saṃgha initiated the order of nuns.

Kyo. ("Doctrine" or "teaching.") The Korean designation for scripturally oriented Buddhist schools, paired against meditation-focused Sŏn as the tradition's two great institutional strands — a distinction sharp enough that Korea's Chosŏn-dynasty state formally recognized only these two categories. Centuries of attempts to reconcile them, from Ŭichŏn's "cultivation of scriptural study and contemplation" to Pojo Chinul's "concentration and wisdom in tandem," eventually collapsed into a simple "Two Traditions, Sŏn and Kyo" designation under King Sejong — a synthesis the modern Chogye order still claims as its own founding premise.

time.basis: the "later dissemination" "commenced in earnest in the eleventh century"

location.label: Tibet (general placeholder — the dissemination spans the whole region)

note: Phyi dar. ("Later dissemination.") The second great wave of Buddhist transmission to Tibet, beginning in the eleventh century after a near two-century "dark period" following the earlier dissemination's collapse — marked by Rin chen bzang po's translation expeditions to India and capped by Atiśa's arrival in 1042. Its fresh "new" translations of tantras became foundational to the Bka' gdams, Sa skya, Bka' brgyud, and later Dge lugs sects, in deliberate contrast to the Rnying ma sect's continued reliance on "old" translations from the earlier dissemination.

time.basis: "(1173–1262)", given directly

location.label: Kyōto, Japan (where he trained at Mt. Hiei and where the Jōdo Shinshū tradition later centered)

note: Shinran. (1173–1262.) Founder of Jōdo Shinshū, who left Tendai training on Mt. Hiei to become Hōnen's disciple, was defrocked and exiled when Hōnen's exclusive-nenbutsu teaching was suppressed, and went on to marry and raise a family while declaring himself "neither monk nor layman." His central concept, shinjin, reframes salvation as arising not from any effort of one's own ("self-power") but purely through entrusting oneself to Amitābha's vow ("other-power") — radical enough that he argued an evil person has an easier path to rebirth in the pure land than a virtuous one, since the virtuous remain attached to the illusion that their own good deeds matter.

time.basis: "(r. c. 605–650)", given directly

location.label: Lhasa, Tibet (capital he established, named directly)

note: Srong btsan sgam po. (r. c. 605–650.) The Tibetan king credited with establishing Buddhism in Tibet and, per later tradition, an earthly manifestation of Avalokiteśvara — though his historical religious commitments remain genuinely uncertain, since he maintained close ties to the indigenous Bon religion throughout his reign. Built an empire rivaling any in Asia, moved his capital to Lhasa, commissioned the creation of the Tibetan script to translate Buddhist texts, and, per Tibetan geomantic legend, constructed a network of "taming temples" across the landscape to pin down a demoness whose subjugation was believed necessary for Buddhism to take root.

Tathatā. ("Suchness" or "thusness.") A term for ultimate reality carrying a more "positive" register than emptiness — reality as it is "ever thus," free of conceptual elaboration, rather than reality defined by what it lacks. Yogācāra reads it as wisdom free of any subject-object split; Madhyamaka collapses it back into emptiness itself, rejecting any attempt to give suchness a positive nature of its own. Its Chinese rendering, zhenru, became one of the most consequential terms in East Asian Buddhist philosophy, anchoring texts like the Dasheng qixin lun.

Viśuddhi. ("Purity.") Distinguished into innate purity — the mind's natural luminosity, present from the start — and purity achieved by clearing away adventitious defilements through practice. Pāli tradition maps a sequence of seven such purities, from morality through mental purification, correct views, and overcoming doubt, to the final purity of knowledge and vision that yields liberation — a structure detailed enough that it supplies the entire outline for Buddhaghosa's Visuddhimagga.

time.basis: his cult "dates back to the first or second century of the Common Era"

note: Akṣobhya. ("Immovable" or "Imperturbable.") The buddha of the East and one of the five tathāgatas, named for his unwavering resolve in mastering the perfection of morality on the way to buddhahood — likely the first buddha cult to emerge after that of Śākyamuni himself, and predating the cult of Amitābha. Despite early popularity across India, Java, and the Himalayan world, and an early Chinese cult dating to the Han dynasty, he never rivaled Amitābha or Vairocana in East Asian devotion, and today survives mainly in maṇḍala iconography — sometimes even displaced there by the healing buddha Bhaiṣajyaguru, who shares his eastern direction.

Āryamārgaphala. ("Noble path and fruit.") The four supramundane paths and their corresponding fruitions marking each stage of sanctity, from stream-enterer through arhat. Attaining a "path" happens exactly once per stage and occurs through direct insight into impermanence, suffering, and nonself; attaining the corresponding "fruit" can recur repeatedly — the technical distinction being that by the path one progressively "becomes" free of the ten fetters, while by the fruit one confirms and rests in that freedom.

Asura. ("Nongods" — demigods or titans.) A class of divinities and the rebirth destiny they occupy, ranked between the divine and human realms yet still counted among the unfortunate destinies. Consumed with envy toward the gods since being expelled from the heaven of the thirty-three by Indra/Śakra, asuras wage endless, futile war to reclaim their lost home — a cosmological grudge match that also became a convenient slot for absorbing local non-Buddhist deities, like the Tibetan srung ma, into the wider Buddhist pantheon.

Dīrghāgama. ("Collection of Long Scriptures.") The Sanskrit-tradition counterpart to the Pāli Dīghanikāya, long known only through a 413 CE Chinese translation attributed to the Dharmaguptaka school until extensive Sanskrit fragments turned up in Afghanistan in the 1990s — fragments that instead point to a Sarvāstivāda or Mūlasarvāstivāda origin. Despite sharing a broad tripartite structure with the Pāli and Chinese versions, two of its three sections diverge so sharply that scholars suspect it descends from a genuinely independent textual lineage rather than a shared original.

Kuśalamūla. ("Wholesome faculties" or "roots of virtue.") The cumulative store of merit-generating qualities built up across past lives, most simply enumerated as nongreed, nonhatred, and nondelusion — the direct inverse of the three unwholesome roots. Vaibhāṣika abhidharma further sorts wholesome roots by where they lead: some toward favorable rebirth, some toward eventual liberation, and a distinct fourfold set toward the direct "spiritual penetration" that opens the path of vision itself, marking the actual attainment of stream-entry.

time.basis: "composed in Sanskrit in the first or second centuries CE"

note: Mūlasarvāstivāda vinaya. By far the longest of the surviving monastic codes — some four times the length of its counterparts — preserved complete only in Tibetan translation, with a massive but partial Chinese rendering by Yijing. Its sheer bulk comes from including far more than bare rules: origin stories for every regulation, extensive narrative material, one of the earliest Sanskrit lives of the Buddha, and practical guidance on matters like escorting images in procession or lending the saṃgha's money at interest — content eclectic enough that it functions almost as a proto-canon in its own right. It remains the monastic code followed in Tibetan Buddhism today.

Sādhana. ("Proof" — in this sense, a logical syllogism.) In Indian logic, a formal proof statement, reduced by the Buddhist logician Dignāga from the Nyāya school's cumbersome five-step syllogism (proposition, reason, analogy, application, conclusion) down to a leaner three: thesis, reason, and exemplification — "the mountain is on fire, because there is smoke, like a stove, unlike a lake." A distinct sense of the same word, referring to tantric ritual technique, is treated separately elsewhere in the dictionary.

time.basis: the tribe's period of greatest attestation, contemporary with the Buddha; chronology convention

location.label: Kapilavastu region, Nepal-India border (the tribe's homeland, named directly)

note: Śākya. The north Indian Kṣatriya-ruled tribe that produced the historical Buddha, ruled in his lifetime by his father Śuddhodana from the capital Kapilavastu, and claiming descent from the legendary solar king Ikṣvāku. Nominally self-governing but subject to the neighboring kingdom of Kośala, the tribe was annexed and largely massacred by the Kośalan king Virūḍhaka after his mother — provided to his father as a bride — was revealed to have been a servant, an invasion the Buddha himself reportedly tried, unsuccessfully in the end, to dissuade.

Śraddhānusārin. ("Follower of faith.") One of seven types of noble ones recognized across Sarvāstivāda and Pāli scholastic traditions: a stream-enterer in whom the faculty of faith predominates over analytical understanding, destined eventually to become someone "liberated through faith." Distinguished from the "dharma-follower," who advances through direct knowledge of the four noble truths and eliminates obstacles all at once rather than progressively — a distinction with real stakes, since Vaibhāṣika abhidharma holds that faith-based arhatship can backslide, while the dharma-follower's attainment cannot.

headword: Tsong kha pa Blo bzang grags pa

time.basis: "(1357–1419)", given directly

location.label: Dga' ldan monastery, near Lhasa, Tibet (founded by him in 1409, seat of the Dge lugs sect)

note: Tsong kha pa Blo bzang grags pa. (1357–1419.) Founder of the Dge lugs sect, trained across Bka' gdams, Sa skya, and other traditions before settling on Prāsaṅgika-Madhyamaka as Buddhism's highest philosophical view, guided in his own account by recurring visions of Nāgārjuna, Buddhapālita, and the bodhisattva Mañjuśrī. His four signature achievements — restoring a Maitreya image, convening a vinaya reform council, inaugurating the Great Prayer Festival at the Jo khang, and founding Dga' ldan monastery in 1409 — anchor a legacy as one of Tibet's most systematic philosophers, author of eighteen volumes including the monumental Lam rim chen mo.

Vajrayāna. ("Adamantine" or "thunderbolt vehicle.") The general term for tantric Buddhism, understood by its own practitioners not as a rival to the Mahāyāna but as its esoteric complement — the exoteric pāramitāyāna of the sūtras and the esoteric vajrayāna of the tantras forming two routes to the same bodhisattva goal. The name evokes the vajra's unbreakable, indivisible quality, typically applied to the inseparable union of method and wisdom that vajrayāna practice is built around.

time.basis: "probably dates from around the second century CE"

note: Vimalakīrtinirdeśa. ("Vimalakīrti's Instructions.") A beloved Mahāyāna sūtra whose protagonist, unusually, is a layman — the Buddha's leading monastic and bodhisattva disciples alike all decline to visit the ailing Vimalakīrti, each recalling a past encounter in which he humbled them. Famous for its climactic teaching on nonduality, delivered through Vimalakīrti's eloquent silence after a series of bodhisattvas fail to adequately describe it in words, and for a scene where a goddess transforms the wise monk Śāriputra into a woman to puncture his conceptual attachments — its original Sanskrit, lost for over a thousand years, resurfaced only in 2001 inside the Potala Palace.

Yakṣa. A class of nature spirits guarding the earth, trees, and buried treasure, wielding powers of flight, shapeshifting, and invisibility for good or ill. Often benevolent protectors of the Buddha and his community — Vajrapāṇi, his personal bodyguard, is the most famous example — yakṣas also have a fearsome female counterpart, the corpse- and infant-devouring yakṣiṇī, who required subjugation by a buddha, arhat, or bodhisattva; Sri Lanka and the mythical continent of Uttarakuru were both considered their traditional homelands.

time.basis: the genre "is often associated particularly with the Chan master Mazu Daoyi (709–788)"

note: Yulu. ("Discourse records" or "recorded sayings.") A Chan literary genre compiling a master's sermons, dialogues, and informal utterances, typically assembled by disciples shortly after his death and prized for preserving the vernacular immediacy of his actual speech — as if the master remained, in some sense, still present and accessible. Particularly associated with Mazu Daoyi and his Hongzhou lineage, the genre expanded to include biography, poetry, and correspondence alongside recorded teachings, functioning as Chan's answer to the secular literati's own personal literary collections.

Āsrava. ("Contaminants" or "outflows.") Mental contaminants — sensuality, continued existence, ignorance, and sometimes views — eradicated only upon reaching arhatship, and shared as a technical term between Buddhism and Jainism, suggesting genuine antiquity. The Buddhist and Jaina interpretations diverge sharply in direction: Buddhists picture the contaminants flowing outward from the mind to color one's engagement with the world, while Jainas picture them flowing inward to defile the self — a small etymological fork revealing two very different theories of what corruption actually is.

time.basis: the earliest surviving recension, from Dunhuang, "dating to the mid-ninth century"

location.label: Dafansi monastery, Shaozhou (Guangdong), China (setting of the sermons, named directly)

note: Liuzu tan jing. ("Platform Sūtra of the Sixth Patriarch.") The transcribed sermons of Huineng, containing the famous poetry contest that won him the Chan patriarchy over his rival Shenxiu and cemented the distinction between Huineng's "sudden" Southern school and Shenxiu's "gradual" Northern school. Central teachings include the identity of concentration and wisdom as essence and function, and "no-thought" as not-thinking even while engaged in thought — doctrines that, despite the text's traditional billing as the Southern school's founding scripture, show clear influence from Northern and Oxhead-school teachings as well. Sir Marc Aurel Stein's discovery of a starkly different mid-ninth-century Dunhuang recension upended the traditional narrative of Chan's early history and launched its modern scholarly reassessment.

Mokṣabhāgīya. ("Aids to liberation.") The second of three Vaibhāṣika wholesome-faculty categories, involving the intent to listen to and reflect on Buddhist teaching until one's actions align with the prospect of liberation — the "remote" path of preparation, built from learning and reflection rather than meditative practice itself. Working by temporarily allaying greed, hatred, and ignorance through their positive counterparts, these faculties develop the first twelve of the thirty-seven factors of awakening, laying groundwork that the more advanced nirvedhabhāgīya factors will later complete.

Pūrvanivāsānusmṛti. ("Recollection of former abodes" — memory of past lives.) One of the six superknowledges and one of the three types of knowledge realized at enlightenment, achieved through deep meditative concentration and thus accessible even to non-Buddhist yogins. The Visuddhimagga ranks recall capacity by spiritual attainment — ordinary disciples reach back a thousand eons, the Buddha's chief disciples an incalculable age, buddhas themselves limitless past lives — while the Buddha's own enlightenment narrative places this recollection in the first watch of the awakening night, followed by the divine eye and finally the knowledge that ends all contamination.

time.basis: excerpts "translated into Chinese as early as the second century CE"

note: Ratnakūṭasūtra. ("Jewel-Heap Sūtra.") Despite its singular title, an early anthology of forty-nine independent Mahāyāna sūtras spanning emptiness, pure land practice, and the specifics of bodhisattva versus śrāvaka monastic discipline, with pieces on both Amitābha's and Akṣobhya's pure lands. Individual sections began reaching China as early as the second century CE, but the collection wasn't assembled into its best-known, massive 120-roll Chinese form until Bodhiruci's Tang-dynasty translation between 703 and 716, incorporating earlier renderings by Dharmarakṣa, Kumārajīva, and others along the way.

Saṃbhogakāya. ("Enjoyment body" or "reward body.") The second of a buddha's three bodies, simultaneously a body of personal enjoyment of the dharma and a resplendent body of "others' enjoyment," visible only to advanced bodhisattvas dwelling in buddha-fields — ordinary humans can perceive only the lesser emanation body. Defined by five certainties: it always resides in an Akaniṣṭha heaven, always teaches Mahāyāna doctrine, lasts until saṃsāra ends, is surrounded exclusively by advanced bodhisattvas, and is adorned with the full complement of a great being's physical marks.

time.basis: period spanning the Buddha's ministry-era visits through the second Buddhist council held there "approximately one hundred years after the Buddha's parinirvāṇa" (chronology convention)

location.label: Vaiśālī, Bihar, India (named directly as the entry's subject)

note: Vaiśālī. Capital of the Licchavi confederacy, visited repeatedly by the Buddha, who accepted a mango grove from the courtesan Āmrapālī and, on the road here from Kapilavastu, granted his stepmother Mahāprajāpatī's request that founded the order of nuns. Also the site of the pivotal second Buddhist council roughly a century after the Buddha's death, convened after the monk Yaśas accused local monks of ten vinaya violations — a dispute that split the saṃgha into the Sthaviranikāya and Mahāsāṃghika and set in motion the eventual fracturing into eighteen mainstream schools.

Vajra. ("Adamant," "diamond," or "thunderbolt.") A symbol of indestructibility central enough to tantric Buddhism to name the entire vajrayāna, and also the ritual scepter paired with a bell in tantric liturgy — vajra for method held in the right hand, bell for wisdom in the left. A five-pointed vajra carries dense symbolic freight: its five lower points represent either the five aggregates or five afflictions, transmuted through practice into the five buddhas represented by its five upper points, with the connecting sphere symbolizing the emptiness that unites them.

time.basis: the tradition "flourished in the seventh and eighth centuries"

location.label: Chang'an, China (general placeholder — Shenxiu and his disciples were part of the metropolitan court elite)

note: Bei zong. ("Northern school.") The early Chan lineage descending from Shenxiu, historically far more influential at the Tang imperial court than later tradition credits it, focused on transcending discursive thought through five expedient methods. Its "gradualist" reputation — and eventual eclipse — was largely manufactured by Heze Shenhui's polemical campaign elevating a rival "Southern school" built on Huineng's sudden awakening, a framing later Chan historiography adopted wholesale despite Shenxiu's genuine contemporary standing. The school's influence reached as far as Tibet, where the Northern-school monk Heshang Moheyan represented the Chinese position in the Bsam yas debate.

Cakravartin. ("Wheel-turning emperor.") An ideal universal monarch who rules in accordance with the dharma, sharing with a buddha the thirty-two marks of a great man and the rule that only one can appear in a world system at a time — indeed, seers reportedly predicted the infant Buddha would become either a cakravartin or a buddha, depending on whether he stayed in the world or renounced it. Four grades exist depending on the metal of the ruler's conquering wheel, from a gold-wheeled ruler who commands the spontaneous surrender of rivals to an iron-wheeled ruler who must fight for every inch — with Aśoka standing as history's most celebrated approximation of the ideal.

Dge bshes. ("Geshe" — spiritual friend.) Originally a general honorific for a saintly Bka' gdams teacher, the term evolved in the Dge lugs sect into a formal academic degree awarded after decades of study at one of Lhasa's three great monasteries, working through five core Indian śāstras via memorization, textbook study, and formal debate. Four grades exist in descending rank, with the top lha rams pa degree restricted to just sixteen candidates a year and serving as the gateway to the highest offices in the Dge lugs religious hierarchy.

time.basis: "(c. 480–c. 540)", given directly

note: Dignāga. (c. 480–c. 540.) The formalizer of Buddhist logic, who streamlined the Nyāya school's cumbersome five-step syllogism into a lean three-step form — proposition, reason, exemplification — and was the first Buddhist thinker to adopt the Vaiśeṣika position that only two means of valid knowledge exist: direct perception and inference. His Pramāṇasamuccaya became the foundational text for centuries of subsequent Buddhist epistemology, most notably taken up and extended by Dharmakīrti.

time.basis: "for the five centuries bracketing the beginning of the Common Era" Gandhāra was a major Buddhist center; conquered "around 185 BCE," Kushan rule extended "between the years 50 and 320 CE"

location.label: Gandhāra region (Peshawar, Pakistan placeholder), named directly as the entry's subject

note: Gandhāra. A cosmopolitan northwest Indian crossroads region — spanning modern northern Pakistan and southeast Afghanistan — where Greek, Central Asian, and Indian cultures mingled along Silk Road trade routes, producing some of the earliest known Buddhist sculpture and the first iconographic images of the Buddha in "Greco-Buddhist" style. A major Sarvāstivāda stronghold alongside neighboring Kashmir, it hosted the fourth Buddhist council under the Kushan king Kaniṣka I, which compiled the massive Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā and gave rise to the Vaibhāṣika school named after it.

time.basis: attributed to translator Kālayaśas, "fl. c. 383–442"

location.label: Turfan region, Central Asia (proposed origin of the underlying visualization practice)

note: Guan Wuliangshou jing. ("Sūtra on the Visualization of [the Buddha of] Immeasurable Life.") One of the three core pure land scriptures, framing sixteen guided visualizations — of the setting sun, Amitābha's pure land, and its resident bodhisattvas — within the story of Queen Vaidehī, imprisoned by her own usurping son and granted release through devotion to Amitābha. No Sanskrit or Tibetan version has ever surfaced despite its claimed Indian origin, and its Chinese-specific content suggests the meditation practice it describes likely originated in Central Asia, possibly the Turfan region, before taking its final form with substantial Chinese admixture.

time.basis: Saichō "left Nara for Hieizan" in 785 and built its founding hall in 788

location.label: Mt. Hiei, Japan (named directly as the entry's subject)

note: Hieizan. The mountain headquarters of Japanese Tendai, settled by Saichō in 785 and built up around the monastery Enryakuji, which grew from religious into major political, economic, and military power across medieval Japan — a power violently curtailed when Oda Nobunaga burned much of the mountain in 1571. Beyond its Buddhist institutions, Hieizan also hosted its own resident kami and became a center for both Shugendō practice and the grueling thousand-day mountain-circumambulation austerity, kaihōgyō.

Maitrī. ("Loving-kindness.") One of the four divine abidings and four immeasurables, defined simply as the wish for others' happiness, capable of producing the first three meditative absorptions but not the fourth, which only equanimity can reach. Buddhaghosa's recommended practice starts self-directed — wishing oneself happiness first — before radiating outward to others, and the cultivation of maitrī is counted among the motivations driving a bodhisattva to work for the liberation of all beings.

Pañcavargika. ("Group of five.") The five ascetics — Ājñātakauṇḍinya, Aśvajit, Vāṣpa, Mahānāman, and Bhadrika — who practiced austerities alongside the bodhisattva and abandoned him in disgust when he accepted a meal, only to become his first disciples after his enlightenment. Their two founding sermons, on the four noble truths and on nonself, brought each of them first to stream-entry and then to arhatship, making them, together with the Buddha, the first six liberated beings in the world — with their long-running karmic ties to him traced back across numerous jātaka tales of his previous lives.

Preta. ("Hungry ghost.") One of Buddhism's unfortunate rebirth realms, its inhabitants marked by distended bellies and needle-thin throats that make satisfying hunger permanently impossible — a punishment for greed and avarice in a past life. Water turns to blood, food turns to spears or molten iron the moment it's approached or swallowed, and feeding these wandering spirits ritually remains an important Buddhist monastic practice across many societies to this day.

Pudgala. ("Person.") A provisional designation for personal identity that every Buddhist school accepts in some form while uniformly denying any permanent, autonomous self behind it — the real philosophical puzzle being how karmic continuity survives across lifetimes without one. The Vātsīputrīya and Sāṃmitīya schools proposed a controversial solution: an "inexpressible" person, neither identical to nor different from the aggregates, that carries karma forward — a position Vasubandhu attacked as a disguised, heretical self by another name.

Saṃjñā. ("Perception" or "conceptual identification.") The mental function that differentiates and labels objects so they can be recognized again later, present in six varieties tied to each sense faculty and counted as the third of the five aggregates — the step where a mere sensation of pleasant or unpleasant becomes conceptually grasped, generating the attraction or aversion that drives further action. In the "equipoise of nonperception," this faculty is deliberately suppressed, a state some traditions read as restful cessation and others warn is a false, nihilistic imitation of real liberation.

Triyāna. ("Three vehicles.") Either the śrāvaka, pratyekabuddha, and bodhisattva paths, or the broader hīnayāna-mahāyāna-vajrayāna scheme — with the Lotus Sūtra famously declaring the first triad merely provisional, expedient devices concealing a single true vehicle to buddhahood for everyone. Whether the three vehicles are genuinely three separate, permanent endpoints or ultimately just one became a real dividing line in Mahāyāna philosophy, with Yogācāra and Faxiang defending three final destinations against Madhyamaka and Tiantai's insistence on a single, universal one.

Varṣā. ("Rains retreat.") A mandatory three-month period of fixed monastic residence during the monsoon, originally intended to spare insects and worms from being trampled on muddy roads, though likely adapted from a wider ascetic practice already current among rival Indian śramaṇa sects. The requirement to stay put for months at a time is credited with directly spurring the rise of permanent monasteries, and monastic seniority itself is measured in the number of rains retreats completed — with breaking the retreat disqualifying a monk from the robe-donation ceremony that traditionally marks its end.

time.basis: attributed to Asaṅga, whose dates are given elsewhere in the dictionary as "c. 320–c. 390 CE"

note: Abhidharmasamuccaya. ("Compendium of Abhidharma.") Asaṅga's systematic five-part treatise on abhidharma categories, distinctive for applying a Yogācāra and Mahāyāna lens to material otherwise inherited from earlier abhidharma theorists — where Sarvāstivāda texts catalogue dharmas to show what perdures across past, present, and future, Asaṅga's version instead uses the same categories to expose their fundamental emptiness. Its sections move from basic factor analysis through the four noble truths, canonical divisions, stages of realization, and finally the techniques of formal debate.

Asaṃskṛta. ("Uncompounded" or "unconditioned.") A term for the small set of factors — chiefly nirvāṇa, and in some schools space — exempt from the impermanence that governs every conditioned phenomenon, since they were never produced by causes and conditions in the first place.

Bala. ("Power" or "strength.") The five spiritual faculties — faith, effort, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom — once fully matured at the threshold of the path of vision, at which point they graduate from mere "faculties" to genuine "powers." A tathāgata's own distinct set of ten powers covers omniscient knowledge of everything from karmic causation to the dispositions of all beings to the final extinction of contamination, while a parallel bodhisattva version of the ten powers is linked specifically to the ninth of the ten bodhisattva stages.

Chuandeng lu. ("Transmission of the lamplight record.") A genre of Chan historical writing constructing genealogical maps of orthodox lineage back to Bodhidharma, using the metaphor of a flame passed lamp to lamp to represent wordless, mind-to-mind transmission of insight from master to disciple. Beyond establishing legitimacy for competing Chan lines, these texts doubled as the primary source for the master-student anecdotes later collected and contemplated as gong'an, making them foundational to both Chan's institutional self-image and its meditative literature alike.

Cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra. ("Conditioned forces dissociated from thought.") A catch-all abhidharma category for factors belonging to neither matter nor mind, invented to explain otherwise awkward phenomena — how a trance state can temporarily suspend both physicality and mentality, or how mere speech sounds manage to convey meaning. Sarvāstivāda's standard list runs to sixteen items, later abhidharma texts trim or expand it, and Yogācāra's hundred-dharma system stretches the category to twenty-four — evidence that this was always a deliberately open, flexible bucket for solving whatever doctrinal puzzle arose next, not a fixed and settled inventory.

Guru. ("Venerable" — religious teacher.) In mainstream monasticism, embodied by the preceptor who ordains and instructs a novice in a relationship likened to father and son; in Mahāyāna literature, elevated into the figure of the essential spiritual guide, as in Sudhana's pilgrimage through fifty-three mentors in the Gaṇḍavyūha. Tantric Buddhism raises the guru's status furthest of all — the very first tantric vow is never to disparage one's guru, considered equal to all buddhas, since it is only through a guru's personal transmission that a student can actually receive the teaching at all.

time.basis: "distinctively Japanese treatments of original enlightenment thought begin in the mid-eleventh century"

location.label: Hieizan, Japan (center of the medieval Tendai oral transmissions that developed the doctrine)

note: Hongaku. ("Original enlightenment.") The doctrine, rooted in the apocryphal Dasheng qixin lun, that enlightenment is already inherently present in every sentient mind — distinguished from "actualized enlightenment," the practical work of putting that latent potential into action. Medieval Japanese Tendai reinterpreted this from a soteriological claim into a more radical ontological one: that everyday reality, just as it is, already constitutes enlightenment, a reading that critics both premodern and modern (notably the "Critical Buddhism" movement) accused of smuggling in a disguised permanent self and of providing convenient religious cover for social inequality.

Indra. The Vedic king of the sky gods, absorbed into Buddhism as guardian of the dharma and ruler of the heaven of the thirty-three atop Mount Sumeru — but always depicted as subservient to the Buddha, holding an umbrella over him or carrying his alms bowl. Functionally interchangeable in Buddhist texts with Śakra, whose full title, "Śakra, king of the gods," is itself simply an epithet built around Indra's name.

time.basis: "(523–592)", given directly

location.label: Chang'an, China (site of Daxingshansi and his own toponym monastery Jingyingsi)

note: Jingying Huiyuan. (523–592.) A prolific Sui-dynasty commentator and putative Di lun exegete, native of Dunhuang, who defended Buddhism in formal debate against Emperor Wu of Northern Zhou during the emperor's persecution of the religion, then helped rebuild the tradition once the Sui dynasty restored imperial favor. His Dasheng yi zhang, a comprehensive encyclopedia of Mahāyāna doctrine, remained a standard reference across East Asia, and his early commentary on the Guan Wuliangshou jing significantly shaped the development of pure land thought in Korea and Japan. His concept of tathāgatagarbha as the shared "essence" underlying both nirvāṇa and saṃsāra was later adapted and popularized by the Huayan patriarch Fazang.

Kongōkai. ("Diamond realm.") One of the two principal maṇḍalas of Japanese esoteric Buddhism, paired with the taizōkai "womb realm," and used by Kūkai to found Shingon's core initiatory rituals. Structured as nine interlocking assemblies spiraling outward from a central image of the cosmic buddha Mahāvairocana surrounded by the four directional buddhas, it visually demonstrates that the entire universe is coextensive with Mahāvairocana's own dharma-body — a teaching relying on no known textual blueprint, evidently having developed through pictorial tradition rather than scriptural prescription.

time.basis: "lived a hundred years after the Buddha's death", per the Aśokāvadāna; chronology convention

location.label: Kashmir (where he was sent to disseminate the dharma, named directly)

note: Madhyāntika. Third in the traditional line of five teachers succeeding the Buddha, sent by his own teacher Ānanda to establish Buddhism in Kashmir, where he is said to have subdued a malevolent nāga and ordained a thousand novice monks. Xuanzang's travel account credits him with commissioning a hundred-foot wooden image of Maitreya, modeled with the aid of a sculptor Madhyāntika sent directly to Tuṣita heaven to study the bodhisattva's actual appearance. Later Chan lineage histories quietly dropped him from the patriarchal roster after the early ninth century, promoting Śāṇakavāsin to third patriarch in his place.

time.basis: historical mahāsiddhas "dating from between the seventh and twelfth centuries CE"

note: Mahāsiddha. ("Great adept.") Tantric Buddhism's ideal practitioner — paralleling the arhat's role in mainstream Buddhism and the bodhisattva's in the Mahāyāna — drawn not from monastic elites but often from society's most despised trades: butchers, fishermen, leatherworkers. Their power comes precisely from transgressing purity codes that ordinary monastic virtue depends on — eating meat, meditating atop corpses, breaking caste taboos — reframing acts that would otherwise lead to hell as the very deeds of a buddha, alongside prodigious magical feats like flying or transmuting metal into gold.

Mainstream Buddhist schools. A modern scholarly coinage for the eighteen (or, by full historical count, over thirty) non-Mahāyāna traditions of Indian Buddhism — Dharmagupta, Mahāsāṃghika, Sarvāstivāda, and the rest — deliberately chosen to replace the polemical Mahāyāna-coined label "Hīnayāna." A neutral, retrospective umbrella term rather than a self-designation any of these schools would have used for themselves.

time.basis: died shortly after giving birth to the future Buddha; chronology convention

location.label: Lumbinī grove (named directly as her son's birthplace)

note: Māyā. ("Illusion.") Mother of the Buddha, who at forty to fifty years old dreamed of a white elephant entering her side on the night of his conception and gave birth standing beneath a tree at Lumbinī, dying seven days later — a death tradition attributes to the unsuitability of any other child ever being conceived in a womb that had held a future buddha. Reborn as a male divinity in Tuṣita heaven, she later descended to hear her son teach the abhidharma in the heaven of the thirty-three; in the Gaṇḍavyūha, she reveals to the pilgrim Sudhana that she is, in fact, mother to all buddhas of past, present, and future alike, Maitreya included.

Paramārthasatya. ("Ultimate truth.") One half of the two truths, paired against conventional truth, and defined variously across schools rather than as a single fixed doctrine — Vaibhāṣika identifies it with indivisible, momentary particles, while Madhyamaka identifies it with emptiness itself. In every formulation, ultimate truth is whatever object, correctly perceived, does not appear falsely and whose understanding actually leads to liberation, making "ultimate truths" properly plural across Buddhist philosophy rather than a single shared referent.

Pratigha. ("Aversion" or "hostility.") A primary mental affliction closely synonymous with dveṣa, ranked second among the six fundamental afflictions in Vaibhāṣika abhidharma and generating a cluster of secondary afflictions — anger, enmity, agitation, envy, harmfulness — all rooted in the same basic repulsion toward a displeasing stimulus. Because it carries both cognitive and emotional weight, it can't be eliminated by insight alone at the path of vision; overcoming it requires the sustained, repeated training of the path of cultivation.

Prayoga. ("Application" or "exertion.") In logic, a formal three-part syllogism — subject, property to be proved, and reason — governed by strict rules about how reason and property must relate.
