In the Abhisamayālaṃkāra's exegetical scheme, prayoga instead names four progressive stages of meditative practice through which a bodhisattva masters, then stabilizes, then perfects, and finally instantaneously realizes every aspect of a buddha's omniscient knowledge — the last of the eight "clear realizations" standing just before omniscience itself is attained.

Saṃyuttanikāya. ("Collection of Related Discourses.") The third of the Pāli sutta collection's five divisions, organized by subject matter into five major sections and fifty-six sub-collections covering everything from causation and the aggregates to the noble eightfold path and meditative absorption. Corresponds roughly to the Sarvāstivāda and Kāśyapīya Saṃyuktāgama, now known only through Chinese translation, though exact sutta counts vary wildly across recensions depending on how a single "discourse" is even defined.

time.basis: Kumārajīva's translations of the school's core texts, dated 404 and 409

location.label: Chang'an, China (Kumārajīva's translation base)

note: San lun zong. ("Three Treatises school.") The Chinese analogue of Indian Madhyamaka, built entirely around three texts translated by Kumārajīva — Nāgārjuna's Middle Treatise with Piṅgala's commentary, Āryadeva's Hundred [Verse] Treatise, and a further Nāgārjuna-attributed introductory manual — none of which survive in Sanskrit or Tibetan. Systematized above all by Jizang, who retrospectively traced the school's lineage to the early exegete Sengzhao and to the Korean-transmitted teacher Sŭngnang, whose "three truths" schema of emptiness, provisional reality, and their synthesis went on to shape both San lun and Tiantai philosophy.

time.basis: site of the Buddha's first sermon, delivered "seven weeks after" his enlightenment; chronology convention

location.label: Sārnāth, near Vārāṇasī, India (named directly as the entry's subject)

note: Sārnāth. The modern name for the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana where the Buddha delivered his first sermon to his five former ascetic companions, converting Ājñātakauṇḍinya first and the rest shortly after — one of Buddhism's four great pilgrimage sites ever since. Aśoka later raised a stūpa and pillar here, including an edict against causing schism in the saṃgha; the site remained an active monastic center visited by both Faxian in the fifth century and Xuanzang in the seventh, and its Dhamek stūpa still stands today as the major surviving structure.

Upekṣā. ("Equanimity.") A term spanning neutral sensation, a virtuous mental factor of undisturbed evenness, a balanced state during concentration practice free of both lethargy and excitement, and — most prominently — the fourth of the four divine abidings, an even-minded regard toward all beings without attachment or aversion. Uniquely among the four divine abidings, equanimity alone can produce all four levels of meditative absorption, where loving-kindness, compassion, and sympathetic joy each top out at the third.

Āryasaṃgha. ("Noble community.") The community of the Buddha's followers who have become noble persons, graded into eight types based on progress through the four paths and fruits from stream-entry to arhatship. Collectively, these eight constitute the "saṃgha jewel" of the three jewels Buddhists formally take refuge in — a technical, restricted definition of "saṃgha" distinct from the broader, everyday sense of the ordained community at large.

Dharmānusārin. ("Follower of the dharma.") One who reaches realization through personal analysis of the teachings rather than through trust in what others report — contrasted with the "follower of faith," and ranked higher among the seven types of noble ones for exactly that reason. Vaibhāṣika abhidharma holds this distinction has real stakes: a faith-grounded arhat can backslide from that attainment, while a dharma-follower's realization, grounded in the irreversible "knowledge of nonproduction," cannot.

time.basis: split from the Sarvāstivāda school "about three hundred years after the Buddha's death" (chronology convention)

location.label: Northwestern India (Peshawar placeholder — inscriptional evidence attested there)

note: Kāśyapīya. ("Followers of Kāśyapa.") One of the eighteen mainstream schools, its founder's identity genuinely disputed among traditional sources — variously Mahākāśyapa himself or a later, unrelated monk of the same name. Doctrinally distinctive for rejecting the Sarvāstivāda claim that factors exist across all three time periods, holding instead that only unfructified past karma, the present, and part of the future actually exist — a position closely allied with, though formally distinct from, the neighboring Dharmaguptaka and Mahīśāsaka schools with which it likely shared a common Vibhajyavāda origin.

time.basis: "(r. 754–799)", given directly

location.label: Bsam yas, Tibet (the monastery he founded, central to his legacy)

note: Khri srong lde btsan. (r. 754–799.) The second of Tibet's three great religious kings, who expanded the empire enough to briefly occupy the Tang capital Chang'an in 763, but is remembered chiefly for founding Bsam yas, Tibet's first monastery, with Śāntarakṣita as preceptor and, after hostile local spirits stalled construction, Padmasambhava's intervention to subdue them. Presided as judge over the pivotal Bsam yas debate between Kamalaśīla and the Chinese monk Heshang Moheyan, ultimately declaring Kamalaśīla victorious and formally establishing Madhyamaka as his kingdom's official philosophy — a ruling that tilted Tibetan Buddhism decisively toward Indian rather than Chinese models.

Mahāvagga. ("Great Chapter.") The first half of the vinaya's Khandhaka division and the earliest systematic narrative of the saṃgha's founding — covering the Buddha's earliest teachings and conversions after enlightenment, the institution of ordination through the threefold refuge, and practical matters like the rains retreat and monastic robes. Its historical account continues directly into the companion Cūḷavagga, which picks up the saṃgha's story after the Buddha's death.

time.basis: "probably composed sometime between the mid-sixth and seventh centuries"

note: Mahāvairocanābhisaṃbodhisūtra. An early Buddhist tantra staged as a dialogue between Vajrapāṇi and the cosmic buddha Mahāvairocana, composed around the time the Mantrayāna was first emerging as its own distinct Mahāyāna strand. Centered on bodhicitta, compassion, and skillful means as the cause, root, and culmination of Mahāvairocana's omniscience, it became — alongside the Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha — one of the two most important tantras for East Asian esoteric Buddhism, reaching China in a 724–725 translation and Tibet with an additional seven chapters not found in the Chinese version.

time.basis: "(709–788)", given directly

location.label: Zhongling, Jiangsu, China (site of Kaiyuansi, where he taught for decades)

note: Mazu Daoyi. (709–788.) Retrospective patriarch of the Hongzhou lineage of Chan, awakened under Nanyue Huairang after being told that sitting meditation, like polishing a roof tile, could never by itself produce a mirror or buddhahood. His radical extension of "original enlightenment" doctrine — declaring "everyday mind is the way" and "mind itself is the Buddha" — insisted sentient beings were never actually deluded at all, a position that drew sharp criticism from Guifeng Zongmi for seemingly excusing practitioners from any need for practice or ethical restraint.

time.basis: internal evidence leads scholars to date the composition "to sometime around the middle of the fifth century"

note: Renwang jing. ("Scripture for Humane Kings.") An indigenous Chinese apocryphon central to "state protection Buddhism," unusual for addressing kings rather than monks or bodhisattvas as its interlocutors — casting royal patronage and monastic virtue as mutually constitutive, so that serving the dharma turns a king into a bodhisattva just as a bodhisattva's vocation renders him a kind of king. Chinese scriptural cataloguers doubted its authenticity as early as 594, citing telltale errors only a Chinese author could make, such as listing two different Chinese translations of the same Indian sūtra as though they were separate texts — yet by 602 it had been officially reclassified as an authentic translation anyway, and has remained so listed ever since.

Trisvabhāva. ("Three natures.") A central Yogācāra doctrine describing all phenomena through three lenses: the imaginary nature, the false appearance of objects as distinct from the consciousness perceiving them; the dependent nature, their real dependence on causes and conditions (ultimately, seeds within the storehouse consciousness); and the consummate nature, the nonduality between consciousness and its objects once the imaginary overlay is removed. In short: the consummate nature is simply the dependent nature once its imaginary distortion has been stripped away.

Wu. ("Awakening" — a common Chinese rendering of bodhi, familiar in English via its Japanese pronunciation, satori.) Most associated in East Asia with Chan's "sudden awakening," the view that the mind's buddha-nature is already complete and needs no gradual purification to be realized, against a rival "gradual awakening" model requiring lifetimes of purifying practice. Guifeng Zongmi and Pojo Chinul refined this into a two-stage model — an initial sudden understanding-awakening that one is already a buddha, followed by gradual cultivation, culminating in a final realization-awakening where one can fully act as one — a debate with real precedent outside East Asia in Tibet's own Bsam yas debate over gradual versus sudden enlightenment.

Wu. ("Not have," "without" — philosophically, "nonbeing" or "nothingness.") A Chinese philosophical term first developed as a technical concept by the Dark Learning (xuanxue) school, whose metaphysical vocabulary went on to significantly shape the language and conceptual categories available to early Chinese Buddhist thought.

time.basis: founder Yangqi Fanghui's dates, "(995–1049)"

location.label: Mt. Yangqi, Yuanzhou, China (named directly as the founder's teaching base)

note: Yangqi pai. One of the two major branches of the Linji Chan lineage, rising to dominance in Song-dynasty Buddhism through Yuanwu Keqin and especially his disciple Dahui Zonggao, who championed kanhua Chan and turned gong'an practice into a tool for realizing innate enlightenment rather than an exercise in literary cleverness — pointedly criticizing rival "lettered Chan" stylists for prizing elegant repartee over genuine breakthrough. Transmitted to Korea by T'aego Pou and to Japan in the thirteenth century, the lineage remains the sole ancestor of every Linji tradition practiced in Japan today.

Yogin. A male practitioner of meditative discipline who has achieved genuine attainment through practice — usable for any accomplished Buddhist adept generally, but applied especially to advanced practitioners of tantra.

Zong. A Chinese term spanning "core teaching" or "cardinal doctrine" on one hand and "school" or "lineage" on the other — used to translate the Sanskrit siddhānta (a philosophical school's axiomatic tenet). Properly rendered "school" only for traditions like Tiantai, Huayan, and Chan that claim an unbroken lineage back to a founding patriarch; purely exegetical traditions built around a single commentarial text, lacking any claimed founder or exclusive lineage, are more accurately called "scholastic traditions" instead.

Zuochan. ("Seated meditation," better known in English by its Japanese pronunciation, zazen.) The archetypal Chan meditative posture, modeled on both the Buddha's own seated enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree and Bodhidharma's nine years of wall-facing meditation. So closely identified with Chan practice that later Chan teachers pushed back against treating it as the only legitimate form — the Platform Sūtra redefines "seated" and "meditation" entirely inwardly, insisting the practice is really about an unmoving, unattached mind sustained through all four bodily postures, not literal sitting alone.

Āryamārga. ("Noble path.") The path of vision, cultivation, and final adept-hood shared by mainstream and Mahāyāna traditions alike, along which a practitioner becomes a noble person through direct perception of truth. The paths of stream-enterer, once-returner, and nonreturner all count as noble paths under this classification.

time.basis: "(c. 500–570)", given directly

note: Bhāvaviveka. (c. 500–570.) An Indian Madhyamaka master retrospectively classed by Tibetans as founder of Svātantrika Madhyamaka, arguing against Buddhapālita that Madhyamaka must state its own position through autonomous syllogisms rather than merely exposing the absurd consequences of an opponent's view — a disagreement Candrakīrti later revived in Buddhapālita's defense, giving rise to the Tibetan Svātantrika-Prāsaṅgika split. His Madhyamakahṛdaya and its autocommentary the Tarkajvālā offer an unusually detailed, spirited survey and refutation of rival Buddhist and Hindu schools, including a pointed rebuttal of Yogācāra's claim that reality could be substantially existent.

time.basis: "founded in 1416"

location.label: 'Bras spungs (Drepung) Monastery, near Lhasa, Tibet (named directly as the entry's subject)

note: 'Bras spungs. ("Rice Heap" — Drepung.) One of the three great Dge lugs monastic seats near Lhasa, founded in 1416 by a leading disciple of Tsong kha pa and swelling to over ten thousand monks under the fifth Dalai Lama, making it the largest monastery in Tibet at its height. Named after the Indian stūpa site where the Buddha reputedly first taught the Kālacakratantra, it became the residence of the early Dalai Lamas' "Palace of Tuṣita" government before that seat moved to the Potala, and though sacked repeatedly across its history — most recently during the Cultural Revolution — it reopened in 1980.

Durgati. ("Unfortunate destinies.") The unfavorable rebirths — hell denizen, animal, hungry ghost, and sometimes demigod — resulting from demeritorious action, each destined to endure vastly different lifespans: a topmost hell's five-hundred-year sentence, calculated by celestial time-scaling, dwarfs an animal's fleeting existence, while a nāga can supposedly persist for an entire eon. The stark asymmetry in suffering and duration across these destinies functions as a vivid moral ledger, mapping precisely how unwholesome deeds translate into unequal portions of misery.

time.basis: "(c. 337–422)", given directly

location.label: Chang'an, China (departure point for his pilgrimage to India in 399)

note: Faxian. (c. 337–422.) Chinese pilgrim-monk whose travel account, the Faxian zhuan, is an invaluable record of early fifth-century South Asian Buddhism. Setting out from Chang'an in 399 in search of a complete vinaya recension, he crossed the Himalayas, spent years studying Sanskrit and copying scriptures in India, then survived a typhoon-damaged voyage home that stranded him five months in Java before he finally reached China in 413 — after which he spent his remaining years translating the texts he had brought back, sometimes alongside the Indian monk Buddhabhadra.

time.basis: elsewhere in this dictionary dated to "perhaps the second century of the Common Era"

note: Gaṇḍavyūha. A Mahāyāna sūtra following the youth Sudhana's pilgrimage through fifty-three spiritual mentors — beginning and ending with Mañjuśrī — as a personification of the full bodhisattva path, culminating in Sudhana's vision-merger with Samantabhadra. Later absorbed as the climactic "Entering the Dharmadhātu" chapter of the Avataṃsakasūtra, it survives in three progressively more complete Chinese translations spanning three and a half centuries, the earliest badly truncated and the last, by Prajña, dedicated specifically to finally rendering the chapter in full.

Lokapāla. ("World guardians.") The four great heavenly kings — Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Virūḍhaka, Virūpākṣa, and Vaiśravaṇa — converted by the Buddha and stationed at the four cardinal gates of Mount Sumeru to protect the world, each commanding his own retinue of demigods (gandharvas, nāgas, yakṣas, and others). Originally indigenous Indian or Central Asian deities absorbed into the Buddhist pantheon, their roots in warrior-caste lineages surface visibly in the suits of armor they acquire as their cult spreads eastward into China, Korea, and Japan.

time.basis: "linguistic elements suggest that portions of the text may date to as early as the second century BCE"

note: Mahāvastu. ("Great Chapter.") The earliest surviving Sanskrit biography of the Buddha, embedded within the vinaya of the Lokottaravāda branch of the Mahāsāṃghika — a placement suggesting Buddha-biography as a genre began life as vinaya introduction before becoming independent literature. Structured in three parts covering the bodhisattva's past lives, his final descent from Tuṣita through enlightenment, and the saṃgha's founding, the text breaks off before the Buddha's death and is packed with interpolated teachings, duplicate narrative episodes, and proto-Mahāyāna elements — like an extended account of the ten bodhisattva grounds — whose relationship to later Mahāyāna doctrine remains genuinely debated.

Mithyādṛṣṭi. ("Wrong view.") Broadly, any mistaken philosophical position such as eternalism or annihilationism; more narrowly, the last of the ten unwholesome actions — specifically, denying that actions have consequences or that rebirth occurs — considered especially dangerous because it removes any deterrent against further unwholesome conduct. Also counted as the most severe of the five root-affliction views, alongside self-view, extremism, attachment to one's own opinions, and misplaced faith in ritual efficacy.

time.basis: "(499–569)", given directly

location.label: Ujjayinī, western India (native place, named directly)

note: Paramārtha. (499–569.) An Indian monk-translator who found imperial patronage in Liang-dynasty China, translating a substantial body of Yogācāra texts even as political upheaval — a rebellion that killed his patron emperor — forced him to relocate south and keep working under local rulers. His controversial claim of an immaculate "ninth consciousness" beyond the storehouse consciousness, developed further by his She lun zong followers, marked a distinctive interpretive path within Chinese Yogācāra; he died in 569 mid-translation of the Abhidharmakośabhāṣya.

Saṃskṛta. ("Conditioned.") The term for all impermanent phenomena produced through the coming-together of causes and conditions, subject to the four-stage cycle of origination, continuance, decay, and cessation. Its status as inherently unreliable and unstable is precisely the standard argument for why conditioned experience should be renounced in favor of seeking the unconditioned — namely nirvāṇa.

Silk Road. A term coined in 1877 by geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen for the sprawling network of Central Asian caravan routes linking China, India, and the Mediterranean world — not a single road but a web of paths skirting the Takla Makan desert through oasis kingdoms like Kucha, Turfan, and Khotan before reconverging at Dunhuang. Beyond trade in silk, spices, and precious metals, the route served for centuries as Buddhism's primary conduit out of India into Central and East Asia, carried by monks traveling alongside merchant caravans — the same routes that later carried Nestorian Christianity, Manichaeism, and Islam in Buddhism's wake.

Ṣoḍaśasthavira. ("The sixteen elders," known in East Asia as the sixteen arhats.) A group of venerated arhat disciples instructed by the Buddha to forgo their own final nirvāṇa and remain in the world, each guarding a specific mythical residence with a retinue of disciples, until Maitreya's arrival — at which point they will gather Śākyamuni's relics into one last stūpa before finally passing into parinirvāṇa themselves. An earlier and narrower tradition, the Śāriputraparipṛcchā, names only four monks entrusted with this task after the Buddha's death: Mahākāśyapa, Piṇḍola, Kundovahan (apparently identical to Bakkula), and Rāhula.

time.basis: renamed Tōdaiji in 747 when major construction began, with "the complex... completed in 798"

location.label: Nara, Japan (named directly as the entry's subject)

note: Tōdaiji. ("Great Monastery of the East.") A monumental Nara-period monastery housing the Great Buddha of Vairocana, at forty-eight feet the largest gilt-bronze image in the world, enshrined within the largest wooden building on earth — a project so vast that its construction, according to monastery records, nearly bankrupted the country. Headquarters of a network of provincial monasteries across the Yamato region, it has been sacked and rebuilt repeatedly across the centuries, and its Shōsōin repository still preserves thousands of eighth-century treasures imported via the Silk Road, from Persian glassware to Indian harps.

Triśikṣā. ("Three trainings.") Morality, concentration, and wisdom — the three overarching categories into which the entire noble eightfold path is traditionally sorted, with wisdom training covering right view and intention, morality training covering right speech, action, and livelihood, and concentration training covering right effort, mindfulness, and concentration itself. Morality lays the necessary foundation on which the subsequent cultivation of concentration and wisdom depends.

Yama. Lord of death and king of hell, whose messengers — birth, old age, sickness, and punishment — are sent among the living as reminders to abstain from wrongdoing. Though karma is supposed to operate as an impersonal natural law needing no judge, Indian sources nonetheless cast Yama as an active interrogator of the dead, a role China expanded dramatically into an entire bureaucratic underworld of ten infernal courts, each presided over by one of the "ten kings of hell" — a system detailed in the indigenous Chinese apocryphon devoted to them.

Daśabhūmikasūtra. ("Scripture of the Ten Stages.") The definitive scriptural source for the ten bodhisattva grounds at the path's upper reaches, correlating each stage with both a core mainstream Buddhist doctrine and mastery of one of the ten perfections. Circulated independently before being absorbed as a chapter of the Avataṃsakasūtra, it became the standard reference point against which rival stage-schemes, such as Asaṅga's seven-stage Bodhisattvabhūmi system, were later measured and reconciled.

Gandharva. ("Fragrance eater.") In Buddhist cosmology, celestial musicians who fly through the sky serving Indra/Śakra's heavenly court and, by tradition, marry the celestial nymphs called apsaras. The same word does separate duty as the technical term for the "transitional being" occupying the forty-nine-day intermediate state between death and rebirth — named for the same presumed diet of pure scent, since it subsists on nothing else while searching for its next parents and destined form.

time.basis: "(c. 800)", given directly

note: Haribhadra. (c. 800.) A Pāla-dynasty Indian exegete, possibly a student of Śāntarakṣita and contemporary of Kamalaśīla, best known for his commentaries on the Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines built on the interpretive scaffolding of the Abhisamayālaṃkāra. His summary commentary became the root text for an entire line of Tibetan exegesis originating at Gsang phu ne'u thog monastery, remaining the most widely studied prajñāpāramitā commentary in Tibetan Buddhism to this day, and his distinctive "false-aspectarian" epistemological position was defined in explicit contrast to Kamalaśīla's rival "true-aspectarian" view.

Huguo Fojiao. ("State-protection Buddhism.") The doctrinally grounded belief that Buddhist ritual and royal patronage of the dharma could shield a state from war, rebellion, and natural disaster — justified by specific chapters in the Lotus Sūtra, the Renwang jing, and the Golden Light Sūtra promising divine protection for faithful rulers. The elaborate "Renwang Assembly of One-Hundred Seats" ritual, performed across China, Japan, and Korea from the late sixth century onward, exemplifies the practice, which in Korea is cited as a defining national characteristic — though revisionist historians argue this framing may reflect modern political concerns, including Japanese Meiji-era ideology, as much as genuine premodern history.

Karuṇā. ("Compassion.") The wish that others be free from suffering, distinguished from loving-kindness's wish for others' happiness, and cultivated by radiating it outward across all directions of space as a tranquility meditation. Mainstream Buddhist compassion is explicitly distinguished from a bodhisattva's "great compassion," which extends to all sentient beings without exception and actively motivates the practitioner to endure three incalculable eons of practice in order to personally end others' suffering, not merely wish it away.

Kṣānti. ("Patience," "forbearance," or "acceptance.") The third of the six perfections, covering a bodhisattva's endurance of abuse and hardship without losing commitment to liberating all beings, but also, in a more technical sense, the receptive acceptance of a hard truth — as in the "acceptance of the fact of suffering," the very first moment of realizing the four noble truths that opens entry into the path of vision. As the third of the four "aids to penetration," it marks an understanding of the four noble truths still slightly less complete than the final, fourth stage that immediately precedes it.

Laukikāgradharma. ("Highest worldly factors.") The fourth and final "aid to penetration," naming the single highest possible mundane mental state directly before the noble path of vision begins — the last moment of being an ordinary person before becoming a stream-enterer. Even the exact composition of this stage was disputed among Vaibhāṣika teachers themselves, though the dominant Kashmiri view held it to be the mental factors that directly trigger irreversible access to eventual liberation.

Lokottara. ("Beyond the world" — supramundane.) A term for anything connected to liberation from saṃsāra, contrasted with "mundane" ordinary experience — in the fifty-two-stage bodhisattva path, roughly the difference between practitioners still at the preparatory ten faiths/understandings/practices stages versus those who have reached the ten bodhisattva grounds proper. The Lokottaravāda subschool of Mahāsāṃghika took its very name from insisting the Buddha's seemingly ordinary acts — eating, sleeping, walking — were only apparent, since he in fact remained perpetually in meditative absorption, entirely free of worldly need.

time.basis: "major independent work of the seventh-century Indian master Candrakīrti", whose dates are given elsewhere as "(c. 600–650)"

note: Madhyamakāvatāra. ("Entrance to the Middle Way.") Candrakīrti's independent verse treatise and primer to Nāgārjuna's Root Verses, organized around the ten bodhisattva stages and their perfections, with an enormous sixth chapter on the perfection of wisdom that became one of Indian Madhyamaka's most influential works. There Candrakīrti extends Nāgārjuna's refutation of a personal self into a celebrated sevenfold analysis — famously applied to a chariot, findable in none of its parts — and mounts one of Madhyamaka's most detailed refutations of Yogācāra's "mind-only" doctrine. Preserved only in Tibetan, it became a core text of the Dge lugs curriculum.

Paratantra. ("Other-powered" or "dependent.") The second of Yogācāra's three natures, covering all impermanent phenomena that arise dependent on causes and conditions — specifically, karmic seeds ripening within the storehouse consciousness into states of consciousness. Ordinary beings fail to see this dependent nature clearly because ignorance distorts it into a false subject-object split, the "imaginary" nature; recognizing the absence of that false split within the dependent nature is what constitutes the third, "consummate" nature.

Parikalpita. ("Imputed" or "imaginary.") The first of Yogācāra's three natures — the falsely perceived existence of objects as separate, external entities distinct from the consciousness perceiving them. Since Yogācāra denies that external objects exist independently at all, everything an ordinary person takes to be a mind-independent external world counts as parikalpita: a projection generated when karmic seeds ripen into both a perceiving consciousness and its perceived object, which ignorance then mistakes for two genuinely separate things.

Prayogamārga. ("Path of preparation.") The second of the five paths, sitting between accumulation and vision, where a practitioner develops concentration equal to or surpassing calm abiding and moves through four increasingly refined levels — heat, peak, forbearance, and supreme worldly dharmas. Not yet a "noble path" since direct perception of reality hasn't occurred, its completion is what finally opens the door to the path of vision and the transition from ordinary being to noble person.

time.basis: "(767–822)", given directly

location.label: Mt. Hiei, Japan (where he founded the Tendai tradition)

note: Saichō. (767–822.) Founder of Japanese Tendai, ordained at Tōdaiji before retreating to Mt. Hiei, where imperial attention followed once the capital moved to nearby Kyōto. His 804 trip to China to study Tiantai doctrine under Jingqi Zhanran's disciples secured imperial backing to found an independent Tendai sect; his later rivalry with Kūkai over tantric initiation, and his prolonged, only posthumously successful campaign to replace Hīnayāna monastic precepts with purely Mahāyāna bodhisattva ordination at Mt. Hiei, both shaped the distinctive institutional shape Japanese Tendai would take.

Sakṛdāgāmiphalastha. ("One who has reached the fruit of once-returner.") The completed counterpart to the once-returner "candidate" (sakṛdāgāmiphalapratipannaka) — the candidate has traversed only the "unimpeded path," while this figure has gone on to the "path of freedom" that actually secures the fruition. In Mahāyāna reinterpretation, the same term is repurposed to describe celestial bodhisattvas in their final life before Tuṣita heaven, on the verge of complete buddhahood rather than mere once-returning.

time.basis: "likely dating from the late seventh century"

note: Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha. ("Compendium of Principles of All the Tathāgatas.") A hugely influential tantra recasting Śākyamuni's enlightenment as achieved not through meditation under the Bodhi tree but through ritual consecration in the Akaniṣṭha heaven — his physical body left behind while a mind-made body traveled to receive empowerment before returning to stage the familiar defeat of Māra as mere theater for the world. Featuring the violent subjugation of Śiva by Vajrapāṇi and formalizing the five buddha families, it became foundational to East Asian esoteric Buddhism via the Vajraśekhara tradition and remained influential in Tibet across both the earlier and later disseminations.

Satyadvaya. ("Two truths.") The exhaustive division of all phenomena into ultimate and conventional truth, defined differently by every school — Vaibhāṣika ties it to whether something can be physically decomposed into parts, Yogācāra to dependent versus consummate natures, Madhyamaka to emptiness versus everything else. Despite being called "truths," conventional truths are in a real sense false, since unenlightened perception ascribes to them more solid reality than they actually possess.

Trilakṣaṇa. ("Three marks.") Impermanence, suffering, and nonself — the three characteristics shared by everything conditioned within saṃsāra. Per the Visuddhimagga, genuinely realizing these three marks is itself what constitutes enlightenment, permanently dismantling belief in a perduring self and guaranteeing stream-entry, with full arhatship and nirvāṇa following within at most seven more lifetimes.

Anuttarasamyaksaṃbodhi. ("Unsurpassed, complete, and perfect enlightenment.") The specific enlightenment of a buddha, categorically superior to an arhat's — where an arhat has overcome only the afflictive obstructions, a buddha has overcome both the afflictive obstructions and the far subtler obstructions to omniscience, the result of the bodhisattva path's many eons of cultivation rather than a single lifetime's effort.

Aśaikṣamārga. ("Path of the adept" — literally, the path where nothing more remains to learn.) The fifth and final stage of the five-path schema, reached once the path of cultivation culminates in an "adamantine-like concentration" that permanently destroys even the subtlest fetters. Having achieved full liberation as either an arhat or a buddha, the adept possesses complete knowledge of the eightfold path and needs no further instruction — hence the name.

time.basis: "stayed at the monastery of Yongningsi in Luoyang from 508 to 512"

location.label: Luoyang, China (Yongningsi monastery, where he did his major translation work)

note: Bodhiruci. (fl. sixth century.) A north Indian translator who reached the Northern Wei capital Luoyang in 508 and, working with Buddhaśānta, translated over thirty Mahāyāna texts reflecting the latest Indian Yogācāra developments, including the Laṅkāvatārasūtra and the Daśabhūmikasūtra commentary that gave rise to China's Di lun zong. Later legend, of doubtful reliability, casts him as a jealous rival who conspired with a Shaolinsi monk to poison Bodhidharma, though he is also credited with converting the monk Tanluan from Daoist longevity practice to pure land teaching. Not to be confused with a later, unrelated Bodhiruci active in Tang-dynasty China two centuries afterward.

time.basis: arrived in China in 693; "(d. 727)"

location.label: Luoyang, China (center of Empress Wu Zetian's court, where he was active)

note: Bodhiruci. (d. 727.) A south Indian translator originally named Dharmaruci, invited to Tang China in 663 but not arriving until 693, where Empress Wu Zetian herself requested his name change. Best known for finally completing, in 713, the massive Chinese translation of the Ratnakūṭasūtra that Xuanzang had left unfinished, alongside assisting Śikṣānanda's translation of the Avataṃsakasūtra — not to be confused with an earlier, unrelated Bodhiruci active two centuries before during the Northern Wei dynasty.

Buddhakula. ("Buddha family" — synonymous with gotra.) The potential inherent in all beings to achieve buddhahood, arising from a confluence of buddhas' compassionate effort, beings' inherently undefiled nature, and belonging to a lineage destined for full buddhahood rather than a merely partial nirvāṇa. In tantric contexts, the term multiplies into five specific buddha families — Vairocana, Akṣobhya, Ratnasambhava, Amitābha, Amoghasiddhi — each corresponding to a distinct personality type dominated by one of the five root afflictions, transformed through practice into its corresponding wisdom.

Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit. A term coined by Sanskritist Franklin Edgerton for the distinctive semi-Sanskritized register found in many Mahāyāna scriptures and the Mahāvastu — the residue of an ongoing, incomplete process of upgrading originally vernacular Prakrit compositions toward the prestige language of Sanskrit. Edgerton distinguished three layers by degree of hybridization, from the Mahāvastu's thoroughly mixed prose and verse, through major sūtras hybridized mainly in their verse portions, down to texts like the Diamond Sūtra recognizable as "hybrid" only through vocabulary.

Darśana. ("Seeing" — vision, insight, understanding.) A term spanning ordinary visual perception through to the five graduated "eyes" of Buddhist literature — physical, divine, wisdom, dharma, and buddha — with the highest subsuming all the others. In its more technical sense as direct insight into the three marks of existence, darśana names the third of the five paths, the pivotal darśanamārga, and is closely related to (though more neutral than) dṛṣṭi, "view," which more often carries pejorative connotations of dogma or wrong belief.

time.basis: "established south of Lha sa in 1073"

location.label: South of Lhasa, Tibet (named directly as the entry's subject)

note: Gsang phu ne'u thog. A Bka' gdams monastery that became, for centuries, the premier center of Tibetan epistemological (pramāṇa) studies, thanks to Rngog Blo ldan shes rab's translations and commentaries on Dharmakīrti, later refined by Sa skya Paṇḍita's own influential 1219 treatise. Also a major hub for Prajñāpāramitā study based on the Abhisamayālaṃkāra and home to Phywa pa Chos kyi seng ge, originator of the distinctive Tibetan textbook genre still used in Dge lugs monasteries today — though like many former Bka' gdams institutions, it faded once the Dge lugs sect rose to dominance.

Huatou. ("Topic of inquiry" or "critical phrase.") A gong'an fragment — most famously Zhaozhou's "no" in answer to whether a dog has buddha-nature — used by Dahui Zonggao as an object of sustained meditative doubt rather than intellectual puzzle-solving. Functioning as a kind of homeopathic dose of conceptual poison meant to cure conceptual thinking itself, the huatou pushes the mind to the very limit of speech and thought, leaving it clear and receptive; the technique reached Korea through Pojo Chinul as hwadu and Japan's Rinzai tradition through Hakuin Ekaku.

Jambudvīpa. ("Rose-Apple Continent.") The southernmost of the four continents surrounding Mount Sumeru, corresponding to India and uniquely privileged in Buddhist cosmology — it is the only continent ruled by a wheel-turning monarch and the sole place where buddhas take their final rebirth and attain enlightenment, always at the vajrāsana at its very center. Triangular in shape with the Himalayas among its mountain ranges and the Ganges among its rivers, its human lifespans fluctuate wildly across cosmic time, from as low as ten years at an eon's end to incalculable lengths at its beginning.

time.basis: "compiled by Daoyuan... in 1004"

note: Jingde chuandeng lu. ("Record of the Transmission of the Lamplight, Compiled during the Jingde Era.") The most influential of the Song-dynasty Chan "lamplight histories," tracing patriarchal succession from the seven buddhas of antiquity down through 1,701 named Chinese and Indian Chan figures. Its final rolls preserve discourse records, poetry, and other Chan miscellany, making the thirty-roll collection an indispensable, if genealogically constructed, source for understanding how the Chan tradition told its own origin story.

time.basis: "composed by the fourth-century master Asaṅga", whose dates are given elsewhere as "c. 320–c. 390 CE"

note: Mahāyānasaṃgraha. ("Summary of the Great Vehicle.") Asaṅga's most complete presentation of Yogācāra theory and practice, detailing the three natures, the storehouse consciousness and its seeds, and the threefold wisdom of hearing, reflection, and meditation through which that consciousness is ultimately dismantled and enlightenment achieved. Lost in the original Sanskrit but preserved in Tibetan and multiple Chinese translations, including by Paramārtha and Xuanzang, it became the founding text of China's She lun zong.

Manomayakāya. ("Mind-made body.") A subtle body acquired through advanced meditation, capable of flight and passing through solid matter, drawn from the physical body the way a sword is drawn from its scabbard upon mastering the fourth meditative absorption. The Laṅkāvatārasūtra distinguishes three bodhisattva versions tied to different stages of the path, and the concept closely parallels the "transitional being" occupying the intermediate state between death and rebirth — both are bodies sustained by joy rather than solid food, invisible to ordinary sight.

headword: Mar pa Chos kyi blo gros

time.basis: "(1012–1097)", given directly

location.label: Lho brag, southern Tibet (birthplace, named directly)

note: Mar pa Chos kyi blo gros. (1012–1097.) Tibetan founder of the Bka' brgyud sect, who made three arduous journeys to India seeking tantric instruction, eventually studying under the siddha Nāropa at the forest retreat of Pullahari and receiving mahāmudrā teachings from Maitrīpa — though contemporary Tibetan sources note Nāropa had likely already died before Mar pa's actual visit, complicating the traditional account. A farmer and family man rather than a monk, he passed his accumulated instructions to four principal disciples, most famously the poet-yogin Mi la ras pa, after his own son and intended heir died in a riding accident.

time.basis: "(1016–1100)", given directly

location.label: Nālandā, India (where he served as abbot and had his pivotal encounter with a ḍākinī)

note: Nāropa. (1016–1100.) A Bengali-born scholar who rose to abbot of Nālandā under the name Abhayakīrti before an encounter with a ḍākinī convinced him he grasped his texts' words but not their inner meaning, sending him in search of the master Tilopa. Subjected to twelve greater and twelve lesser trials involving genuine physical suffering, he finally received Tilopa's realization through a blow from his guru's own shoe, and his compiled instructions — the "six doctrines of Nāropa" — became central to the Bka' brgyud lineage, transmitted (at least by tradition, since the chronology doesn't quite hold up) through Mar pa to Mi la ras pa.

time.basis: "reached its greatest glory during the reign of the third Mauryan emperor, Aśoka"

location.label: Pāṭaliputra, near modern Patna, Bihar, India (named directly as the entry's subject)

note: Pāṭaliputra. Capital of Magadha and later the entire Mauryan empire, prophesied for greatness by the Buddha himself when it was still the humble village of Pāṭaligāma, and reaching its imperial peak under Aśoka, whose realm stretched from Afghanistan to Bengal. Site of the third Buddhist council according to Pāli chronicles, from which missions were reportedly dispatched to nine neighboring lands — a claim partially corroborated by Aśoka's own inscriptions describing diplomatic outreach. Known to the Greeks as Palibothra and described firsthand by the envoy Megasthenes, it later served again as Gupta imperial capital before falling to ruin, finally destroyed in the Muslim invasions of the twelfth century.

Pratyakṣa. ("Direct perception.") One of only two forms of valid knowledge in Buddhist epistemology, alongside inference — cognition that correctly grasps its object without the conceptual mediation of an image. Four types exist: sensory perception through the five senses, a fleeting mental perception bridging sensory input into conceptual thought, self-knowing perception that makes memory possible by observing consciousness observing itself, and yogic perception, achieved only on the noble path through a union of calm and insight.

time.basis: origins "traced to the founding of Dpal spungs monastery, established in 1727"

location.label: Sde dge, Kham, eastern Tibet (center of the movement's origin)

note: Ris med. ("Unbounded" or "impartial" — nonsectarian.) A religious ideal, most associated with nineteenth-century eastern Tibet, promoting the study of multiple sects' teachings without erasing the distinctions between them — epitomized by 'Jam mgon kong sprul, a Bka' brgyud lama raised Bon and ordained Rnying ma, whose scholarship modeled genuine cross-sectarian engagement while carefully preserving each lineage's separate identity. Despite popular Western framing of this as an organized "nonsectarian movement," historians note it was really a shared ideal expressed through a few towering individual careers rather than a coordinated institutional reform — though it has since become a durable symbol of unity for the Tibetan exile community.

Rūpāvacaradhyāna. Meditative absorption tied to the subtle-materiality realm, unfolding across four progressively subtler stages as five hindrances are allayed one by one and the five constituents of absorption fall away in sequence — from all five present in the first absorption down to only one-pointedness remaining in the fourth. Mastering the fourth stage is a prerequisite for developing supranormal powers and for advancing into the four still-subtler immaterial absorptions, and can itself result in rebirth as a Brahmā god within the corresponding heavenly plane.

time.basis: personal name of the Buddha before enlightenment; chronology convention

location.label: Kapilavastu/Lumbinī area, southern Nepal (associated with his princely years)

note: Siddhārtha. ("He Who Achieves His Goal.") The Buddha's given name, used during his years as prince and ascetic before enlightenment, after which he becomes known instead as Gautama, Śākyamuni, or simply the Tathāgata — the Lalitavistara instead names him Sarvārthasiddha, "He Who Achieves the Welfare of All." The name is likely best known in the West as the title of Hermann Hesse's 1922 novel, whose protagonist, despite the title, is explicitly not the historical Buddha.

Smṛtyupasthāna. ("Foundations of mindfulness.") A fourfold meditative training contemplating the body, sensations, mental states, and mental factors in turn — from breath and posture awareness to noticing whether the mind is elated or distracted to observing the five hindrances and five aggregates directly. As the first of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, it establishes mindfulness's foundational role within the noble eightfold path itself.

time.basis: father of the Buddha, contemporary with his son's life; chronology convention

location.label: Kapilavastu (where he ruled, named directly)

note: Śuddhodana. ("Pure Rice.") The Buddha's father, king of the Śākya clan at Kapilavastu, who built three pleasure palaces in a failed attempt to shield his son from the sufferings that would eventually drive him to renounce the world. Reconciled to his son's path after his enlightenment, though he objected when the Buddha ordained his young grandson Rāhula without parental consent — prompting a new rule requiring parental permission for ordination going forward — Śuddhodana himself became a stream-enterer and, shortly before his death, an arhat.

Vyāpāda. ("Malice" or "ill will.") Ninth of the ten unwholesome courses of action (alongside killing, stealing, lying, and the rest), and elsewhere in Buddhist literature also counted among the five hindrances to meditative absorption, where it specifically blocks the physical rapture that absorption depends on. Its standard counteragent is the cultivation of loving-kindness, the divine abiding whose deliberate radiating outward is meant to directly dissolve ill will at its root.

time.basis: "(635–713)", given directly

location.label: Śrīvijaya (Palembang, Sumatra) — where he composed his travel record and translated for decades

note: Yijing. (635–713.) A Chinese pilgrim inspired by Faxian and Xuanzang, who sailed to India by the southern sea route in 671, studied a decade at Nālandā, then spent roughly thirty years based in Śrīvijaya (Palembang), composing his invaluable travel record and beginning his massive translation of the Mūlasarvāstivāda vinaya. Returning to China in 695 with some four hundred Sanskrit manuscripts and relics, he was welcomed by Empress Wu Zetian and spent his remaining years translating Yogācāra texts and tantras, as well as compiling biographies of fellow East Asian pilgrims to India.

Baxiang. ("Eight episodes.") The standard set of archetypal events marking any buddha's life story — descent from Tuṣita, conception, birth, renunciation, subjugating Māra, enlightenment, the first turning of the dharma wheel, and final parinirvāṇa — with an alternate version substituting specific narrative beats like the four portents and ascetic practice in the Himalayas. A staple organizing scheme in Buddhist art across Asia.

Cittamātra. ("Mind-only.") The Laṅkāvatārasūtra's doctrine that the external sensory world has no existence independent of mind, giving Yogācāra its alternate name. Built on an eight-consciousness model — the familiar six plus an afflicted mentality and a storehouse consciousness — the theory holds that mental states "perfume" the storehouse consciousness with residual impressions that later ripen into new experience; Vasubandhu, converted to the view by his brother Asaṅga, argued in his Thirty Verses that no atomic basis for external objects could exist, leaving mind-only as the only coherent explanation for both ordinary experience and its eventual purification.

Dbu ma chen po. ("Great Madhyamaka.") A term central to Tibet's "self-empty, other-empty" debate over which Indian thinkers count as Madhyamaka's true representatives. Dge lugs orthodoxy holds Candrakīrti's reading of Nāgārjuna as the definitive account of a purely negative emptiness; the Jo nang pa and allied thinkers instead elevate a positive "other-emptiness" — an eternal, self-arisen wisdom consciousness empty only of extraneous defilement, not of its own true nature — relegating Candrakīrti's negative dialectic to a lesser, "one-sided" Madhyamaka in favor of Nāgārjuna's devotional hymns and thinkers the Dge lugs classify as Yogācāra.

time.basis: "in its present form, it probably dates from the fourth-century CE"

location.label: Sri Lanka (Mahāvihāra tradition, source of the chronicle)

note: Dīpavaṃsa. ("Island Chronicle.") The earliest surviving Pāli chronicle of Sri Lanka, compiled from older Sinhalese Mahāvihāra commentaries and covering Theravāda history from the third-century-BCE conversion of King Devānaṃpiyatissa through the fourth-century-CE reign of Mahāsena. Preserves the earliest Pāli account of Aśoka's patronage of the third Buddhist council and its missionary dispatches abroad, and directly supplied the outline later expanded into the more famous Mahāvaṃsa.

time.basis: Mahayŏnsa, one of its primary monasteries, "built by Ŭisang in 676"

location.label: Kŭmgangsan (Diamond Mountains), Kangwŏn Province, North Korea (named directly as the entry's subject)

note: Kŭmgangsan. ("Diamond Mountains.") Korea's most celebrated Buddhist sacred mountains, identified since the Silla dynasty with the Avataṃsakasūtra's description of a mountain where the bodhisattva Dharmodgata perpetually preaches — a connection the Huayan exegete Chengguan explicitly drew to Korea. Once home to some 108 monasteries before the devastation of the Korean War, including Ŭisang's 676 foundation Mahayŏnsa, it remains an active pilgrimage site today, though continued access has been repeatedly disrupted by the volatile politics of the divided peninsula.

Li. ("Principle" or "pattern.") Originally a term for the natural grain in a piece of jade, extended by early Chinese philosophy into a general concept of the underlying pattern governing reality — taken up by Wang Bi as synonymous with metaphysical nonbeing, then absorbed into Chinese Buddhist thought by Daosheng as a synonym for buddha-nature. Huayan philosophy gave the term its most sophisticated development: Dushun used it for the proposition that phenomena are empty, Fazang identified it with the mind of suchness, and Chengguan extended it into the essential quality pervading all four realms of reality — a trajectory that would later feed directly into Song-dynasty Neo-Confucian metaphysics.

time.basis: contemporary and elder of the Buddha ("he was older than the Buddha"); chronology convention

location.label: Magadha (general placeholder — childhood region shared with Śāriputra)

note: Mahāmaudgalyāyana. The Buddha's other chief disciple alongside his childhood friend Śāriputra, unmatched among the saṃgha in supranormal powers. Born to a wealthy family and moved to renounce the world after a shared moment of existential disillusionment at a public performance, he and Śāriputra first studied under the skeptic teacher Sañjaya before parting ways in search of a satisfying teacher — each vowing to inform the other first if either succeeded. When Śāriputra achieved stream-entry on hearing a brief verse of the Buddha's teaching from the monk Aśvajit, he immediately shared it with Mahāmaudgalyāyana, who attained the same realization just as quickly.

time.basis: son of Aśoka, active during his reign, "(r. c. 268–232 BCE)" per the Aśoka entry; converted Sri Lanka "in the third century BCE"

location.label: Anurādhapura, Sri Lanka (where he established the Mahāvihāra monastery)

note: Mahinda. Aśoka's son, ordained at twenty and immediately attaining arahantship, who led the Buddhist mission that converted the Sinhalese king Devānaṃpiyatissa and inaugurated Buddhism in Sri Lanka. After preaching successive sermons that made the king's court stream-enterers and then once-returners, he arranged for his sister Saṅghamittā to travel to the island (bringing a Bodhi tree cutting) since he himself, as a monk, could not ordain the women requesting entry into the order. He established the Mahāvihāra monastery in a royal garden gifted by the king, which became Theravāda's headquarters on the island, and died at sixty, his ashes enshrined near the great stūpa he had helped found.

Nāmarūpa. ("Name-and-form" — mentality and materiality.) The fourth link of dependent origination, where "name" covers the four mental aggregates and "form" the physical body — read by some traditions as marking the exact moment consciousness from a prior life enters the womb to inhabit a new embryo. The two are said to depend on each other completely, like a lame man riding on a blind man's shoulders: without form there is nothing for consciousness to inhabit, and without consciousness the embryo cannot develop, so neither can exist without the other, like two bundles of reeds propped against each other.

time.basis: "(1222–1282)", given directly

location.label: Mt. Minobu, Yamanashi, Japan (where he retired and wrote his major later works)

note: Nichiren. (1222–1282.) Founder of Nichirenshū, who broke decisively with Hōnen's pure land nenbutsu practice after concluding the Lotus Sūtra alone contained the Buddha's ultimate, definitive teaching — proclaiming in 1253 that reciting its title, Namu Myōhōrengekyō, sufficed for liberation in the current degenerate age. His confrontational lobbying of the Kamakura government to suppress rival schools and adopt the Lotus Sūtra led to repeated arrest and exile, including a period on Sado Island where he composed several major treatises, before retiring to Mt. Minobu to write and teach until his death, leaving behind fierce disputes over his succession.

Niḥsvabhāva. ("Lack of self-nature" or "absence of intrinsic existence.") Madhyamaka's core diagnosis: the root of all suffering is mistakenly believing that persons and phenomena possess an independent, autonomous identity, when in fact none do — a synonym for emptiness so central that Madhyamaka is sometimes called niḥsvabhāvavāda, "proponents of no intrinsic existence." Yogācāra repurposes the term across its three natures, describing each as lacking self-nature in a different way: the imaginary lacks defining characteristics, the dependent lacks independent production, and the consummate lacks any ultimate difference between subject and object.

Pārājika. ("Defeat.") The gravest category of monastic offense, triggering automatic and — in the Pāli tradition — permanent expulsion from the saṃgha: sexual intercourse, theft, killing a human being, or falsely claiming spiritual attainment for monks, with nuns bound by an additional four rules concerning physical contact and complicity. Pāli tradition compares the offender to a severed head or a stone split in two, beyond any possibility of repair, though other traditions like the Mūlasarvāstivāda allow a diminished but still-monastic status of "pārājika penitent" rather than total exile.

Ponsa. ("Foundational monastery.") Korea's district-level head monasteries, an institution the state used repeatedly to exert administrative control over Buddhism — first consolidated under Chosŏn king T'aejong in 1407, discontinued when the Kyo and Sŏn schools were abolished, then revived under Japanese colonial administration in 1911 with thirty-one designated districts. The modern Chogye order inherited and adapted the system, organizing today's twenty-five ponsa (including Chogyesa, Haeinsa, and Pulguksa) each overseeing a network of smaller affiliated branch monasteries in its region.

time.basis: "an important and persistent philosophical debate in Tibetan Buddhism, dating to the fifteenth century"

note: Rang stong gzhan stong. ("Self-emptiness, other-emptiness.") A fifteenth-century Tibetan doctrinal fault line pitting the Dge lugs, who hold that all phenomena — even a buddha's omniscient mind — are equally empty of any intrinsic nature whatsoever, against the Jo nang, who argue for a positive "other-emptiness": an eternal, self-arisen wisdom consciousness empty only of extraneous defilement, not of its own true nature. Both sides claim Candrakīrti and Nāgārjuna as authorities, with the Jo nang relegating Candrakīrti's negative dialectic to a "one-sided" reading and instead privileging Nāgārjuna's more positively worded devotional hymns as his truest final view.

Saṃbhāramārga. ("Path of accumulation.") The first of the five paths, opening with either disgust for saṃsāra (for those seeking nirvāṇa) or the generation of bodhicitta (for those on the Mahāyāna path), and subdivided into small, middling, and large stages tied respectively to the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, and the four bases of psychic power. Like the path of preparation that follows it, it is not yet a "noble path," since direct perception of reality has not yet occurred — Mahāyāna abhidharma likens its three stages to earth, gold, and finally the capacity to see a buddha's emanation body directly.

Saṃvṛtisatya. ("Conventional truth.") The half of the two truths carrying built-in connotations of deception and concealment — objects of ordinary experience, misperceived through ignorance, yet still possessing genuine conventional utility, unlike a purely nonexistent object like a permanent self. Some schools split it further into "correct" conventional truth (an actual face) versus "incorrect" conventional truth (its mirror reflection), based on whether the object can actually perform the function its appearance suggests.

Ti. ("Body," "essence," or "substance.") A term paired philosophically with "function" (yong), elevated from its ordinary Confucian sense of physical body into a metaphysical concept by Wang Bi, who used it as a synonym for Daoist nonbeing. Chinese Buddhist thinkers from Sengzhao to Guifeng Zongmi adopted and systematized the ti-yong pairing — Zongmi identifying ti with the unchanging essence of true thusness and yong with its diverse functional manifestations — a framework later exported wholesale into Neo-Confucian metaphysics by thinkers like Zhu Xi.

Vajrasattva. ("Vajra Being.") A tantric deity of purification worshipped as a primordial buddha, sometimes counted as a sixth member of or substitute within the five-buddha system, and identified with both Vajrapāṇi and Vajradhara depending on context. East Asian esoteric Buddhism casts him as the second patriarch of its teaching lineage, receiving the doctrine directly from Vairocana before passing it down through Nāgārjuna to the tradition's later transmitters; in Tibet, reciting his hundred-syllable mantra one hundred thousand times is a standard preliminary purification practice required before any tantric instruction can be received.

Vibhaṅga. ("Analysis.") The second book of the Pāli abhidhamma canon, often treated as a supplement to the first book, the Dhammasaṅgaṇī, though it applies its own distinct analytical methods across eighteen self-contained chapters covering topics from the aggregates and sense bases to the eightfold path and meditative absorption. Most chapters follow a three-part structure — sutta-style analysis, technical abhidharma categorization, then a closing catechism of questions — and the text's most influential commentary, Buddhaghosa's Sammohavinodanī, was written in the fifth century.

Wu jia qi zong. ("Five houses and seven schools.") The traditional map of mature Chan's institutional development, tracing five "houses" — Guiyang, Linji, Caodong, Yunmen, and Fayan — back to the two great disciples of Huineng, Nanyue Huairang and Qingyuan Xingsi. The Linji house later split during the Song dynasty into the Huanglong and Yangqi lineages, whose addition to the original five produces the full count of "seven schools" — a framework historian Guifeng Zongmi traced back further still to earlier lineages eventually eclipsed by these flourishing later houses.

Ānimitta. ("Signless.") One of the three "gates to deliverance" alongside emptiness and wishlessness, cultivated by halting perception at the level of bare recognition rather than reacting to an object's generic and secondary characteristics — the discipline behind the sūtra refrain "in the seen, there is only the seen," free of the ego's usual superimpositions. Produced through insight into impermanence, it counters sensory attachment directly and, since nirvāṇa itself carries no sensory signs to grasp onto, mastering signlessness is what finally allows the mind to turn toward it.

Apāya. ("Falling away" — baleful destinies, synonymous with durgati.) Rebirth as a hell denizen, animal, or hungry ghost (sometimes with demigod added as a fourth), resulting from any of ten classified wrong deeds spanning bodily acts like killing and stealing, verbal acts like lying and harsh speech, and mental acts like covetousness, malice, and wrong views. Other scriptural sources add reviling noble ones and acting on wrong views as further direct causes of this unfortunate rebirth.

time.basis: compiled by Yuanwu Keqin, whose dates are given elsewhere as "(1063–1135)"

note: Biyan lu. ("Blue Cliff Record.") One of Chan's two most influential gong'an anthologies, built around Xuedou Chongxian's earlier hundred-case collection with verse commentary, to which Yuanwu Keqin added introductory pointers, interlinear capping phrases, and extensive prose commentary. So closely identified with attachment to clever language that Yuanwu's own foremost disciple, Dahui Zonggao, reportedly burned the text for fear his students would become fixated on Xuedou's and Yuanwu's words rather than genuine realization — it remains, alongside the Wumen guan, foundational to Japanese Rinzai training today.

Bodhyaṅga. ("Branches of enlightenment.") Seven qualities that unfold in sequence at the path of vision — mindfulness, investigation of factors, energy, rapture, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity — each arising as a direct consequence of the one before it, from investigating the Buddha's teachings with energy through to the rapture, tranquility, and finally deep concentration that produces complete composure. Their cultivation leads to the threefold knowledge culminating in realizing that the contaminants have been permanently extinguished.

time.basis: the magnum opus of "Āryadeva, a third century CE Indian monk"

note: Catuḥśataka. ("Four Hundred [Stanzas].") Āryadeva's sixteen-chapter Madhyamaka masterwork, opening with refutations of permanence, satisfaction, purity, and a substantial self before turning to the bodhisattva path, the three poisons, and a sustained series of arguments against rival Buddhist and non-Buddhist schools, all converging on emptiness as reality's fundamental nature. Its relationship to the shorter, similarly themed Śataśāstra remains debated — rather than one simply summarizing or expanding the other, the two are more likely independent works addressing overlapping ground, possibly reflecting different stages or interpretations of Āryadeva's own thought.

time.basis: "(d.u.; c. seventh century)"

location.label: Mathurā, India (birthplace and later monastic residence, named directly)

note: Guṇaprabha. (c. seventh century.) A Mathurā-born scholar who began as a Yogācāra writer and adviser to King Harṣa before shifting to śrāvakayāna vinaya specialization, becoming Tibet's most revered authority on the Mūlasarvāstivāda monastic code. His Vinayasūtra condensed the massive Mūlasarvāstivāda vinaya to roughly a quarter of its length, functioning as a practical primer on actual monastic conduct rather than scripture, and became so foundational to Tibetan Buddhism that it forms one of the five core texts of the Dge lugs curriculum — despite a legend that his one trip to consult Maitreya directly in Tuṣita heaven taught him nothing new at all.

Jñānadarśana. ("Knowledge and vision.") Direct insight into impermanence, suffering, and nonself, marking the culmination of a stock meditative sequence: having suffused the mind with concentration and purity through the four absorptions, the meditator turns toward this vision, recognizes the self as merely a physical body bound to a dependent mentality, releases attachment to both, and thereby gains the knowledge of freedom from further rebirth. In Mahāyāna usage, the "perfection of knowledge and vision" serves as an alternate name for the perfection of wisdom itself.

Kalpa. ("Eon" or "age.") Buddhism's unit of cosmological time, layered into nested scales: an "intermediate" kalpa spans a full decline in human lifespan from near-immortality down to ten years, eighty of these make a "great" kalpa cycling through creation, abiding, dissolution, and nothingness, and the almost incomprehensibly vast "incalculable" kalpa — a great kalpa raised to the sixtieth power — measures out the three full eons the bodhisattva path to buddhahood is said to require. A kalpa graced by an actual buddha's appearance earns the special designation "fortunate."

Mahāsthāna. ("Great site.") The canonical list of four (or, expanded, eight) Indian pilgrimage sites tied to pivotal moments in the Buddha's life — birth at Lumbinī, enlightenment at Bodhgayā, first sermon at Sārnāth, and final nirvāṇa at Kuśinagarī, with the expanded list adding sites of specific miracles at Śrāvastī, Sāṃkāśya, Rājagṛha, and Vaiśālī. These eight sites recur constantly in Pāla-period Indian sculpture and were essential stops for Chinese and Korean pilgrims like Xuanzang traveling the subcontinent.

time.basis: "probably emerged some three centuries after the demise of the Buddha" (chronology convention)

note: Mahīśāsaka. One of the eighteen mainstream schools, likely named after its brāhmaṇa founder — a former district governor turned arhat — and classed, alongside its likely offshoot the Dharmaguptaka, within the broader Sthaviranikāya lineage descending from the Sarvāstivāda. Distinctive doctrines include denying any intermediate state between death and rebirth (holding instead that a subtle form of the aggregates carries forward directly) and classifying the Buddha as, in fact, a member of the saṃgha — a position with real consequences for how monastic property and alms were divided. Its vinaya recension was recorded by the Chinese pilgrim Faxian in Sri Lanka, and Asaṅga himself is said to have first been ordained within this school.

Mūlasarvāstivāda. ("Root Sarvāstivāda.") A subsect of the Sarvāstivāda mainstream school whose precise doctrinal distinction from its parent tradition remains genuinely unclear even to modern scholarship — the name itself, claiming to be the "root" or original form, may reflect a polemical claim of institutional priority rather than a settled historical fact. Its monastic code, the Mūlasarvāstivāda vinaya, survives as by far the longest of the extant vinayas and remains the disciplinary code still followed in Tibetan Buddhism today.

time.basis: "internal and external evidence... suggests that the Yingluo jing is a Chinese apocryphon from the fifth century"

note: Pusa yingluo benye jing. ("Book of the Original Acts that Adorn the Bodhisattva.") A Chinese apocryphal sūtra highly influential on Chan and Tiantai exegetes, best known for synthesizing competing path schemas into a comprehensive fifty-two-stage bodhisattva career — adding a preliminary "ten faiths" stage to the Avataṃsakasūtra's forty-two named stages — and for its widely cited threefold classification of bodhisattva morality into restraint, cultivation of virtue, and active service to other beings. Its attribution to the translator Zhu Fonian remains disputed, complicated by borrowed passages from other indigenous Chinese sūtras and its genuine but distinct namesake, the authentic third-century translation Pusa benye jing.

time.basis: "fifth-century commentary... written in Sri Lanka by... Buddhaghosa", whose dates are given elsewhere as "fl. c. 370–450 CE"

location.label: Sri Lanka (Mahāvihāra tradition, where Buddhaghosa composed it)

note: Samantapāsādikā. ("Entirely Pleasing.") Buddhaghosa's fifth-century commentary on the vinaya, opening with an extensive historical introduction running from the Buddha's death through the first three councils to the vinaya's recitation in Sri Lanka under King Devānaṃpiyatissa. Rich in historical and geographical detail on Indian monasteries, kings, and Aśoka's missionary dispatches across South and Southeast Asia, it also preserves an account of Moggaliputtatissa, compiler of the Kathāvatthu.

Saṃtāna. ("Continuum.") An uninterrupted sequence of cause and effect — especially mental moments — used to describe how mind and body persist across time despite containing nothing permanent, extending both within a single lifetime and across many. The concept does real philosophical work: it explains how karmic continuity and rebirth remain coherent even without a permanent self, breaking down only at an arhat's final thought-moment, when the continuum's next step shifts to the unconditioned realm and no further conditioned thought can ever arise again.

time.basis: foundation "traditionally attributed to the Chan master Baizhang Qinggui (749–814)"

note: Sengtang. ("Saṃgha hall" or "monks' hall.") The architectural and practical center of Chinese Chan monastic life, where monks ate, slept, and meditated together on long communal platforms arranged by seniority — a practice traditionally credited to Baizhang Qinggui and later codified into the standard plan of every large Song-dynasty public monastery. Introduced to Japan by Dōgen in 1236, it became closely identified with the Sōtō tradition specifically, since Rinzai instead reserved a separate, meditation-only zendō, using the saṃgha hall model solely for eating and sleeping.

time.basis: restored and expanded by Pojo Chinul "in 1197"

location.label: Mount Chogye, South Chŏlla Province, Korea (named directly as the entry's subject)

note: Songgwangsa. ("Piney Expanse Monastery.") One of Korea's three "jewel monasteries," representing the saṃgha jewel through its succession of sixteen state preceptors during the Koryŏ dynasty, and expanded from a small foundation by Pojo Chinul in 1197 into the seat of his Samādhi and Prajñā Community. Renamed Susŏnsa by royal decree in 1208 — a name its meditation hall still bears — the monastery today functions as one of five ecumenical training centers in the modern Chogye order, teaching the full range of Korean Buddhist practice under its alternate name, Chogye Ch'ongnim.

*Svātantrika. ("Autonomist.") One of two retrospective Tibetan classifications of Indian Madhyamaka — a label that never actually appears in Indian sources — coined to describe Bhāvaviveka's insistence on using autonomous syllogisms in philosophical debate, a method Candrakīrti explicitly rejected in founding what Tibetans would call the rival Prāsaṅgika approach. Tibetan doxography further splits Svātantrika into a Sautrāntika-aligned branch founded by Bhāvaviveka and a Yogācāra-aligned branch founded by Śāntarakṣita.

Wushi. ("Five periods.") Tiantai's chronological classification of the Buddha's teaching career, explaining doctrinal inconsistency across scriptures by assigning each text to a stage in a deliberate pedagogical arc: the sublime but incomprehensible Avataṃsakasūtra immediately after enlightenment, simplified āgama teachings at the Deer Park to accommodate confused disciples, intermediate Mahāyāna-favoring vaipulya sūtras, the boundary-dissolving prajñāpāramitā literature, and finally the Lotus Sūtra and Nirvāṇa Sūtra as the "consummate" teaching revealing the Buddha's truest intention — a progression Tiantai further likened to the successive stages of refining milk into ghee.

time.basis: "(778–897)", given directly

location.label: Zhaozhou, Hebei, China (Guanyinyuan, where he taught for his final forty years)

note: Zhaozhou Congshen. (778–897.) A Tang-dynasty Chan master who studied for decades under Nanquan Puyuan before settling at eighty into a small monastery in Zhaozhou, teaching through understated verbal exchange rather than the shouting and beating favored by contemporaries — Yuanwu Keqin later said "Zhaozhou's Chan lies on the lips." His most famous exchange, in which he answered "no" to whether a dog possesses buddha-nature, became the single most cited case in all of Chan literature and, through Dahui Zonggao's promotion, the archetypal huatou of kanhua Chan meditation — even though his own dharma lineage died out not long after his death.

time.basis: "(705–774)", given directly

location.label: Chang'an, China (where he spent most of his career)

note: Amoghavajra. (705–774.) A likely Central Asian émigré monk who, alongside his teacher Vajrabodhi and later Xuanzang, ranks among Chinese Buddhism's most prolific translators, bringing back a wealth of esoteric scriptures — including the Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha — from a journey to India and Sri Lanka in the 740s. Rising to construct imperial consecration altars and establish esoteric ritual chapels within the palace itself, he survived the disruption of the An Lushan rebellion to be honored with the purple robe, the highest distinction available to a Buddhist monk in Tang China.

time.basis: contemporary and lay disciple of the Buddha; chronology convention

location.label: Śrāvastī (named directly as his home city)

note: Anāthapiṇḍada. ("Feeder of the Defenseless.") A wealthy Śrāvastī merchant declared foremost among lay disciples for his generosity, who purchased and built the Jetavana grove — the Buddha's favorite residence — by literally covering its grounds in gold coins. Reduced to poverty in his later years yet still feeding monks from his own cooking pot until his death, his deathbed conversation with Śāriputra, in which he begged that deeper teachings reserved for monks be shared with the laity too, stands as one of the Pāli canon's most affecting exchanges — he was reborn that same night in Tuṣita heaven.

time.basis: "(r. c. 465–413 BCE)", given directly

location.label: Rājagṛha, Magadha (his capital, named directly)

note: Bimbisāra. (r. c. 465–413 BCE.) King of Magadha and the Buddha's foremost royal patron, who donated the Veṇuvana bamboo grove and repaired the road to Vaiśālī for the Buddha's convenience, declaring that his life's five great ambitions — becoming king, hosting the Buddha, serving him, receiving his teaching, and understanding it — had all been fulfilled. Murdered by his own son Ajātaśatru at the instigation of Devadatta, who saw the king's devotion to the Buddha as an obstacle to seizing control of the saṃgha himself; Pāli tradition holds Bimbisāra was reborn as a yakṣa and later visited the Buddha in that form.

Bodhipākṣikadharma. ("Factors pertaining to awakening" — wings of awakening.) A comprehensive list of thirty-seven practices assembled from seven originally distinct sets — the four foundations of mindfulness, four right efforts, four bases of psychic power, five spiritual faculties, five mental powers, seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path. Likely one of the earliest "matrices" (mātṛkā) in Buddhist literature, this list came to be treated as an exhaustive summary of the Buddha's entire teaching, later absorbing further meditative categories as it evolved into a foundational framework for abhidharma itself.

Cariyāpiṭaka. ("Basket of Conduct.") The fifteenth and final book of the Khuddakanikāya, thirty-five verse stories of the Buddha's past lives illustrating seven of the ten Pāli perfections — generosity, morality, renunciation, truthfulness, resolution, loving-kindness, and equanimity — that parallel corresponding prose accounts found in the Jātaka. Tradition holds it was preached by the Buddha at Śāriputra's request and later used by the missionary Mahinda to convert thousands of Sri Lankans when he recited it at Anurādhapura.

Divyacakṣus. ("Divine eye" — clairvoyance.) One of the six superknowledges and three knowledges of enlightenment, granting the ability to see distant events, observe mind-made bodies, and — most significantly — witness beings' rebirth destinies unfold according to their past deeds, seeing wrongdoers descend to lower realms and the virtuous ascend to higher ones. The Buddha attained this power during the second watch of his enlightenment night; though classed as a merely mundane achievement reachable through deep meditative absorption alone, it forms a crucial link toward the truly liberating third knowledge that follows it.

time.basis: "most likely an indigenous Chinese scripture... composed during the middle of the fifth century"

note: Fanwang jing. ("Brahmā's Net Sūtra.") A Chinese apocryphal scripture whose second roll — far more influential than its rarely-studied first — sets out ten major and forty-eight minor bodhisattva precepts open to laypeople as well as monastics, becoming a popular East Asian alternative to the traditional 250 monastic vinaya rules. Explicitly correlating its precepts with Confucian filial piety and buddha-nature, it was embraced wholesale by Saichō in Japan, who rejected traditional monastic ordination entirely in favor of these purely Mahāyāna precepts, while Korea treats them as complementary to, rather than a replacement for, standard monastic vows.

Gozan. ("Five mountains.") A medieval Japanese ranking system for state-sponsored Zen monasteries, adapted from Chinese precedent and first implemented under the Kamakura shogunate before being reordered repeatedly as political power shifted between Kamakura and Kyōto. By the Muromachi period the system had expanded to roughly three hundred officially ranked monasteries across three tiers, and came to denote not just institutions but entire prestigious lineages renowned for their classical Chinese literary and artistic accomplishment — with a parallel, far less documented five-mountain convent system existing for Japanese nuns.

Lam rim. ("Stages of the path.") A major Tibetan literary genre and study framework tracing back to Atiśa's Bodhipathapradīpa, organizing the entire Buddhist path around three progressively broader levels of spiritual motivation — seeking merely a better rebirth, then personal liberation, then full buddhahood to benefit all beings. Though most associated with the Dge lugs sect, which counts eight canonical lam rim treatises headlined by Tsong kha pa's massive Lam rim chen mo, the genre appears across every major Tibetan Buddhist tradition.

time.basis: "written most probably in the fifth century CE"

location.label: Sri Lanka (Mahāvihāra tradition, source of the chronicle)

note: Mahāvaṃsa. ("Great Chronicle.") Sri Lanka's most celebrated Pāli chronicle, expanding on the earlier Dīpavaṃsa's outline with a more elaborate and coherent narrative running from Buddhism's origins through the three Indian councils to Mahinda's mission and the reign of Mahāsena — though it drops some material found in its source, such as the lineage of nuns.

time.basis: "built in the third century BCE"
