location.label: Anurādhapura, Sri Lanka (named directly as the entry's subject)

note: Mahāvihāra. ("Great Monastery.") The headquarters of orthodox Theravāda in Sri Lanka, built for Mahinda at Anurādhapura following King Devānaṃpiyatissa's conversion, and site of the first-ever commitment of a Buddhist canon to writing, undertaken by five hundred of its monks in the late first century BCE. Its authority was twice challenged by breakaway fraternities and its buildings vacated for nine years under a hostile royal decree, but it remained influential enough that Buddhaghosa composed his sutta commentaries there before it finally declined after the Sri Lankan capital relocated in the ninth century.

time.basis: presumed contemporary of Asaṅga, "fourth century CE" (Asaṅga's dates given elsewhere as "c. 320–c. 390 CE")

note: Maitreyanātha. ("Protector Maitreya.") The name scholars have given to a possibly historical Indian teacher, contemporary with Asaṅga, credited with authoring some or all of the "five books of Maitreya" — including the Abhisamayālaṃkāra and Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra — texts that tradition instead says were delivered directly to Asaṅga by the bodhisattva Maitreya in Tuṣita heaven. The name itself is ambiguous between "Protector Maitreya" and "Protected by Maitreya," reflecting the genuine uncertainty over whether a real human author stands behind the attribution.

Nirodhasamāpatti. ("Equipoise of cessation.") The highest meditative attainment recognized in mainstream Buddhism, transcending even the four immaterial absorptions — a state of suspended animation where the meditator remains technically alive while all physical and mental activity, including basic mentality, completely stops for a fixed period. Because even thought itself is absent, it's classified as a "conditioned force dissociated from thought" in both Sarvāstivāda and Yogācāra systems, with Yogācāra crediting the storehouse consciousness alone with keeping the meditator's body alive throughout.

Nirodhasatya. ("Truth of cessation.") The third of the four noble truths, referring in its fullest sense to nirvāṇa — the permanent cessation of action, affliction, and the suffering they generate — and, in abhidharma's finer analysis, to the specific, permanent destruction of each affliction tied to each of the three realms of existence. Despite completing the causal chain as an "effect" of the fourth truth (the path), cessation isn't an ordinary effect at all: it's classified as a "disconnection fruition," since the path doesn't produce nirodha so much as simply uncover it by removing what obscured it.

Pañcajñāna. ("Five wisdoms.") Five facets of a buddha's perfect enlightenment — the wisdom of the dharma-realm, mirror-like wisdom, the wisdom of equality, discerning wisdom, and the wisdom of accomplished action — mapped in Yogācāra onto the transformation of each of the eight consciousnesses once purified. In tantric practice, each wisdom corresponds to one of the five buddha families, and the entire path is framed as the deliberate transmutation of the five root afflictions into these five wisdoms in exact, one-to-one correspondence.

Sāsrava. ("With outflows" — contaminated.) A term for anything, animate or not, that can serve as an occasion for the afflictions to increase — broader than mere "defilement" since even objects and wholesome states leading to future happiness still count as contaminated if that future state itself has further outflows. The Abhidharmakośabhāṣya names only four truly uncontaminated dharmas, three of them permanent (space and the two forms of cessation) and only the truth of the path itself impermanent yet uncontaminated — everything else that composes a person falls under the single sweeping category of the "contaminated aggregates."

time.basis: originated with Śreṇika Vatsagotra, "a contemporary of Gautama Buddha"; chronology convention

note: Śreṇika heresy. The mistaken view, traced to the wanderer Śreṇika Vatsagotra, that the impermanent body houses a permanent self — illustrated by Śreṇika's own image of a house burning down while its owner escapes unharmed outside, directly inverting the Buddha's own fire-simile teaching that nothing "goes anywhere" when the aggregates cease. The charge resurfaces repeatedly in East Asian Chan polemics, leveled against Mazu Daoyi's "mind itself is buddha" teaching by Nanyang Huizhong and later against similar claims by Dōgen, who worried any doctrine implying an eternal, unchanging mind-nature beneath an impermanent body collapsed straight back into this same ancient error.

time.basis: "scholars speculate that the text originated in India in the fourth century"

note: Suvarṇaprabhāsottamasūtra. ("Sūtra of Supreme Golden Light.") A hugely influential East Asian Mahāyāna sūtra, rich in dhāraṇī and sometimes classified as proto-tantric, central to "state-protection Buddhism" through its promise that faithful rulers who uphold it will be divinely protected while negligent ones will see their kingdoms fall to ruin. Also the scriptural source for the "water and land ceremony" for universal salvation, illustrated by the sūtra's own story of a past-life Buddha who saved a pond of dying fish and, in another tale, of Prince Mahāsattva's self-sacrifice to feed a starving tigress — one of Buddhist literature's most famous instances of the "gift of the body."

time.basis: "established by the vinaya master Chajang... in 646"

location.label: Yangsan, South Kyŏngsang Province, Korea (named directly as the entry's subject)

note: T'ongdosa. Korea's "buddha-jewel monastery," one of three representing the three jewels, founded by the vinaya master Chajang in 646 to enshrine relics and a robe he received from Mañjuśrī on pilgrimage at Wutaishan. Uniquely for a main shrine hall in Korea, its taeung chŏn contains no buddha image at all — instead a rear window looks out onto the Diamond Ordination Platform where the actual relics are enshrined — and generations of monks protected those relics through repeated Japanese invasions, hiding them in forests and even carrying them as far as the Diamond Mountains before finally restoring them to the monastery for good in 1603.

Upāsaka. ("[Male] lay disciple.") A layman formally committed to Buddhism through the three refuges and five basic precepts, permanently binding, supplemented on full- and new-moon fasting days by three further precepts — no eating after midday, no entertainment or adornment, no luxurious beds — that together make eight, with celibacy substituting for the usual sexual-conduct precept on those specific days.

Vihāra. ("Abode" — monastery.) The dwelling place that formal monasticism grew out of once the Buddha instructed wandering monks to settle in one place during the rains retreat to avoid trampling insects on muddy roads — a practical rule that snowballed into the entire institution of permanent monastic residence. Vinaya regulations govern everything from a vihāra's layout (rooms arranged around a courtyard typically holding a Bodhi tree sapling or stūpa) to its permanence as saṃgha property once donated, which can never be reclaimed; the Indian state of Bihar takes its very name from the many vihāras once scattered across the region.

Yamāntaka. ("Destroyer of Death.") One of the Dge lugs sect's three principal tantric deities, a fully enlightened buddha who appears exclusively in wrathful form — by legend, the bodhisattva Mañjuśrī's own transformation into a terrifying bull-headed figure in order to defeat Yama, Lord of Death, who was ravaging the land. His nine heads, thirty-four arms, and sixteen legs are each loaded with symbolic meaning, mapping onto everything from the two truths of Madhyamaka to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment to the sixteen forms of emptiness, and his three root tantras — Black, Red, and the "Three Summaries" — define the three main Tibetan variants of his practice.

Āsravakṣaya. ("Extinction of the contaminants.") The supranormal power produced by perfected insight, and the third and final of the three knowledges realized at enlightenment — its attainment is precisely what makes someone an arhat, guaranteeing that at death they pass into nirvāṇa and are never reborn again.

Aśubhabhāvanā. ("Contemplation on the impure" or "foul.") A meditation countering lust by visualizing either the body's thirty-one or thirty-two unglamorous physical parts or the graphic stages of a corpse's decay — bloating, discoloration, infestation by worms, dissolution to bare bone — described in vivid detail across Buddhist commentarial literature and included as standard training in Theravāda monastic ordination. The Chinese tradition supplements this with a parallel sevenfold contemplation on the body's inherent foulness from conception through death, and sustained practice can, once the meditator masters a stable mental image of decay, lead all the way to the fourth level of meditative absorption.

Avīci. ("Interminable.") The deepest and most tortuous of the eight great hells, reserved for those who commit the five most heinous acts — patricide, matricide, killing an arhat, wounding a buddha, or causing schism in the saṃgha — whose relentless, uninterrupted burning gives the hell its name. Like every hell realm, though, avīci is ultimately temporary: however many eons of suffering are required to exhaust the underlying unwholesome karma, that being will eventually be reborn elsewhere once the debt is paid.

Buddhadhātu. ("Buddha-element" or "buddha-nature.") The inherent potential of all sentient beings to achieve buddhahood, first appearing in the Mahāyāna recension of the Mahāparinirvāṇasūtra, which declares that every sentient being possesses this element regardless of their present conduct or spiritual state. The term is easily confused with its Chinese rendering foxing (literally "buddha-nature"), which has sometimes been mistakenly back-translated into a nonstandard Sanskrit form rather than the accepted buddhadhātu — and dhātu alone, elsewhere in Buddhist Sanskrit, can also simply mean a physical relic of the Buddha, an entirely separate sense of the same word.

Dunwu jianxiu. ("Sudden awakening followed by gradual cultivation.") A path schema associated with Guifeng Zongmi and Pojo Chinul, in which an initial sudden "understanding-awakening" — knowing oneself to already be a buddha — is only the beginning, not the end, of the path. Genuine buddhahood still requires a long process of gradual cultivation to erode deeply ingrained habitual patterns, until knowledge and action finally coincide in a final "realization-awakening" — a process Zongmi and Chinul compare to an infant born with full human faculties who nonetheless still needs years to mature into functioning as an adult.

time.basis: per the Dīpavaṃsa, arose "during the second century after the Buddha's death" (chronology convention)

location.label: Himalayan region (general placeholder — named directly, "Inhabitants of the Himālayas")

note: Haimavata. ("Inhabitants of the Himālayas.") One of the eighteen mainstream schools, named for its Himalayan homeland and, according to a Sarvāstivāda-authored account often dismissed as polemical, the first school to split from the Sthaviranikāya lineage. That same account links it to Mahādeva's controversial five theses questioning arhats' spiritual perfection — the very propositions blamed for triggering the second council's schism between the Sthaviras and the emerging Mahāsāṃghika — while crediting the school with several distinctive positions of its own, including that bodhisattvas remain ordinary beings until buddhahood and that non-Buddhist ascetics simply cannot develop genuine supernatural powers.

time.basis: "(1133–1212)", given directly

location.label: Mimasaka province, Japan (native place, named directly)

note: Hōnen. (1133–1212.) Founder of Japan's Jōdoshū, orphaned by his father's violent death and raised by an uncle before training at Mt. Hiei. His teaching that reciting Amitābha's name alone suffices for rebirth in the pure land — the "easy path" set against traditional Tendai practice — drew a large popular following, including his disciple Shinran, and provoked enough establishment backlash that Hōnen was exiled to Tosa in 1207 before being pardoned; his still-unpublished masterwork, the Senchakushū, was significant enough that Shinran was personally permitted to copy it.

time.basis: "established by the Tibetan king Srong btsan sgam po... around 640 CE"

location.label: Lhasa, Tibet (named directly as the entry's subject)

note: Jo khang. ("House of the Lord.") Tibet's earliest and most sacred temple, built around 640 CE by King Srong btsan sgam po and his two queens directly atop the heart of a demoness the Tibetan landscape was believed to embody — a foundational act in Tibet's own Buddhist origin myth. Home to the Jo bo Śākyamuni statue, said to have been sculpted during the Buddha's own lifetime and brought from China by Princess Wencheng, it anchors Lhasa's central pilgrimage circuit and gave the city itself its name, having survived Cultural Revolution-era desecration — including use as a pigsty — to be restored and named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2000.

time.basis: "dates to the first Karma pa, Dus gsum mkhyen pa", whose dates are given elsewhere as "(1110–1193)"

location.label: Mtshur phu Monastery, Tibet (the sect's traditional seat)

note: Karma Bka' brgyud. The oldest and most politically prominent of the Bka' brgyud sect's four subsects, headed by the succession of incarnate lamas known as the Karma pa and wielding major political power from the late fourteenth century until the Dge lugs sect's ascendancy under the fifth Dalai Lama. Distinctive for placing equal weight on scriptural study and meditative practice, especially mahāmudrā, it remains a vigorous tradition in exile and is sometimes mistakenly called the "Black Hats" in the West, after the Karma pa's distinctive ceremonial crown.

time.basis: "(1308–1364)", given directly

location.label: G.yo ru, central Tibet (birthplace, named directly)

note: Klong chen rab 'byams. (1308–1364.) The Rnying ma sect's foremost systematizer of rdzogs chen, believed to be the reincarnation of two figures central to that teaching's transmission, who trained widely across Rnying ma, Sa skya, and Bka' brgyud traditions before abandoning institutional scholarship in disillusionment to become a wandering ascetic. Received the core rdzogs chen teachings from the yogin Kumārarāja at Bsam yas, later composing his most celebrated works — including the "Seven Treasuries" — partly during a decade of political exile in Bhutan, where he also founded eight monasteries; his elegant, poetic writing later inspired the Rnying ma revival led by the treasure-revealer 'Jigs med gling pa.

time.basis: "an important Indian kingdom during the Buddha's time"; chronology convention

location.label: Śrāvastī (its capital, named directly)

note: Kośala. One of the two most powerful kingdoms in India during the Buddha's lifetime, alongside Magadha, ruling over the smaller neighboring Śākya tribe from its capital Śrāvastī, where the Buddha spent much of his teaching career at the Jetavana monastery. Eventually conquered by King Ajātaśatru of Magadha, absorbing it into the larger kingdom's growing power, and later counted among the twenty-four sacred sites associated with the Cakrasaṃvaratantra.

time.basis: the cult of Kṣitigarbha "gained popularity by at least the fifth century" in China

location.label: Jiuhuashan, Anhui, China (where Chinese tradition places his monk-form residence)

note: Kṣitigarbha. ("Earth Store.") A bodhisattva devoted to rescuing beings trapped in the hell realms, largely overlooked in India and Tibet but transformed in China, from the fifth century onward, into a full-fledged Lord of Hell counterbalancing the Jade Emperor of native Chinese cosmology — a role reinforced by his prior-birth legend as a filial daughter who saved her mother from the Avīci hell. Uniquely depicted as an unadorned, shaven-headed monk rather than in bodhisattva finery, he became known in Japan as Jizō, protector of children, travelers, and community boundaries, with statues of him still dressed in bibs today in memory of stillborn and aborted children.

time.basis: site of the Buddha's parinirvāṇa; chronology convention

location.label: Kuśinagar, Uttar Pradesh, India (named directly as the entry's subject)

note: Kuśinagarī. The town where the Buddha passed into parinirvāṇa beneath twin śāla trees, having earlier declined — after his attendant Ānanda failed to catch the hint — an offer to extend his own life for a full eon. When Ānanda protested that such an obscure "back-woods" town seemed unworthy of the Buddha's death, the Buddha reminded him it had once been the splendid capital of an earlier cakravartin king; after cremation, the brāhmaṇa Droṇa divided the Buddha's relics into eight shares for rival claimant kingdoms, building a stūpa at Kuśinagarī itself to house the vessel that had briefly held them — making the site one of Buddhism's four great pilgrimage destinations.

Mahābhūta. ("Great elements.") The four fundamental physical qualities composing the material world in abhidharma analysis: earth providing solidity, water providing cohesion, fire providing heat, and wind providing mobility. Every physical object is understood to contain all four elements simultaneously, simply in differing proportions, rather than being made of just one.

time.basis: contemporaries of the Buddha; chronology convention

location.label: Kapilavastu (associated with the Buddha's cousin Mahānāman and the Śākya clan's destruction)

note: Mahānāman. A name shared by at least two, and by some accounts three, distinct early Buddhist figures. One was among the five ascetic companions who first heard the Buddha's inaugural sermon and quickly attained arhatship; the other, the Buddha's cousin and Aniruddha's elder brother, was declared foremost among generous lay almsgivers — but whose prideful deception, marrying off a slave-born daughter to King Prasenajit under false pretenses of pure lineage, was discovered a generation later and triggered the eventual massacre of the entire Śākya clan by the resulting grandson's vengeance. A third, unrelated Mahānāma is credited as the fifth-century author of the Pāli chronicle Mahāvaṃsa.

Mahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa. ("Marks of a great man.") Thirty-two physical marks — golden skin, webbed hands, a protrusion atop the head, a white tuft between the eyebrows, forty perfectly even teeth — shared by both buddhas and wheel-turning emperors, each understood as the specific karmic fruit of a particular virtue cultivated over countless past lives. Accompanied by a further eighty minor marks and most fully manifest on a buddha's resplendent enjoyment-body, this list functioned as a kind of physiognomic checklist for recognizing extraordinary beings on sight, with individual marks like the cranial protrusion and the brow-tuft attracting entire traditions of their own elaborate commentary.

time.basis: led the third council during Aśoka's reign, "(r. c. 268–232 BCE)" per the Aśoka entry

location.label: Pāṭaliputra (site of the third Buddhist council, named directly)

note: Moggaliputtatissa. The monk who presided over the third Buddhist council at Pāṭaliputra, called in by Aśoka to resolve a seven-year crisis in which non-Buddhist mendicants had donned monastic robes purely for livelihood, forcing a suspension of the ordination ceremony until Aśoka personally interrogated the saṃgha and defrocked the pretenders. With the saṃgha purified, Moggaliputtatissa convened the council to rehearse the canon and composed the Kathāvatthu, the abhidhamma's seventh and final book, specifically to refute heretical views.

time.basis: "based on a series of lectures Zhiyi delivered in 594"

note: Mohe zhiguan. ("The Great Calming and Contemplation.") Tiantai Zhiyi's magnum opus on meditative theory and practice, transcribed from his 594 lectures by his disciple Guanding, balancing "calming" (śamatha) and "observation" (vipaśyanā) across three complementary readings of each term. Its most celebrated doctrine, "the trichiliocosm in a single instant of thought," holds that any single moment of mind perfectly encompasses the entirety of reality — though the text itself breaks off incomplete partway through its seventh of ten planned chapters.

time.basis: traditionally attributed to "the great fifth-century Pāli scholar Buddhaghosa"

note: Nidānakathā. ("Account of Origins.") The introduction to the Jātaka collection and the earliest continuous narrative biography of the Buddha in Pāli sources, running in three sections from the ascetic Sumedha's vow before the buddha Dīpaṃkara, through the descent from Tuṣita and enlightenment, to the donation of Jetavana in the Buddha's early ministry. Deliberately incomplete as a life story — it skips over the intervening jātaka births entirely and ends well before the Buddha's death — it nonetheless became the template for later, more expansive Buddha biographies.

Nirodha. ("Cessation," "extinction," or "suppression.") The extinction of a specific affliction or group of afflictions — nirvāṇa itself counts as a form of nirodha, since it is the cessation of all action and affliction entirely. Abhidharma distinguishes an "analytical cessation" achieved through meditative insight from a "nonanalytical cessation," a mere absence (like hunger fading after a meal) or a permanent block on certain factors ever arising again.

Pañcabala. ("Five powers.") Faith, effort, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom — the same five spiritual faculties matured into full "powers," each serving as the specific antidote to one of the five hindrances blocking meditative absorption: faith against ill will, effort against sloth, mindfulness against sensual desire, concentration against restlessness, wisdom against doubt. Counted among the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, with prajñāpāramitā literature placing their fuller development at the more advanced "forbearance" and "highest worldly dharmas" stages of the path of preparation.

Pariniṣpanna. ("Perfected" or "consummate.") The third and highest of Yogācāra's three natures — the recognition that no object exists as something materially separate from the consciousness perceiving it, once the false imaginary overlay has been stripped from the dependent nature underneath. Described in the Saṃdhinirmocanasūtra as the ultimate lack of intrinsic nature, this consummate nature is Yogācāra's candidate for the highest reality accessible to a purified mind.

Praṇidhāna. ("Vow" or "aspiration.") A solemn statement of intent to achieve a specific aim, most famously the bodhisattva's vow to reach buddhahood for the sake of all beings — a "prior vow" whose eventual fulfillment is guaranteed once buddhahood is actually attained. The best-known example is Dharmākara's forty-eight vows before the buddha Lokeśvararāja, which culminated in his becoming Amitābha and creating the pure land Sukhāvatī, foundational to all of East Asian pure land practice.

Samāpatti. ("Attainment" or "trance.") Eight levels of deep meditative concentration correlating with the eight absorptions of the subtle-materiality and immaterial realms, sometimes extended to a ninth — the attainment of the cessation of perception and sensation. Achieving any of these states through meditation while human determines rebirth into the corresponding cosmological level in the next life, a stratified attainment-scheme with parallels in non-Buddhist yogic systems as well.

time.basis: "Eighth-century Indian monk of Nālandā monastery"

location.label: Nālandā, India (named directly as his monastic home)

note: Śāntideva. (Eighth century.) Author of the enormously influential Bodhicaryāvatāra and its companion Śikṣāsamuccaya, known at Nālandā monastery only as an apparently indolent monk until fellow monks, hoping to humiliate him, dared him to recite scripture before the assembly — whereupon he delivered the entire Bodhicaryāvatāra from memory and, on reaching its ninth chapter on wisdom, is said to have risen into the air and vanished, leaving real textual disputes over how that chapter actually ends. Tibetan doxographers classify him as Prāsaṅgika-Madhyamaka, and the Bka' gdams tradition counted his masterwork among its six foundational treatises.

Śuddhāvāsa. ("Pure abodes.") The five highest heavens of the subtle-materiality realm's fourth meditative absorption, serving as a final way station for nonreturners — advanced practitioners in their last life before arhatship, who need never again be reborn in the sensuous realm below. Believed to sit empty for entire eons when no buddha is present in the world, and, in Mahāyāna sources, home to the divinities who present the four portents that drive a bodhisattva-in-training to renounce the household life.

time.basis: invited to Pāṭaliputra by King Aśoka, "(r. c. 268–232 BCE)" per the Aśoka entry

location.label: Mathurā, India (named directly as where he lived)

note: Upagupta. An Indian arhat unknown to Pāli canonical sources but prominent in Sanskrit avadāna literature, famed for taming Māra by hanging a garland of corpses around his neck, and later invited by Aśoka to personally tour him around the great Buddhist pilgrimage sites. Listed as the fifth Indian patriarch in Sarvāstivāda sources (fourth in the Chan tradition's count), his cult became especially prominent in Southeast Asian and Burmese Buddhism, where he is believed to reside in a southern-ocean pavilion and is ritually invited ashore to ward off Māra's interference.

Vajradhara. ("Vajra Holder.") A primordial buddha of the tantric systems, closely identified with (and possibly originally identical to) Vajrapāṇi, and the principal deity of the mahāmudrā lineage he is said to have revealed to Tilopa, transmitted onward through Nāropa and Mar pa to Mi la ras pa. Regarded in Tibet as the primordial buddha of the three "new" tantric sects — Sa skya, Bka' brgyud, and Dge lugs — alongside Samantabhadra, the separate primordial buddha of the Rnying ma sect.

Vajrakula. ("Vajra family" or "vajra lineage.") One of tantric Buddhism's classificatory lineages — three in earlier systems (vajra, lotus, buddha families) or five in later anuttarayogatantra schemes (adding jewel and action families) — each linked to its own buddha, aggregate, wisdom, root affliction, element, and color. The vajra family itself is headed by Akṣobhya or Vajrasattva and corresponds to the consciousness aggregate, mirror-like wisdom, the affliction of anger, the element water, and the color white.

Yāna. ("Vehicle" or "conveyance.") A literal term for transportation repurposed by Mahāyāna literature into a defining metaphor for the entire tradition — a mode of conveyance along the path to enlightenment, sorted polemically into two or three rival vehicles (bodhisattva, pratyekabuddha, śrāvaka; or simply Mahāyāna versus the dismissively named Hīnayāna). The Lotus Sūtra's parable of the burning house, where a father promises three different carriages but delivers only one magnificent one, remains yāna-rhetoric's most celebrated expression; tantric Buddhism later split the Mahāyāna itself into the sūtra-based "perfection vehicle" and the tantra-based "mantra vehicle," better known as the vajrayāna.
